Title: Benin Ivory
Description: Arm-cuff, one of a pair; made of elephant ivory. Depicts the Oba (king) in centre of first and third rows flanked by two warriors.;
Curators Comments:
Pair with Af1922,0313.05; Plankensteiner 2007:
These luxurious armlets are among six very similar works by one of Benin's extraordinary 18th century ivory carvers.  Throughout much of Benin's history, the use of ivory was restricted, and anyone who wished to commission the Igbesanmwan placed his request through the Oba.  During the 1700s, this prohibition was relaxed.  The Dutch had replaced the Portuguese as the principal European traders on the rivers of the Niger Delta.  Their efforts to fill the demand for ivory in Europe brought unparalleled wealth for whoever supplied their ships.  Elephant hunting was intensified, and firearms increased the efficacy of the hunters.  Thousands of tusks were exported to Europe each year (Ryder 1969:133).  Hundreds were retained for skilled artists, who created the earliest of Benin's richly-carved altar tusks, as well as ivory containers, ornaments, and armlets.
Many of the images used by the artist who carved these armlets resemble motifs inherited by the Igbesanmwan (Blackmun 1984, II).  However, the guild is divided into hierarchies of specialists, and the style of this master is unique.  The surface of each armlet is divided into four rows of standing figures.  Each row of these images is repeated once, so that the first and third rows are duplicates, as are the second and fourth rows.  Throughout the surface, intricate forms are interwoven with the figural motifs, to link each of the rows with the next.
The Oba of Benin appears in the centre of the first and third rows, accompanied by two helmeted warriors.  He wears an elaborate crown and a beaded band diagonally across his chest.  A leopard-face mask on his left hip secures the stiffened end of his wrapped kilt, which rises behind him.  His right hand grasps a ceremonial 'eben' sword, and with his left hand he firmly holds the forearm of one of the warriors.  This central royal figure, with its restraining gesture, is repeated on all but one of the six armlets.  With variations, the Oba's gesture is also found on ancestral altar tusks.  The motif seems to indicate that Benin's military might is under the Oba's control.
The central motif in rows two and four is another richly dressed figure, also with an 'eben'.  He wears the leopard teeth necklace, quadrilangular bell, and tight chest band of a warrior, combined with the peaked helmet, beaded collar and stiffened hip ornament of a prominent titleholder.  He is accompanied by two active Europeans, and the artist has added an odd detail: the foreign figures wear the chest bands of Edo warriors.  These bands are designed to increase endurance and strength, and their portrayal by the artist suggests that the Europeans may be military allies.  More-over, the cntral figure with the peaked helmet is a common central motif on ancestral tusks, where it is always accompanied by Benin's warriors.  Today's carvers no longer remember that figure's identity.  However, it is unlikely that it portrays a ruler, and the image implies military strength.  A similar ivory figure depicted on a number of Ugie Oro idiophones suggests that it represents the hereditary war commander, the Ezomo of Benin
If the figure portrays the Ezomo, the two superb armlets (and three of the four that resemble them) present his status as equal to the Oba of Benin.  This unusual emphasis suggests that the armlets were commissioned by the Ezomo himself, who maintained a lavish court outside Benin City.  Ezomo Ehenua rivaled both Oba Akenzua I and Oba Eresoyen in political power.  Later, the wealth of Ezomo Odia and Ezomo Ekeneza far surpassed the resources available to Oba Akengbuda, Benin's ruler during the second half of the century (Egharevba 1969c:18-22).  Any one of Benin's three 18th-century war commanders could have commissioned these extraordinary ivories.

Title: Benin Ivory
Description: Arm-cuff; made of elephant ivory inlaid with brass, one of a pair. Depicts eben swords and the heads of Portuguese in large hats, between braided edging.;
Curators Comments:
Pair with Af1922,0313.3.; Plankensteiner 2007: 
When dressed in elaborate beaded regalia, the Oba often covers each wrist with an armlet of ivory.  This solid cylindrical cuff will not snag on he networks of beads, as he deftly twists the ‘eben’ ceremonial sword.  Titleholders also need armlets, particularly when they must toss the ‘eben’ repeatedly during the annual festival of Igue.  Theirs are typically commissioned from the Igun Eronmwon bronze casters, and hammered and forged bronze can also be used.  During some periods of history, elite officials have also commissioned armlets of ivory from specialist masters.  Although these armlets are among the most unusual of Benin’s ivory cuffs, they have very little in common, other than the similar materials from which they are made.
The alternating ‘eben’ ceremonial swords and abstract faces that appear on this armlet, which builds a pair with another example at the British Museum, are entirely traditional in origin.  A master carver has sculpted the edges of this intricate ivory in a delicate braided form that also appears on other armlets of this quality.  Inside of the braided border, two rows of tiny knots appear to fasten each ‘eben’ handle to the braid.  A second tier of ‘eben’ is attached to the first, and the third tier rests upon similar rows of knots and braids around the other border of the ivory.  Portuguese heads with bulbous, patterned hats are compressed to fill the spaces between the multiple images, and small bronze discs are inlaid into the ivory to form their eyes.  The heads orient the design, to make it appear that the ‘eben’ swords on the surface are all suspended downwards.  This position indicated an acknowledgement of ancestral influence in Benin’s affairs.
Although patterns of repeated ‘eben’ and foreign heads are not unusual in Benin, this master carver enriched the ivory surface of each ‘eben’ with inlays of carefully-shaped metal, a painstaking procedure that was also employed in creating a number of other 18th-century ivories.  The process implies that these carvers worked in tandem with equally talented artists from the Igun Eronmwon bronze caster’s guild.
In contrast to this original treatment of an often-repeated Benin design, the artists who created the inlaid armlet were inspired from abroad.  From the 16th century onward, the kingdom’s crafts guilds were in contact with sea traders and crewmen who made regular journeys to India, Ceylon, Japan, and China.  It is therefore not surprising that at least one very delicate carved armlet found in Benin City was certainly imported directly from Asia.  This Asian armlet, now in Philadelphia, features repeated medallions that alternate with tiny linear figures of the Oba of Benin (Hall 1922:146, 148, figs. 62-63).  The diminutive scale of the embossed lines that form these images is unknown on any other Edo artwork.  The medallions on this fragile Asian ivory were once inlaid with metal, which has since been lost.
Two other inlaid Benin armlets on display were apparently inspired by this Asian prototype.  Wherever the metal is missing from their inlaid medallions, the ivory shapes that remain are nearly identical to those on the Asian example.  The metal decorations that remain on the surfaces of these two armlets were also apparently imported.  They appear to have been pre-cast in either Asia or Europe, and the armlets were carved to receive these uncharacteristic shapes as inlays.  The result is a reminder that West Africa has a very long history of contacts with other cultures.  Benin was not at all isolated from the rest of the world.
It might be possible for a specialist to locate the origin of the imported Asian prototype armlet, along with the time period during which it was made.  The unusual metal decorations that remain on the inlaid armlet could also be investigated, to determine their source.  There are also other anomalous ivory objects in Benin with inlaid designs that imply overseas origin or influence.  Without further research into Benin’s internationally-inspired art, it is difficult to establish the age of these unusual ivories.

Title: Benin Coral
Description: Apron, regalia; made of coral beads strung on vegetable fibre thread arranged in an open net-like pattern. Waist-band made of natural-coloured cotton cloth.;
Curators Comments:
Plankensteiner 2007: 
‘A child surpasses beads’.  This Edo adage compares offspring to costly red coral (ivie ebo’ or ‘European beads’) and stone beads (‘ivie egbo’ or ‘forest beads’).  The latter, brownish-red agate or jasper (both varieties of chalcedony), are older imports from the north.  The Portuguese introduced red Mediterranean coral in the last 15th century; its colour fit pre-existing tastes and symbolism – red is power, blood and danger.  In Benin, both types are collectively referred to as ‘ivie’ and called ‘coral’ by English-speakers.
The monarch’s identity is linked to coral.  After the 1897 invasion, Oba Ovonramwen faced the British in a white wrapper ‘covered with masses of strings of coral, interspersed with larger pieces […] His head dress […] was composed wholly of coral of excellent quality, meshed closely together, and must have weighed very heavily on his head, for it was constantly being temporarily removed by an attendant.  His wrists up to his elbows were closely covered with coral bangles, so were his ankles’ (Roth 1968:xiii).  These...belongings are very similar to today’s royal dress.
...Beaded regalia, it would have been assembled and maintained by the Enisen, members of the palace Iwebo society.  These official dressers assist the Oba, his mother and the more important chiefs.   
[This] coral apron, probably worn over white, is uncommon.  Nevadomsky observed the current Oba donned a shawl-width netted garment as the Crown Prince; until his installation, it was the longest beaded item he was permitted (Nevadomsky and Inneh 1983:53).  Beaded accessories accentuate wealth.  
Coral beads have a mystical, medicinal aspect and are protective.  In Renaissance Europe, coral averted the evil eye, a belief probably communicated to Africa.  Its defensive use in Benin is supported by an annual ‘charging’ at the Ugie Ivie ceremony, held at Oba Ewuare’s shrine.  The Oba’s and his chiefs’ coral are touched with sacrificial animal heads to purify and reinvigorate it; in centuries past, a slave was killed for this purpose.; Note from E P S Roupell (3 June 1898):
"Apron. Worn by king's wife when summoned into his presence."

Title: Benin Coral
Description: Fly-whisk, regalia (ugbudien ugie); made from coral and agate beads. Whisk has long strings of coral beads with four beaded flaps at top; handle composed of four large agate beads with cluster of coral beads at top.;
Curators Comments:
Plankensteiner 2007: 
‘A child surpasses beads’.  This Edo adage compares offspring to costly red coral (ivie ebo’ or ‘European beads’) and stone beads (‘ivie egbo’ or ‘forest beads’).  The latter, brownish-red agate or jasper (both varieties of chalcedony), are older imports from the north.  The Portuguese introduced red Mediterranean coral in the last 15th century; its colour fit pre-existing tastes and symbolism – red is power, blood and danger.  In Benin, both types are collectively referred to as ‘ivie’ and called ‘coral’ by English-speakers.
The monarch’s identity is linked to coral.  After the 1897 invasion, Oba Ovonramwen faced the British in a white wrapper ‘covered with masses of strings of coral, interspersed with larger pieces […] His head dress […] was composed wholly of coral of excellent quality, meshed closely together, and must have weighed very heavily on his head, for it was constantly being temporarily removed by an attendant.  His wrists up to his elbows were closely covered with coral bangles, so were his ankles’ (Roth 1968:xiii).  These...belongings are very similar to today’s royal dress.
...Beaded regalia...would have been assembled and maintained by the Enisen, members of the palace Iwebo society.  These official dressers assist the Oba, his mother and the more important chiefs.
...Beaded accessories accentuate wealth.  Horse-tail whisks are popular prestige objects throughout Africa, raised and shaken in approbation, appreciation and acknowledgement.  This unusual example replaces hair with coral strands; its 2.5 kilogram weight (Fagg 1978:28) speaks to the importance of status over comfort.  Oba Ovonramwen owned at least one other example (Pitt Rivers 1977: pl26).
Coral beads have a mystical, medicinal aspect and are protective.  In Renaissance Europe, coral averted the evil eye, a belief probably communicated to Africa.  Its defensive use in Benin is supported by an annual ‘charging’ at the Ugie Ivie ceremony, held at Oba Ewuare’s shrine.  The Oba’s and his chiefs’ coral are touched with sacrificial animal heads to purify and reinvigorate it; in centuries past, a slave was killed for this purpose.; Read & Dalton 1899:
Fly whisk of the King of Benin, formed of strings of coral beads with a handle of four large beads of red jasper.
The coral beads are no doubt of European make, as well as the jasper ones. These last are similar in shape to the long carnelian beads which were exported from Europe for use in the slave trade.; Note from EPS Roupell (3 June 1898):
"Coral. Fly whisk carried before the king by female naked youth - the ordinary fly whihsk is made from a horses tail this is evidently made from that idea. "

Description: Arm-ring; lost-wax cast in brass. Penannular in form, D-shaped in section, heavy, with straight-cut terminals. Decorated on outer surface with three bands of raised decoration (possibly cowrie shells?) arranged in three sets around the arm-ring. Hatched lines at each end close to terminals.;
Curators Comments:
Herbert Alexander Child was captain of the Niger Coast Protectorate yacht 'Ivy' that transported the deposed Oba Ovonramwen to exile in Calabar following the British Expedition to Benin City in 1897. Child made a significant collection while he was based in Nigeria, including objects looted from Benin City in 1897. 
In 1925 Child's widow deposited 105 'West African curios' on loan to Poole Museum in Dorset, including objects from Benin City. 
In 1934 Harry Beasley purchased 50 objects from the Trustees of the Herbert Child Estate for the Cranmore Ethnographical Museum. The remaining objects in the Child collection stayed in Poole until 1954 when they were donated to the National Museum Lagos, Nigeria (accession numbers 54.9.1-70).; The Beasley Collection ledger entry for 1 May 1934 reads: 'BENIN:- A heavy bronze twisted bangle with three raised portions of ornamentation each consisting of three ridges.'; See Collection File: Af1944,04.1-77.

Title: Benin Ivory
Description: Altar tusk; made of elephant ivory carved with human and animal figures in relief.;
Dimensions: 215.00 centimetres inner curve: tip to base (approx) ;  229.00 centimetres outer curve: tip to base (approx) ;  12.00 centimetres base (approx) ;  13.00 centimetres base (approx) ;
Curators Comments:
Read & Dalton 1899:
Elephant tusk carved in relief, in the same style as Af1224.2. The plaited band at the base is much decayed; there are twelve figures on the outer curve in the usual variety of dress, one of them being a European with two half figures of Europeans apparently as attendants; beyond these, on the sides of the tusks, are two other Europeans each shooting at a deer with a cross-bow. (See Fig 6 on details image.) The eighth figure from the bottom represents a chief or god with curved appendages in place of legs ending in cat-fish heads, his head-dress also represents a cat-fish, and a snake issues from each hip; he holds in his right hand a knife-dagger and in his left a jointed staff. (Fig. 7, details image.) A similar figure, but with crocodiles issuing from his head, is on the side of the tusk, but in the last a crocodile comes from between the cat-fish legs and is attacking a deer. Another figure on the side represents a Bini chief riding a horse and holding a spear ; the last figure next the point of the tusk has a cat-fish head-dress, and holds a cat-fish in each hand; two of the same creatures proceed from his hips. (Fig. 9, details image.) On the inner curve are several conventional cat-fish; from the mouth of one of them issues a snake, which appears to be disgorging two cat-fish. Among the other subjects are figures of Europeans, birds devouring snakes, deer, &c. The point of the tusk is carved to represent a chief's head with two faces.

Description: Odudua helmet mask; lost-wax cast in brass. In form of human head with central crest; tiered hairstyle and beaded headband. Four raised scarification marks over each eye; pupils inlaid with iron. Teeth bared. Pierced with holes around base.;
Curators Comments:
This brass helmet is used in the Ododua ritual, in honour of the father of Oranmiyan, the legendary founder of the ruling dynasty. The dance is performed by seven masqueraders who wear brass helmets and carry ceremonial swords to signify their high status. They dance back and forth before the Oba seven times as a sign of their commitment and loyalty.
P. Girshick Ben-Amos, The art of Benin (London, The British Museum Press, 1995); Read & Dalton 1899:
Life-sized model of the head of a native in brass. The hair is cut in parallel lines, and the brows are encircled by a fillet of coral beads, to which are attached larger beads. On the top is a high crest with three groups of tubes (beads ?), and an openwork border formed of a plaited strip supporting fusiform beads. On either side of the head are four plaits and on each eyebrow four cicatrices. The pupils of the eyes are of iron.

This is an altar of the hand for a Queen Mother, similar in form to that used by her son the Oba (king) to strengthen his own good fortune. A stake driven through the hole in the centre of the altar held a small carved ivory tusk. 
The Queen Mother had a separate court at Uselu outside Benin City where female title-holders replaced the male officials of the Oba's court.; The possession of an altar of the hand - ikegobo - was a privilege reserved to personalities of the highest status in the Kingdom of Benin (Oba, Iyoba, chiefs, smiths, carvers, wealthy traders, warriors, etc).

Description: Odudua helmet mask; lost-wax cast in brass. In form of human head with tapering projection from top of head. Three vertical scarification marks above each eyebrow. Serpents and long-nosed crocodiles crawling down the projection and on cap. Serpents and crocodiles on chin. Under chin and on right and left sides of neck are crosses. Bottom of mask pierced with holes.;
Curators Comments:
The Beasley Collection ledger for 20 October 1932 reads: 'BENIN:- A bronze headdress of unusual proportions having the features unlike the usual Benin type. From the top of the head projects an ornamented tube. Length overall:- 28". Collected by Dr Robert Allman, a member of the Benin expedition 1897. Bought:- Fosters Auction Rooms. lot 160.'
The auction catalogue records this mask under 'Other Property' with the correct auction lot number as 110. 
An annotated copy of the Fosters auction catalogue in the Wellcome Institute has number '125' marked at the side of lot 110 and sale price of £190.  This lot was not however listed in the 'purchases' list compiled by Mr Stow on behalf of the WHMM in the annotated catalogue. It there seems that it was purchased directly at the Fosters sale by Beasley.; This is also seemingly the same head published by Nancy Cunard, 1934, Negro Anthology, p.666 as 'one time in the collection of Mr Curtis Moffat, London'.; This male Ododua helmet mask cast in brass possibly dates to the eighteenth century and used to be one of the characters of the Ododua masquerade at the Ague Osa ritual, as part of the New Yam festival (Ague), an agricultural rite marking the end of the year. According to tradition, the Ododua royal masquerades were introduced under Oba Oresonyen's reign (c.1735), as a subsidiary performance to the New Yam festival. The Ododua masquerade is said to honour Ododua, the progenitor of the Benin royal dynasty, and the royal ancestors. 
The Ododua masks have important political significance which is suggested by their predominant royal symbolism.  This mask represents a mythic healer. The iconography of the mask, including the serpents and crocodiles, as well as the grimace of the face, refers to the close relationship between the cosmological order or disorder, the natural world and kingship. It reflects also the symbolic relation between identified animal species and the powers of the king. The mask integrates also important Yoruba references including the name 'Odudua' which refers to the earth deity of the Yoruba people and founder of the ancient Ife.; See Collection File: Af1944,04.1-77.

Description: Crown; made of cloth and beads; circularcrown with flat top made of cardboard? covered with cloth; outside of crown decorated with three bands of multicoloured glass beadwork, top and bottom showing human figures, middle band showing zigzags; four beadwork birds sewn around outside edge of top of crown; beadwork pole attached at centre of top of crown with four beadwork birds sewn on sides and one bird on top of pole with tail hanging down; beadwork tassels sewn around bottom rim ofcrown.;
Curators Comments:
See the essay on this crown and the associated regalia by Moyo Okediji in John Mack (ed), ‘Africa, arts and cultures’, BM 2000, pp.18-21.; Beaded and veiled crowns, ade ileke, are traditionally worn by those kings who could trace their ancestry to Ododua, the mythic founder and first king of the Yoruba people. The crown is called an orisha, a deity, and is placed upon the king's head by his female attendant. Powerful medicines are placed at the top of the crown to protect the king's head and thus his future. The veil that covers the king's face hides his individuality and increases attention on the crown itself, the real centre of power. The birds decorating the crown represent the royal bird, okin.

Title: Lower Niger Bronzes
Curators Comments:
The presence of the Aro knot twidted into the form of this object may mean it can be described as a Lower Niger Bronze. 
The term ‘Lower Niger Bronze Industry’ was created and first used by William Buller Fagg (1957, 1963, 1970) to identify a miscellaneous group of lost-wax cast objects which were stylistically and/or iconographically distinct from Igbo-Ukwu, Ife and Benin City pieces. The objects are associated with various locations in southern Nigeria, south of the confluence of Benue and Niger Rivers and between the borders with the Republic of Benin and Cameroon. Description: Brass cast bell in the form of a human head; lost-wax cast in copper alloy; clapperless; conical form with small looped strap handle. In the form of a face and neck with asymmetrical hairstyle. Low relief decoration emerges from both corners of the mouth.;
Curators Comments:
A very similar face bell was exhibited in Tom Phillips (ed), 'Africa, the art of a continent', Royal Academy 1995, cat.5.74, with a text by Henry Drewal. 
'Brass face bells (omo) are owned by the Olisa and prominent chiefs in Yorubaland, particularly among the Ijebu Yoruba. Special sounds announce the presence of powerful persons. Worn on a sash over the right shoulder so as to hang down at the left hip, the face bell is associated with transitions and the transfer of power, each occupant casting one for his successor. Almost all examples of such face bells have three long striations (with or without textured patterns between them) that curve outwards from the corners of the mouth around the sides of the full face to the ears. This pattern occurs in relief faces on an Ijebu bronze stool that served in enthronement rites. The double crescent marks on the forehead appear most frequently in the arts of the Oshogbo society, whose members supervise the selection and installation of rulers. The wrapped projections that rise on the left side of the head and the long braided loop that descends on the right may refer to itagbe [see Af1886,1209.3], woven cloths with wrapped tassels often draped on the head or shoulder during ceremonies. During the British expedition to Benin City (Edo) in 1897 objects made of brass, ivory, coral, and wood were looted by British soldiers from the royal palace, its storerooms, and compounds.   
Some of these objects were sold or exchanged in West Africa. However, many were brought to the UK where they were retained by soldiers of the expedition and subsequently inherited by their families; put up for auction; or donated, lent, or sold to museums.; Plankensteiner 2007:
The custom of placing an altarpiece called aseberia in a queen mother's shrine seems to have begun no earlier than the late 17th century.  On this aseberia, the platform is relatively simple and it is undecorated along the corners and upper edges, style elements considered to be characteristics of the early 18th century. The six figures and two leopards that attend the queen mother are arranged symmetrically on the plain upper surface, on either side of the wide opening in the centre. Her figure stands at the back of the platform, with her left hand holding a knobbed staff with spiral decoration on the shaft.
On either side, one of the queen mother's female attendants holds a mirror charm high above the group. Historically the Edo have conceptualized reflective surfaces as windows in the world of spirits and deities, just as other cultures have been awed by surface of crystal balls (Omoisigho Osaigeide, personal communication, April 23rd, 1982; Ogiemwonyi Ugiagbe, personal communication, May 1982; Bradbury [1957-1961]: BS 478). Mirrors in Benin were hidden inside wooden cases. The cover was more than mere protection from breakage; it closed the cosmic window, shielding the owner from any beings that might emerge undetected from the reflection (see Egharevba 1968a: 31).  At public ceremonies, mirror charms have been used for generations to protect the Oba and Iyoba, by deflecting hostile spiritual energies that are sent to attack them. The hidden mirror catches whatever illl fortune is intended and reflects it back towards the being that sent it (Blackmun 1984: 307-311).
The other figures on the aseberia represent male officials who served the lyoba. She appointed her own Ewua officials, as well as her warrior bodyguards. The leopards are symbols of her son's kingly powers, as are the abstracted elephant heads with the trunk ending in a human hand. These appear twice in relief, on the front of the platform.  The other images in relief represent the heads or skulls of animals that have been sacrificed to revitalize the lyoba's spirit: cattle, antelope, leopards (four skulls), and two mudfish.; See Collection File: Af1954,23.315.a-b.

Description: Presentation paddle carved from wood.;
Curators Comments: This belongs to the class of decorative paddles, often sold to visiting Europeans by the Itsekiri (who controlled the coastal trade from Warri), of which there are many other examples in the BM. A similar paddle in the Pitt-Rivers Museum , collected in 1901, is illustrated in Michael Sadler (ed.) ‘Arts of West Africa’ London 1935, plate XXX. According to the accompanying text by Richard Carline, this was 'in native use at the time it was collected’. According to information given to him by the curator Henry Balfour, ‘the perforated openings in the blade are said to provide a better grip of the water than a plain surface’. It is, however, certain that many or most of these paddles were sold as unusable curiosities: Af1954,23.774, for example, is only held together by rings along the shaft.
Acq notes (acq): Af1913,1211.3 to 42 are a miscellany of objects transferred to the BM from the Foreign Office in 1913 without any record of their previous history. The attributions of origin now on the database are those made by BM curators when they arrived in 1913. The objects themselves are probably all from the 19th century.

Description: Commemorative head of an Oba (uhunmwun elao); lost-wax cast in brass. Human head depicted wearing beaded coral regalia in form of openwork cap with side wings, strings of beads at sides and back of head, beaded wires projecting across face, and high beaded collar. Head has three raised scarification marks above eyes, two inset vertical marks on forehead and irises inlaid with iron. Line of impressed circles below eyes. Flanged base has motifs of leopards, stone axe-heads, elephants trunks terminating in human hands holding leaves and cow heads. Central circular hole in top of head. Red earth encrustation, especially at back of head.;
Curators Comments:
Reproduced by Frank Willlett, 'African Art, an introduction', London 1971, p.104: 'Bronze head of the late period of Benin art: a massive casting intended to support an ivory tusk on an ancestor altar in the Palace. The projecting decorations on the crown are said in Benin to have been introduced by Oba Osemwede (1816-48). The head therefore cannot be earlier than this time.'; Read & Dalton 1899:
Pedestal in the form of a human head, with a circular hole in the top, and a cap of beadwork, from the sides of which project two curved wings and two horn-like objects in front of the face.  A high bead collar covers the chin, and the sides and back of the head are partially covered by pendant plaits and strings of beads.  Over each eyebrow are three cicatrices and a longer band, the latter like the pupils of the eyes, inlaid with iron.  A flange projects round the base upon which are various symbolic objects in relief.  In front is a cow’s head between two polished axe-heads and two elephant heads with human arms for trunks.  At the back is another axe-head between two rudely executed masks beyond which are two fish and another cow’s head.
Note- Af1897,1217.1,2 and 3 are not made of iron as stated in The Studio, Vol XV., p. 178, December 1898; Int. Archiv für Ethnographie, Vol. XI. (1898),p 237, but of bronze, like No. 4.

His symbol is a kind of crown covered with many cowries, the maker of which is given presents of food etc during the whole time of its manufacture. Ori is regarded as the luck-bringer; if adversity pursue you, it is said ‘Your Ori has turned his back on you’, whereas if you meet with good fortune, you sacrifice to it in thanksgiving. In some respects it resembles the Ibo Ikenga.”

Description: Cloth (aso oke); woman's wrap-around garment, partly incomplete. Composed of thirteen narrow strips, hand sewn together. Warp stripes in beige sanyan (wild silk) and white cotton. Hidden dark beige sanyan supplementary weft float bands.;
Curators Comments:
The cloth has been damaged and is possibly incomplete. When acquired it had been resewn using a sewing-machine. This was unpicked by the collector and the cloth re-sewn in Ghana by one of the few remaining tailors who can do this work (who was commissioned through Duncan Clarke). It is easy to see the holes created by the sewing machine. The sequence of the strips was left as found, but is probably not original. The plain strip at one outer edge shows no signs of earlier sewing and is probably original; but the other edging strip shows evidence of old machine holes and so cannot be original. The two plain strips that meet each other towards the center of the cloth are unusual, and it may be that it and the five adjacent strips should be detached and inverted; this would create a pattern (which might be the original) of five mixed stripes separated by a central plain strips and with plain edging strips on the two sides.The original hems at either end were unpicked and have not been resewn.; Yoruba prestige cloths and garments sometimes use a form of locally available wild silk called 'sanyan' which is produced by several species of the Anaphe moth. This silk is a light beige colour and is lustreless once processed. This local silk continued to be used in women's wrap-around garments and men's gowns until the early twentieth century when it was replaced by a beige imported European cotton. This was also (confusingly) called sanyan but is of a different colour, and is of machine-made thread. The original African sanyan is always a hand-spun thread and was produced locally, proncipally in Nigeria.
Traditionally male Yoruba weavers used the double-heddle loom to create the aso oke cloth strips.

Description: Bell, upper section (a); lost-wax cast in low tin bronze. Elliptical form; with small looped strap handle and hole at top for clapper. Upper section decorated with geometric desings arranged in horizontal bands. Clapper (b) in form of small bell attached with metal wire through hole at top of bell.;
Production place: Made in: Nigeria (a);  Made in: Europe (b:?)
Dimensions: 13.20 centimetres a ;  3.00 centimetres b ;  400.00 grammes a+b ;  9.90 centimetres a ;  3.00 centimetres b ;  7.80 centimetres a ;  3.00 centimetres b ;
Curators Comments:
The term ‘Lower Niger Bronze Industry’ was created and first used by William Buller Fagg (1957, 1963, 1970) to identify a miscellaneous group of lost-wax cast objects which were stylistically and/or iconographically distinct from Igbo-Ukwu, Ife and Benin City pieces. The objects are associated with various locations in southern Nigeria, south of the confluence of Benue and Niger Rivers and between the borders with the Republic of Benin and Cameroon. They are thought to have been made prior to European contact, circa pre-1500 A.D. Sometimes referred to as the ‘Lower Niger Bronze Industries’ or ‘Lower Niger Bronzes’.

Title: Lower Niger Bronzes
Description: Bell; lost-wax cast in gun-metal. Cylindrical form; with elliptical cross-section and rounded shoulders, slightly waisted. Curators Comments:
The term ‘Lower Niger Bronze Industry’ was created and first used by William Buller Fagg (1957, 1963, 1970) to identify a miscellaneous group of lost-wax cast objects which were stylistically and/or iconographically distinct from Igbo-Ukwu, Ife and Benin City pieces. The objects are associated with various locations in southern Nigeria, south of the confluence of Benue and Niger Rivers and between the borders with the Republic of Benin and Cameroon. They are thought to have been made prior to European contact, circa pre-1500 A.D. Sometimes referred to as the ‘Lower Niger Bronze Industries’ or ‘Lower Niger Bronzes’.

Description: Cloth (aso-oke), part of; nine narrow strips hand-sewn together. White cotton and natural-coloured fibre warp stripes. Dark red/maroon-dyed cotton supplementary weft bands. Hemmed at both ends.;
Curators Comments:
The series of cloths registered as 2018,2036.1 to 75 consists of Yoruba aso oke cloths, woven by men on a narrow strip loom; the cloths themselves, however, are almost entirely of a smaller size intended to be worn by women as skirts round the hips, or occasionally on the upper half of the body. Several are shawls or head-ties. The cloths are arranged in an order that is more or less chronological, but within this groups cloths of similar materials or techniques together. The sequence is first sanyan (1-9); then indigo (10-42); then alaari (43-54). The first 54 cloths probably date between the late XIXc and the 1930s; 55-75 are thought to be post-WWII.
The first sequence from 1 to 9 is of cloths using cotton and 'sanyan', the locally collected wild silk from cocoons of an African variety of moth (see comment on 2018,2036.2). 
The first cloth is incomplete, missing at least one strip. It is the only cloth in the collection to use dyed raffia in the warp. The magenta weft bands are in alaari (imported European silk: for which see 2018,2036.44). It originally had a matching head-tie (now in a private collection).

Description: Key-hook; made of iron with trefoil-shaped brass finial inlaid with agate.;
Curators Comments:
Herbert Alexander Child was captain of the Niger Coast Protectorate yacht 'Ivy' that transported the deposed Oba Ovonramwen to exile in Calabar following the British Expedition to Benin City in 1897. Child made a significant collection while he was based in Nigeria, including objects looted from Benin City in 1897. 
In 1925 Child's widow deposited 105 'West African curios' on loan to Poole Museum in Dorset, including objects from Benin City. 
In 1934 Harry Beasley purchased 50 objects from the Trustees of the Herbert Child Estate for the Cranmore Ethnographical Museum. The remaining objects in the Child collection stayed in Poole until 1954 when they were donated to the National Museum Lagos, Nigeria (accession numbers 54.9.1-70).; This key-hook was purchased by Harry Beasley on 1 May 1934 from the Trustees of the Herbert Child Estate.
The Beasley Collection ledger reads: 'A large bronze turn latch, the end cruciform and inladi with coral.'; Plankensteiner 2007:
A variety of brass keys are still used to lock palace rooms where valuable objects such as the king's regalia are stored.  They are also employed to secure palace shrines, and especially those large quadrangles - only one of many still exists - more publicly accessible and that contain carved ivories, staffs, and cast brass objects.  The key holder knocks three times on the large timbered door to ensure that the spirits of the deceased are awake, inserts the key and with a twist, lifts the hook off its latch.  This releases the bolt that locked the door.  The hooks operate in much the same way as the cast keys.  Inserted at an angle, the hook key catches the slide and lifts it, the hooked part of the key holds the slide securely and ensures that the slide does not fall to the ground.
Locks of a more conventional padlock type also existed.  Insertion of a key into the side of the lock released a mechanism that held the padlock together.  Made of brass, these padlocks often had designs of the king, chiefs, or other court dignitaries, and various animals making them decorative and symbolic at the same time.
Some keys are fairly simple as in the iron hooked rod type, although these often have intriguing cast brass handles with agate inlay.  Agate is the traditional bead of authority; only later was Mediterranean coral incorporated as beads of a king's or chief's rank.  The equal arm cross is highly symbolic and represents, among other things, the crossroads or junction that serves as the point of connection between the natural and the spiritual worlds and the keys serve to open doors that link the living and the dead...  Like the quatrefoil the brass trefoil of [this key] is symbolic: the numbers 3, 4, 7 and 14 are ritually significant in divination and in the calculation of ceremonies, and they are significant in different ways in many societies.; See Collection File: Af1944,04.1-77.

Title: Asante Gold
Description: Hollow lost wax casting in gold of a bead in the form of an aquatic shell pierced for suspension at the larger end. The shell is modelled with a continuous series of evenly spaced conical spines that form a continuous spiral around the exterior of the shell from top to bottom.;
Ethnic name (assoc): Associated with: Asante (?);  Associated with: Edo
Curators Comments:
Temporary Register,1861-1921; no individual description. Slip 98,6-30.6 has drawing and written description: 'gold model of spiral shell'.	See correspondence in Collection File: Af1898,0630.; Note from EPS Roupell (3 June 1898):
"Small gold shell. Of this nothing is known except that it formed part of a necklace of one of the king's wives. The Bini are not acquainted with gold & did not recognise its value."; The wearing of real and cast gold shells originated from a widespread belief among Akan communities that they protected people from lightning strikes, from bullets and other projectiles. Sea creatures with shells such as crabs and sea/land snails were also seen to inhabit two or more spheres and as a result, their hard carapaces symbolised to others that the wearer could do the same as well as provide a measure of physical and spiritual protection.  
This is an extremely heavy thick-walled casting and is unlike any other in the Asante Gold collection.

This object is known as a 'Birmingham bell' and was cast in the late 19th century. Although made in Birmingham (UK) bells such as this are in fact sand box cast copies of 'Forcados style' crowned bell head forms. For examples of 'Forcados style' bell heads, see Af1909,0811.3-6.

Most of the CMS objects would have been collected by CMS missionaries in the field. None of the unregistered objects have collection dates or field collector names. The CMS, and other missionary societies, regularly organised missionary exhibitions for the British general public. Objects collected by the CMS were exhibited and some were also available for sale. Description:
Register 1979
Gourd, very large, with incised decoration.;
Curators Comments:
Exhibited in Tom Phillips (ed), 'Africa, the art of a continent', Royal Academy 1995, cat.5.76, with catalogue text by Nigel Barley: 
'Calabash gourds of the Cucurbitaceae family are prevalent throughout sub-Saharan Africa, occurring in a great diversity of shapes and sizes. Naturally spherical, tubular and bottle-shaped fruits may all be further varied by tying the growing gourd. This gourd has a variable thickness that in places exceeds 4cm, and the artist has exploited this for decorative effect. Except around the aperture, where a snake and various zigzag motifs are preserved in the outer integument, the smooth exterior has been completely removed. A chequerboard design of alternating bevelled diamonds and raised squares has been used to cover the entire surface of the vessel. To maintain the formal rigour of the pattern, the artists has had to vary the size of each motif and the depth to which it is cut to accommodate the irregularities of the vessel. Carving within the depth of a gourd is a common Yoruba technique. Sometimes chalk may be rubbed into the design to accentuate the perception of depth, but there is no sign of this in the present piece. Gourds vary enormously in the uses to which they are put. Large gourds form a prominent part of altars of the Yoruba god of thunder, Shango, and it is not impossible that a work of such consummate artistry had such a role.'

Curators Comments: The Asante had trade links with many other West African cultures. This iron padlock and key was made by the Hausa of northern Nigeria; they exchanged finely worked metal objects such as this for Asante kola nuts. Although the lock is a utilitarian object that could have been used on a chest, door or treasure-bag, it gives a fascinating insight into Asante culture. In Asante proverbs locks imply private possession of valuables or property and their unequal distribution: the development of private wealth. Keys were often worn or displayed as an indication of this.
Bib references: McLeod 1981 / The Asante; McLeod 1977 / T. E. Bowdich: an early collector in West Africa; Bowdich 1819 / Mission from Cape Coast Castle to Ashantee

Description: Commemorative head of an Oba (uhunmwun elao); lost-wax cast in brass. In form of human head depicted wearing coral bead regalia: openwork cap with side wings, strings of beads at sides and back of head, beaded wires projecting across face, and high beaded collar. Central coral bead suspended from centre front of cap. Head has three raised scarification marks above eyes; irises inlaid with iron. Inner eyelids incised with short marks. Flanged base decorated with figures of leopards and stone axe-heads.;
Curators Comments:
The Beasley Collection ledger entry for 28 July 1933 that probably refers to this commemorative head reads: 'BENIN:-   'A large head with reticulated headdress with feathers of exceptional size. Ex:- Sir Cecil Armitage Colleciton. Taken at the capture of Benin City in February 1897. Bought:- Sotheby's Auction Rooms. Lot 183. '; This head, typical of the late period in Benin art, shows the Oba (king) of Benin wearing elaborate neck and hand ornaments of coral. It is not a portrait of a particular Oba, but a generic royal image. The royal palace of the Edo peoples was the centre of their world and the Oba was believed to be descended from the Creator God of Benin. The king was also considered to be the counterpart, as ruler of the land, to the god Olokun, ruler of the waters. The king's wealth and power is believed to originate with the fifteenth-century Oba Ewuare, who is said to have gone to the river and brought back the coral beads and riches from Olokun's kingdom. This may, in fact, refer to the arrival of Portuguese travellers in the fifteenth century who brought coral from across the seas. Coral is of great significance to the Edo peoples, as only the Oba wears coral, in a complete costume of beadwork. They are said to contain the power of ase, that is, whatever is said with them in possession will happen. Thus they are the emblem and insignia of the king's divine status.
Commemorative brass heads of deceased Obas or chiefs are placed in shrines dedicated to royal ancestors. On the top of each head is placed an ivory tusk with carved images of former kings, warrior chiefs, soldiers and animals with symbolic royal powers.
P. Girshick Ben-Amos, The art of Benin (London, The British Museum Press, 1995); See Collection File: Af1944,04.1-77.

Description: Carved wooden box (a) and lid (b) decorated with embossed sheet brass strips. Lid in form of cow or antelope head with human hands grasping the horns.;
Dimensions: 19.50 centimetres a+b ;  9.00 centimetres a ;  10.60 centimetres b ;  12.10 centimetres a+b ;  11.90 centimetres a ;  11.30 centimetres b ;  32.40 centimetres a+b ;  32.00 centimetres a ;  29.20 centimetres b ;
Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: label inside box lid Inscription language: English Inscription quoted: 97-500. Benin City. C.F.18 June 1897. Cockburn. Inscription note: Registration number. Findspot. Christy Fund. Date of acquisition. Name of vendor.;
Curators Comments:
Plankensteiner 2007:
These ivory and wood containers (orievbee) are prestige objects created for the presentation of kola nuts (the fruit of a tropical rain forest tree in the Malvaceaae family).  In traditional practice, householders welcome guests by offering them kola nuts, a symbol of peace, order and civilisation.  The kola nuts are broken into segments and distributed according to relative rank followed by a prayer blessing those present.  While it is permissable to offer kola nuts by hand or on a china plate, chiefs and wealthy men can purchase elaborately decorated containers from the carvers' guild.  Orievbee are usually carved from wood...[and] covered with the ubiquitous guilloche designs (oba n'iri agbon, 'the rope of the world pattern'), some of the wooden ones are further enhanced by strips of brass sheet (a similar one is illustrated in Pitt Rivers 1977, pl. XLIV). 
Kola nut containers are found in a number of different shapes - rectangular, circular, and, in cases such as this, having the form of an animal's head.  The animal represented has been variously identified as an antelope or a cow - both creatures that are considered to combine physical beauty (shapely horns, smooth attractive skin, and easy gait) with a lack of aggressiveness towards humans.  A pair of hands grasp the horns in a gesture that symbolizes the right of humans to sacrifice antelopes and cows with impunity.
This type of carving appears to have a long history in Benin.  There are several 16th-17th century brass plaques which depict various types of court officials holding orievbee in the shape of a horned animal.  Some officials are solitary figures (Read and Dalton 1899: pl. XXVIII 3 and 4) while others are part of the entourage of a chief (Ezra 1992: 116, pl.36 & pl.42).  According to Dark (1960:32) this kind of kola nut box was introduced by the great 15th century king Oba Ewuare.

Curators Comments:
This sculpture combines attributes of bird, wild animal and human within a single figure. It would originally have formed merely one element of a complex shrine.
This was exhibited in Tom Phillips (ed), ‘Africa, the art of a continent’, Royal Academy 1995, cat.5.58, with catalogue text by Nigel Barley, comparing this Ijo figure with a similar Urhobo one  in the exhibition (Af1949,46.188, qv for a general account of such ivwri figures).
“The sculpture from the Ijo is a similar conception yet is different in so many particulars [from the Urhobo figure] that the piece reads like the same statement in two different dialects. The Urhobo ivwri rounds out its forms whenever possible, whereas the Ijo efri squares all its shapes off. The function of the piece is the same as that of the Urhobo, and it exhibits the same aggression. Nowhere can the stylistic differences between neighbouring peoples be better demonstrated.”
Reproduced in William Fagg & Margaret Plass, 'African Sculpture, an anthology', Dutton Vista (London) 1964, p.34.

Description: Wrapper; title cloth (aso olona); composed of three panels hand-sewn together. Natural handspun cotton warp and weft with grey cotton warp stripe. Supplementary weft float patterns in imported red-, yellow- and dark indigo-dyed cotton with densely worked patterns of snakes, frogs and crocodiles. Each panel ends with band of weft stripes in red-, indigo- and yellow-dyed cotton. Fringed red cotton border woven in along one side.;
Technique: plain weave; supplementary weft; dyed; sewn
Curators Comments:
The group of cloths registered as 2018,2036.106 to 112 are all from Ijebu Ode, the Yoruba Nigerian city lying between Lagos and the Niger Delta, and all were woven on the woman's vertical loom as title cloths for members of the Oshogbo society, by whom they are known as 'aso olona' (ie cloth with patterns'). In modern times the cloths fall into two types: there are four-panel cloths sewn together and worn toga-style, and there are single-panel cloths worn over the shoulder called 'itagbe'. See the article on these cloths by Lisa Aronson in 'African Arts', July 1992, pp.52-63.
Ijebu Ode was an important centre of weaving, producing blue and white textiles that were traded both westwards and eastwards to the Niger Delta from town of Ndoki. There was also a large local market for the 'aso olona' cloths, which were used by members of the Oshogbo society (called Ogboni elsewhere in the Yoruba area). The designs used on these cloths are specific to the Oshogbo society, and include patterns identified as crocodiles, frogs, fishheads and snakes (for the full list see Aronson). Outside Ijebu Ode (but not in Ijebu Ode), these motifs are generically known in the Niger Delta as 'ikakibite' (tortoise cloths - 'ikaki' being the tortoise').
This cloth has unusual features, notably the three-panel construction (later cloths such as eg.2018,2036.107 have four panels) and the fringe of red that has been woven in along the bottom side (as seen when worn). The cotton is handspun, while the red cloth has been unravelled from imported European red cloth (the twist within the thread is still evident).These features are also found in the two earliest such cloths that are so far recorded: a cloth in the National Museum in Edinburgh acquired in 1790s, and a cloth in Berlin acquired by Nachtigal in the 1860s. The BM cloth belongs in this group, and is complete and in good condition apart from some threads that have become detached in one corner.
Condition: Good.

Description: Piece of cloth composed of three narrow strips of handspun cotton, hand-woven and hand-sewn together along the selvedges (one is sewn in the opposite direction to the others). Each strip has the same pattern produced from indigo and white cotton in both warp and weft. This creates a pattern of light white strips against indigo, which becomes a more intense white when the white threads cross each other. The cloth has not been hemmed.;
Curators Comments:
WA slip records: "Africa West. Small piece of cotton cloth made of three breadths sewn together of a blue and white pattern in oblong panels. Given by Major Denham and Capt. Clapperton."
The WA [West Africa] series was created in ca.1877 (the date found on some of the slips) and included newly arrived as well as earlier textiles.
Acq notes (acq):
The BM printed synopsis of 1835, pp.5-6 (the same text is repeated in the editions of 1836,1837,1838 and 1842) lists three cloths from the 1822-4 African expedition of Denham and Clapperton on display in the Ethnographic Room, cases 12 and 13. ‘A piece of cloth, 16 ¼ ft long by 7 ¼ feet wide, decorated with borders and various stellated patterns, produced by discharging the deep colour of the indigo; it is woven in narrow strips each 3 inches wide [Af,WA.11]. Another piece of cloth, formed of similar strips, but the check pattern produced in the weaving [Af,WA.14]. A piece of very narrow cloth, of the original width before it is made up for use [unidentified]. From Africa. Presented by Major Denham and Captain Clapperton.’
These must all come from the expedition of 1822 to 1824, for which see Major Denham, Captain Clapperton and the late Dr Oudney, 'Narrative of travels and discoveries in northern and central Africa in the years 1822, 1823 and 1824' (London, John Murray, 1828). Unfortunately there is no mention of these cloths in any of their narratives. The expedition from Tripoli across the Sahara reached Bornu, from where Denham explored around Lake Chad, while Clapperton travelled west to Kano and Sokoto. 
The cloth therefore was probably a product of northern Nigeria, or somewhere nearby in the Sahel.

Description: Display cloth (ndop), made of narrow strips of handspun and hand-woven cotton, hand sewn together along the selvedges. Resist dyed using raffia stitching to produce a regular geometric pattern in dark indigo with the design in white/light indigo lines. The warp ends of the cloth are not hemmed.;
Curators Comments:
Picton & Mack in 1989 captioned a detail of the cloth as follows: 'Detail of resist-dyed cotton textile, Abakwariga, Nigeria. An example of the so-called Cameroun cloths produced by the Abakwariga, the Junkunized Hausa craftsmen of the Wukari area. The cotton fabric is stitched with raphia before dyeing. This cloth has been burnished to create the sheen made possible by excess indigo on the surface of the fabric.' 
See the account of stitch-dyeing by C K Meek, ‘The Northern Tribes of Nigeria’, OUP 1925, p.163: “I noticed a curious method of decorating gowns in use among the Abakwariga – an ancient pagan Hausa settlement south of the Benue. Designs are stencilled with charcoal on a white gown, and along the line of the design strips of fibre are sewn. The gown is then thrown into indigo dye, and when it is taken out the fibre strips are removed, leaving the white lines of the stencilled design. This stopping-out method of dyeing, which is known to the Yoruba (and incidentally to the natives of Borneo and Java) is not, as far as I am aware, followed by any Hausa other than the Abakwaringa.”
The cloth was lent to the exhibition in the Metropolitan Museum in New York in 2008, and the following passage from the catalogue relates to this cloth: ‘The term ndop is often used to refer to hand-woven textiles with bold designs produced by indigo resist-dyeing. This tradition appears to have originated in the Wukari region of Nigeria, where it is practiced by individuals belonging to Abakwariga families that have settled in Jukun communities but are of Hausa origin. Such textiles are used in Jukun culture as funeral shrouds, or akya, but they are also in great demand for export to royal patrons in neighbouring Cameroon. There they provide an impressive backdrop for leaders on important occasions of state’. (A. LaGamma and C. Giuntini, 2008. The Essential Art of African Textiles: Design Without End. The Metropolitan Museum of Art: New York).
NB This cloth is so large (over 5 metres long) that it has not yet been photographed as a single object; there are only details.
The tradition of indigo resist-dyeing continued in Wukari into the twentieth century. In 1919 Olive Temple wrote in her book, ‘Notes on the tribes, provinces, emirates and states of the northern provinces of Nigeria’, 1919, p.178 (on the Jukun of Wukari) “They still work the salt-pans at Akwana, but have practically ceased weaving the cloth for which they were once famous.” The tradition did however continue, mainly as exports made for the market in the Cameroons.

Gourd bowl with lid, the latter hinged with plaited vegetable-fibre string; a nut tied on as a handle; incised decoration in black, brown and yellow.;
Curators Comments: Nos.91 to 97 were attributed by W B Fagg to south-east Nigeria. There seem to be no similar gourds in the BM collection; the nearest parallel is with later Ibibio gourds, and these might be an unrecorded early variety of Ibibio decoration.
Acq notes (acq):
According to Braunholtz's entry in the BM Register, this was acquired by Beasley on 1.1.1937. Braunholtz added a note on nos.91 to 97:  'These all seem to be from the John Jamieson collection 1840-1850". Many other African works with a recorded acquisition date of 1.1 1937 were entered by Braunholtz as from the John Jamieson collection, and it seems certain that all the objects with a date of 1 January 1937 belong to a single collection. 
The problem is to identify 'John Jamieson' who seems to be unrecorded. This problem disappears if the collection was that of Robert Jamieson (qv), who was the leading British Africa merchant of the 1840s and 1850s, or another member of his family.

Description: Rectangular cloth; plain weave; natural-coloured raffia palm fibre warp and weft. Weft stripes in varying widths in indigo-dyed cotton. Loose warp fringes at both ends.;
Curators Comments:
Recorded in register:"Mat brought by the negroes from the west coast of Africa to Bahia, made from the leaves of Borassus flabellifer L var aethiopum (?). J Wetherell Esq. [James Wetherell, HBM vice consort, Bahia]."
This can be elaborated by a passage in Wetherell's book, 'Brazil. Stray notes from Bahia', ed. by W. Hadfield. Liverpool 1860, p.73: ‘A handsome coast cloth is thrown over the shoulder. These cloths are woven in small stripes of coloured cotton from two to four inches wide in striped or checked patterns, and the slips sewn together form a shawl. Those imported from the coast of Africa of the best description are worth at least 50,000 mileries, about £5 sterling. The most expensive, and of course the favourite colour now, is a bluish grey ground with dull crimson stripes.’
This and other passages in the book show that the freed slaves in Brazil were importing many types of clothing and objects from Africa for their own use in Brazil.
Evidence for this is to be found in the catalogue of the 1862 London International Exhibition, in the section on pp.5-6 supplied by the Commercial Association of Abeokuta:
"Sundry native manufactures.
[Nos.1 and 2 are raw materials]
Cotton is obtainable in any quantity, and is now grown extensively throughout the Yoruba country, especially to the east and north. Great quantities of cotton cloths, of a strong texture, are annually made, finding their way to the Brazils, and into the far interior. To obtain a largely increased supply of cotton, it is only necessary to open roads, and bring money to the market. Upwards of 2,000 bales have been exported this year, and the quantity would have been doubled or trebled if the country had been at peace. The present price is 4 1/2d. per lb. The other fibres are not at present made for exportation, though doubtless, some of them— jute, for instance — would be, if in demand. Of the native manufactures, the grass cloths, made from palm fibre, and the cotton cloths, are most prominent. Very nice leather work is done. The art of dyeing Morocco leather different colours has been introduced from the interior. Indigo is almost the only dye which can be obtained in considerable quantities. The natives manufacture all their own iron implements, and the quality of the metal is considered good." (AVG)

Acq notes (acq): Entered the British Museum as part of a donation of material in 1855 by Haslar Hospital Museum. There were several unregistered objects (known as ‘duplicates’) from the Haslar Hospital donation in the BM collection. In 1866 and 1868, A. W. Franks requested permission from the Trustees to transfer the Haslar duplicates to the Christy Collection. Some of these were registered as part of the Christy Collection while others were added to the duplicates collection used for exchanges. The Royal Hospital Haslar in Gosport was founded in 1762 to provide medical care for the Royal Navy. Attached to the hospital was the Haslar Hospital Museum, founded in 1827. The museum held a large collection of medical, natural history and ethnographical objects collected by Naval surgeons and officers in the field. It is unknown how, when or where the objects were acquired.

(modern description)
A single strip of hand-woven cloth to be used as a head-tie; the pattern is warp-faced and uses three kinds of hand-spun thread: a magenta alaari silk, a white cotton, and a light brown fibre derived from the silk-cotton tree. The pattern is formed by stripes of equal width that alternate across the cloth: most are white and brown which are edged and separated by single lines of alaari; there are also two wide bands of alaari, one at one side, the other in the centre, while the second edge has a much narrower stripe of alaari. The weft is of doubled rows of white thread. At both ends of the cloth there is a band of openwork created by using the weft to tie the warps together. The warp ends have been twisted to form tassels.;

Description: Qur'an case made of leather, with Qur'an book; a) long rectangular leather cover which folds in four places and wraps over itself, with leather tie to wrap around and hold it closed, tooled on outside with geometric designs; b) stack of papers with Qur'anic text.;
Curators Comments:
First written by Egyptian scholar Khalil ibn Ishaq al-Jundi in the1300s, the Mukhtasar Khalil was a legal handbook for the Maliki school of Islam  prevalent in West Africa. This manuscript comprises the first half of the Mukhtasar. Notes at the beginning and end states that it was copied in  Kano by the scribe Ali ‘son of Abi Bakr and his mother Atika’ and was purchased in 1874 by the Sultan of Hadejia for the price of 150 cowrie  shells. 
	The copying and annotation of works such as this were essential to cultures of learning across subSaharan Africa. Here, the Arabic text written  in larger letters is supplemented by explanatory notes in both Arabic and Hausa ‘Ajami (the Hausa language in Arabic script).
Acq notes (acq): Af1978,09.1 to 46 was given by Mr K Kissack. It is recorded in the donation book as 'A small collection of ethnographic material from Northern Nigeria collected by a Captain Campbell. Some of the material is described as coming from Hadejia'. To judge from the objects, the collection was made before the First World War, perhaps when the British were occupying the area in the extreme north of Nigeria in which Hadejia lies.

Description:
(description from 1843-5 Register)
Hank of raw green silk of two different shades intermixed, and not spun into thread. To it is attached the following memorandum: "No.2 green silk sold at Brini Canu by the Arabs. Purchased at Egga. Paid 150 cowries." 4 1/2 ins length.;
Curators Comments:
Brini Canu has been identified by Marion Johnson as Brini Kano, ie the city of Kano.
ADD  The label attached to the companion hank of spun silk (Af1843,0710.18) suggests that it is most probably the European waste silk, dyed with the colour magenta (alaari) in north Africa, and carried across the Sahara by Arab traders to the market in Kano in northern Nigeria, where it was hand-spun into silk thread for use in weaving prestige cloth. This bundle of unspun green silk would also have been dyed in north Africa and exported to northern Nigeria. Red and green were highly desired colours in 19th century Nigerian weaving, and could not be produced locally, so had to be imported. These and the cloths from the Egga expedition of 1841 are probably the earliest datable examples of this trade. (AVG)

Description: Cosmetic container (a) made of hide, with globular body and long cylindrical neck. Cover (b) made of hide with black hair, bound horizontally with white-haired strips.;
Curators Comments:
Register entry: "Bottle for galena. Made at Egga. Paid 100 cowries".
See W. Allen and T. R. H. Thompson, ‘Narrative of the expedition into the river Niger in 1841’, London 1846, II p.105:
'The custom of painting the eye-lids of a dark blue colour with ‘galena’ prevails here [in Nupe country] to a great extent indeed. It has been generally seen especially among the females since we left Eboe [Aboe, Igbo] … The galena is generally contained in small leathern bottles with rounded globular bottoms, and long narrow necks. In the stopper of the bottle a long pencil is fixed, with which the staining of the eye-lids is performed. Kohol is the Arabic name of this dye.’
This is the earliest datable Hausa cosmetic bottle in the BM. See the account by C K Meek, ‘The Northern Tribes of Nigeria’, OUP 1925, p.161: “Various skin-vessels such as the bottles used for carrying galena stain, snuff or tobacco boxes, and the larger vessels used for carrying honey or butter, are made from undressed cow hides. The method of manufacture is noteworthy. A clay mould of the shape required is first made. The worker then takes a piece of hide which has been soaked in water and shaves of the hairy outer covering, using for this purpose a knife with a crescent-shaped blade. The moist inner skin is then cut into a series of thin strips, and with these the mould is encircled. The strips knit together when left to dry in the sun, and the mould inside is removed by being gently tapped with a piece of bone until it breaks. Skin vessels made of strips of skin in this way will open up if exposed to wet. They are usually decorated on the outside with strips of hairy hide.”

Af1843,0311.1 to 66 is the famous 'Egga collection' which was brought back to London from the 1841 Niger expedition, which was widely thought to have been a disaster as the mortality was so high among those participating. Description: Woman’s wrapper composed of 18 hand woven strips of handspun cotton and alaari silk (aso oke), hand sewn together along the selvedges. A narrower 19th strip of cotton dyed in two shades of indigo added along one side has an extension at one end that serves as a tie. The body of the cloth is made of paired strips of three patterns, which are arranged in the order A,B,A,C,A,B,A,B,C. The strips all have a warp-faced pattern, using narrower or wider stripes of white and indigo cotton (dyed to different shades) and magenta alaari silk. In some strips a pattern is introduced in the weft by varying the weft thread between white and indigo. The warp ends are unhemmed.;
Curators Comments:
See ‘Journals of the Rev. Frederick Schon and Mr Samuel Crowther who accompanied the expedition up the Niger’, London 1843, p.173:
[Schön’s account of Egga market]: 'The manufacturing of country cloths deserves the first notice: with nothing of African industry that I ever saw was I  more pleased. There are no less than about two hundred looms employed in various parts of the town, and sometimes as many as ten in one place. The looms are very simple and the cloth made is uncommonly neat, never being wider than three inches. Some is quite white; some striped white blue and red. They make the pieces about fifty or sixty yards long, which are afterwards sewed together to any length or width which may be required. The make tobes of them which require no less than fifteen or sixteen yards of calico; and smaller cloths for their heads and to cast around their shoulders. The due is likewise made by themselves. The blue colour is made with indigo, of which they possess a large quantity; dye-pits are seen everywhere, and perceived from a distance from the bad small they produce. The red colour is obtained from camwood, but in what manner I am unable to say: there is very little of it to be seen here which is probably imported from other places. The natives use it for other purposes than dyeing cloths… [that is for dyeing the skin].'; (description from orignal label transcribed in the 1843-5 register)
"No.3 Female dress cloth  used by higher classes partly sewed up with raw silk sold at Brini Caun [Canu] by the Arabs, made at Egga. Purchased at Kibami or Kinami [sic]. Price 5000 cowries. 17 breaths of 2 1/2 inches; length size 6 ft by 4 ft. Cotton."
Brini Canu has been identified by Marion Johnson as Brini Kano, ie the city of Kano. Kinami is the town south along the Niger from Egga. It is shown on the map in Schön & Crowther's account of the Expedition, and is also the modern name; 'Kimani' does not exist.

Curators Comments:
See W. Allen and T. R. H. Thompson, ‘Narrative of the expedition into the river Niger in 1841’, London 1846, I p.395:
The rich wear a very full dress, called in the Haussa language ‘Rigah’ or shirt; also ‘Tobo, Toba, Toga or Itoga. It is made like a surplice, with very large open sleeves, the arm-hole in fact reaches from the shoulder to within two inches of the bottom of the dress. The common tobes are white, blue or chequered: the latter is called ‘Rigah’n Zabbo’ from its being speckled like a guinea-fowl. The best kind have sometimes a green or red silk stripe. On particular occasions the richest people and kings wear silk tobes which are brought by Arab across the desert. Cotton tobes vary in price from ten to sixty and even a hundred thousand cowries, those with a red silk stripe being the dearest. All are worked or embroidered in front with silk or cotton. When a blue tobe is worn, a white one is generally put on beneath it, as the indigo not being well fixed comes off and soils the skin. They are never washed but are worn until they become both of a colour and drop off in rags. Turkish trousers, a scarlet cap, and sandals complete the dress of a gentleman of the first rank and fashion.; (description from label recorded in 1843-5 register)

Curators Comments:
(description from original label transcribed in the 1843-5 register)
"No.35 Blue glazed tobe used by the higher classes. After the tobe is taken out of the indigo blue, it is hung up to dry, then afterwards taken and spread on a roller and rubbed as hard as the strength of the wrist could bear; that makes it glaize. Manufactured at Egga, purchased at Egga. Paid 7000 cowries.'
See Marion Johnson, ‘Cloth on the banks of the Niger’, Journal of the Historical Society of Nigeria, VI 1973, p.359:
"The third tobe is in some ways the most interesting; it is very large, dyed a very dark blue with a shiny glaze; the indigo still dyes the hands blue on touching it, and it has clearly never been opened up since the day the dye was polished into it. Here we have the famous "elephant shirt", the kore nyffe , which was, with the "guinea- fowl" shirt, the most famous of the Nupe exports to the north, where these shirts were valued sometimes as highly as the "guinea-fowl" shirts. … This tobe, made in Egga, cost 7,000 cowries; it was probably of better quality than the 23 Kore Nyffi that Barth bought in Katsina in 1853 for an average of 6,5000 cowries. Cheaper "Black Nupe tobes of common manufacture" (probably unglazed), were bought by Barth at Gando for as little as 3,300, and sold at Say on the Niger for 5,000. In Kano, cloth was (and is) glazed by beating with mallets; a similar process is described by Laird and Oldfield: the cloths were laid on a flat block, smoothed by hatchets and knives, and "a man beats them with a wooden instrument, not unlike an English cricket bat, till they become sufficiently smooth and glossy ..." This was at Addakuda, near the confluence; at Egga, it is clear that a quite different technique was in use. This different technique may explain why the Nupe people did not produce for export the turkedis and rawanis (glazed women's cloths and face veils) for which Kano was famous, while the Kano people could not produce the giwa (glazed elephant shirts), but imported them from Nupe and re-exported them. It is interesting that Mockler-Ferryman, referring to "dark-blue Kano cloth" at Bida in about 1890, adds a footnote "This Kano cotton stuff is dyed with indigo, and highly glazed, the glaze being obtained by means of wooden rollers". This is the Nupe technique, which he must have seen or heard of at Bida … At Sokoto in Lander's time, there was a considerable production of white cotton cloth, "both for home consumption and for exportation to Kano and Nyffe"; the cloth for export was largely made up into tobes and shirts."

Description: Vessel made from a gourd with incised decoration, with a bean stopper attached by string.;
Curators Comments:
On the utility of gourds in Africa, see William Smith, ‘A new voyage to Guinea’, London 1744, pp.29-30:
“Nevertheless they are abundantly stocked with great choice of extraordinary good vessels which grow wild almost everywhere: I mean, the Gourd, or Callabash, whose leaf is like that of a pumpion, nor is the fruit when green unlike it. Such as grow near the negroes hutts generally creep up and cover the whole roof, being of no less use for shading the negroes from the sun, than that of Jonas was to him. When the callabash is ripe, they cut it from the Stalk, and set it to dry for three or four days in the sun, which not only hardens the outside, but consumes everything within, except the seeds, which may easily be shook out. They are shaped like Florence flasks most commonly, but they may be formed to any shape while young. They grow of very different sizes, so as to contain from half a pint to eight or ten gallons. When they are sawed down the middle they make very good platters, bowls, or drinking cups, according to their size; and those with very long necks make good ladles; and, lastly, when whole they are as good as bottles to keep liquor in.”

Description: Cloth (aso oke); woman's wrap-around garment. Composed of fourteen narrow strips, hand sewn together. Alternating warp strips in plain white handspun cotton and beige sanyan (wild silk). Outermost strips on both sides have openwork (onjawa) decoration. Hemmed at both ends.;

Curators Comments:
Boxes of this type were used to hold kola nuts, medicines, sacrificial offerings or small gifts. They were carved by members of the Omada palace organsiation. Parents often enrolled their sons in Omada at an early age where they learnt the skills of carving in a classroom-type setting. Working outside the formal palace guilds Omada carving is often characterised by images from secular life and has a freedom of expression and composition.; The Beasley Collection ledger entry for 3 May 1932 reads: 'BENIN:- A wooden kola box in black wood carved with twined design & centrally a bird with expanded wings holding a snake. Bought:- Curtis Moffat Ltd, 4 Fitzroy Square. W1.'
Beasley purchased the box from Moffat for £2.10s.; See Collection File: Af1944,04.1-77.

Acq notes (acq):
During the British Expedition to Benin City (Edo) in 1897 objects made of brass, ivory, coral and wood were looted by British soldiers from the royal palace, its storerooms and compounds.   
Some of these objects were sold or exchanged in West Africa. However, many were brought to the UK where they were retained by members of the expedition and subsequently inherited by their families; put up for auction; or donated, lent, or sold to museums. 
This box was previously in the collection of the Cranmore Ethnographical Museum established by Harry Geoffrey Beasley and his wife, Irene Marguerite Beasley, in 1928. It was recorded in the Cranmore Museum ledger by Harry Beasley on 3 May 1932.
Much of the Beasley collection was distributed following Harry Beasley’s death in 1939. This object formed part of the donation made by Irene Beasley to the British Museum in 1944 (for the full gift see Af1944,04.1-337).
