Description: Stool (agba); made of wood of mortice and tenon construction. Carved on top surface with central figure of Oba holding eben sword. Flanked by European trader in boat on right and attendant holding umbrella over Oba's head on left. Images of trade goods, a crocodile and two snakes between. Four rectangular legs of stool also carved on front surfaces with human and animal figures. Secured to top surface with ? brass nails. Inset circular mirrors in centre of stretchers on four sides.;
Curators Comments:
Plankensteiner 2007
This chair hails from the collection of Ernest Roupell, who took part in the Punitive Expedition of 1897 and was later a district administrator in Benin.  According to the British Museum’s inventory, this object was in the possession of the last king, ‘Overami’.  According to Roupell, the attendants of the Oba always carried it with them, and Oba Ovonramwen was sitting on it when he was sentenced to exile in September 1898.
In Benin, three types of stools were in use: the barrel-shaped ekete, nowadays covered with white fabric, on which the king sits during all public ceremonies; the erhe or round bronze or wooden stool (Hess 1983).  Interestingly, the rectangular type is considered in Benin to be the oldest form of throne, supposedly introduced by the second Ogiso ruler Ere.  This type of chair is particular, however-consisting of several parts joined together by tenons- appears to have been fashioned after European models.
The chair displayed here consists of nine interlocking parts, all richly carved with ornaments and figurative scenes.  In the centre of the scene, on the seat, stands a king in his ceremonial coral attire, with upraised eben sword and a Y-shaped object, the ends of which are formed from two hands.  Standing to his right and shielding him with a parasol is a dignitary with the characteristic uguakpata hairstyle, still common today (see Aisien 2001).  Near the king on the left is a European standing in a boat depicted with upraised sabre, and wearing a suit and hat.  On the outside of the boat, below it and above the king on the right, barrels are portrayed – presumably the sort in which palm oil, an important commodity in the 19th century, was traded.  Furthermore, various vessels, a stemmed glass, and animals are associated with the god of sea- crocodiles and snakes – can be seen.  Three dignitaries and a European are depicted on the four legs of the stool.; Read & Dalton 1899:
Stool of brown wood on four legs connected by shaped rails, all carved in relief. On the top the king stands dressed in a shirt, cap and anklets, all apparently made of coral beads; in his right hand he holds a dagger, in his left a bifid object; an attendant on his left holds an umbrella over him, and on his right hand is a European in a boat holding up a chain and a cutlass; the field is filled with figures of snakes, a crocodile, barrels, cannon, etc. On the four legs are (1.) a chief holding up a dagger and an elephant's head; below, a fish; (2.) a man in profile with spear and curved sword; below, a European with cutlass, hooked staff and drinking glass; (3.) a chief standing, holding a spear and curved dagger; below, a leopard; (4.) a European standing with cutlass and walking stick; below, a leopard; this last subject is upside down. The circular panels on the rails have had trade mirrors set in them and three still remain.
This stool is said to have belonged to Overami, the late King of Benin.; Note from EPS Roupell (3 June 1898):
"Overami's stool. This is the stool used by him since he came to the throne some 9 years ago. It was carried in by an attendant when he came in to submit & also at his trial."

Description: Epa wooden mask representing an armed man on horseback; the whole mounted on an Epa-style head.;
Curators Comments:
Exhibited in  T. Phillips (ed.), 'Africa, the Art of a Continent' (London, Royal Academy, 1995) cat.5.80 (p.420) with catalogue text by John Picton:
The helmet mask with a super-structure carved from a single block of wood is known as an epa-type given the frequency of the generic term epa, but also elefon, or aguru, depending upon local usage. Both epa and elefon are sometimes found in the same community as distinct mask forms. Sometimes the generic term for any mask form is egigun, sometimes imale, and there is a widespread belief that to carve an image or a mask and to sacrifice it is to create a metaphysical presence.
This mask is carved in a style characteristic of the village of Oye-Ekiti, close to Ire, from which it can be inferred that it would probably have been performed during the feast of Ogun. It came to the Museum in 1924, at a time when sculptors were actively still producing such work in this area. The eroded state of the face would be due to successive applications of sacrificial blood and palm wine (the only reason for suggesting that it dates from the late 19th century).
The figure surmounting the mask is a warrior on horseback with shield and spears in one hand and a severed head in the other; he wears the long cap in which the hunters keep their powder dry. The equestrian imagery does not derive from local warfare, but from the cavalry used by the Oyo kingdom and empire that dominated the region from the Middle Niger to the coast from the 17th to 19th centuries, and by the emirate of Ilorin established in north-central Yoruba in the early 19th century by the Fulani.
Bib references: Phillips 1996 / Africa: The Art of a Continent; Underwood 1948 / Masks of West Africa

Description: Gown (tobe, boubou, riga): oblong shaped body with broad sleeves flared towards the top. Composed of 66 narrow strips about 4 inches wide, uniformly woven from dark indigo-dyed handspun thread, which has been given a checkered ‘guinea-fowl’ pattern (called ‘saki’ by the Hausa, and ‘etu’ by the Yoruba) by running threads of white cotton (also hand-spun) regularly along both warp and weft. A small pocket has been sewn to the front, and both front and back have been embroidered in white cotton. The embroidery is in the ‘eight knives’ (aska takwas) pattern, using chain and buttonhole eyelet stitch; there is a large spiral at the front and another on the back. The knives themselves are embroidered on top of extra pieces of cloth that have been cut to shape. The tunic is unlined, but hemmed around the neck and sleeves.;
Curators Comments: The embroidery is of very high quality, and the small area occupied by the decoration suggests that this is an early example, dating from the second half of the XIXc. It is very similar to the embroidery on the famous gown brought back by Heinrich Barth in 1855, and now in Berlin. See Bernhard Gardi, ‘Le boubou c’est chic’, 2002, pp.74-5. See also the somewhat later example in the BM brought back by Freeman and securely dated to 1887-91 (Af1948,25.9).

Description: Standing figure of a man carved in wood.;
Curators Comments:
Recorded in the register as "Wooden figure, male, crudely carved. Munshi, North Nigeria."; Text from William Fagg, ‘The Tribal Image’, BMP, 1977, no.31:
The original documentation attributing this piece to ‘Munshi’ (the Tiv) appears evidently incorrect, and it was reattributed thirty years ago from its resemblance to another piece assigned to the ‘Ashani’ in an exhibition at Lagos. These, however, have not been traced, though they were said to be near the Cameroon border. Professor Rubin, who has an excellent knowledge of the Upper Benue Valley, suggests plausibly that the piece is in a Jukun style of the nineteenth century. This is a very old piece, as was the only other known piece of the type, and the style may well now be long extinct. A number of pieces recently found among the northern Jukun, however, would seem to be closely related. This magnificent piece was given by Dr Parsons in 1909.
Bib references: Underwood 1947 / Figures in wood of West Africa

Description: Cloth (Abakwariga), composed of 30 hand-woven narrow strips hand-sewn together along the selvedges, made from hand-spun cotton. The original cloth of undyed cotton has been resist dyed (with starch or wax) to create two desgins reminiscent of a union jack. These are bordered by a single line of zig-zags which is itself bordered by a net of zig-zags. The textile has been double dyed to create a light indigo pattern on a dark indigo back ground. The cloth has not been hemmed.;
Curators Comments:
Register 1954:
Cotton cloth (74" x 180") hand-spun and woven into strips 2 1/2" wide, dyed dark blue with a resist pattern in pale blue. 
(curatorial observation) Abakwariga cloth from Wukari. This is a type that was much exported to the Cameroons. For an earlier example see Af,WA.11.
For C K Meek’s account on Jukun stitch-resist indigo dyed cloth, see his book, ‘A Sudanese Kingdom’, London 1931, pp.432-3. He notes that in Wukari the gowns presented by the king to high officials were always decorated by this method. “Designs are stencilled with charcoal on a white gown, and along the lines of the design rolled strips of palm-fibre (ba) are sewn. The gown is then thrown into indigo dye, and when it is taken out the fibre strips are removed, leaving the white lines of the stencilled design. The process is known as 'bu sese'.”

Description:
Gown (tobe, boubou, riga). [NB This cloth has been wrongly folded, and the photograph is incomprehensible. It should be turned 90 degrees, and folded along the centre in the other direction, in which case it would look (as it should) like Af1966,01.7. The following description assumes this correct layout.]
Gown (tobe, boubou, riga): oblong shaped body with broad sleeves flared towards the centre. Composed of 79 narrow strips about 4 ½ inches wide, uniformly woven from dark indigo-dyed handspun thread, which has been woven by the Yoruba with a variety of the checkered ‘guinea-fowl’ pattern (called ‘etu’ by the Yoruba) by running threads of white cotton (also hand-spun) regularly along both warp and weft. Each of the strips has three bands of alaari magenta silk regularly placed within the ‘etu’. A small pocket has been sewn to the front, and both front and back have been embroidered in white cotton. The embroidery is either by the Nupe or Hausa in the ‘eight knives’ (aska takwas) pattern, using chain and buttonhole eyelet stitch; there is a large spiral at the front and another on the back. The knives themselves are embroidered on top of extra pieces of cloth that have been cut to shape and couched down. The neck is stated to be lined with European white calico cotton which has been dyed blue locally. The open edges have all been hemmed by hand.;
Curators Comments: This gown appears never to have been used, and is both a superb piece and in magnificent condition. Like Af1966,01.7 it must date from the second half of the XIXc.

Description: Musical horn, perforated at tip, made of animal horn.;
Curators Comments:
"Transferred from Zoology Department. Dr. Baikie. Tschadda [ie Benue] expedition. Temp.J.E.Gray". This information is found on an unnumbered slip written in the 1870s or 1880s (from which it was transferred to the Q register). 
Dr J E Gray (d.1875) was Keeper of the Zoology Department. Dr Baikie distributed the material he had collected on the 1854 Niger-Benue expedition to different bodies; this horn went to the Zoology Department of the BM (not yet separated and sent to South Kensington), and was then passed to the Ethnography section, where it was never given a register number. It belongs with Af1979,01.623.
Both belong to the group Af1856,0218.1 to 13 (Baikie gift from Benue made by him to the BM in 1855, at a time when he was in charge at the Haslar Hospital). See letter in Christy Correspondence. A letter from Dr Baikie, Haslar Hospital, Gosport, 4 June 1855, probably addressed to A W Franks:
"Dear Sir, By the railway this morning I send a large box, addressed to Mr Hawkins, containing a few Ethnological specimens from the Kwora and Tshadda [ie Niger and Benue]. The mats numbered 1, 2 and 3 are made by the Igbira races along the lower part of the Tshadda; that marked 2 is a tribe named Ado, on the west side of the Kwora, opposite Idda. There are a few plain calabashes, from the confluence & lower part of the Tshadda. There are also in the box some musical instruments & carved images, got at Fernando Po, from the coast of Lower Guinea, I think from the neighbourhood of the Congo, and the box is filled up with things from Haslar Museum.
I have a good many other things to send, but have kept them for examination. Please have the box returned to Haslar Museum, as I am short of packing cases.
Yours truly
Wm. Balfour Baikie.
PS There are two horns in the box addressed to Dr Gray."
These are the two horns in the Af1979,01 series.

Curators Comments:
See comment on Af1856,0218.10.
The slip records: "Hamarua" -  identified in the 1960s by P A Allison as being Muri, on the north bank of the Benue.
See Baikie's 'Narrative of an exploring expedition', p.152: 24 September 1854, at Hamaruwa, being the furthest point along the Benue reached by the expedition:
"The road to Hamaruwa [from the river] they considered to be fully a dozen miles; and from its very bad nature, especially after the then recent heavy rains, it was not until sunset that they reached the town. They were well and comfortably lodged, and in the morning the Sultan, in his anxiety to see them, granted them an early audience, contrary to the long established custom of the country, which requires messengers to wait for thirty days before being heard. He received them most favourably, gave them presents, and had a long conversation with them. Mr. Crowther asked him among other matters, if he would object to our sending teachers to instruct the barbarous people who inhabited many of his villages. The Sultan, shrugging his shoulders, replied certainly not ; but they were such Keferi, such savages, that he doubted much whether anything could be made of them. He then gave Mr. Crowther a large piece of native cloth to take to me, and also sent by him a letter in Arabic, of which the following translation I owe to the kindness of Edwin Norris, Esq.: " In the name of God ! Praise be to God, the sufficient One ! Salutation to Mohammed ! The Emir Mohammed to you. He bids you have patience, and to stay in this place until he sends to the north countries, to the Emir Bawsh, and to the first Emir. Whoever wishes to buy of you the things which you have, let him buy what he likes. This is the Emir's command to you until tidings of you reach these countries. Every one may get what he wants through you, for all the shopkeepers of the place run to you to get what you have with you. Health ! "
[p.158, still at Hamaruwa] We amused ourselves by purchasing mats, rings, ear-rings, wristlets, hairpins, and other ornaments, made of lead, copper, or brass, for which we gave trinkets, and handkerchief pieces. Razors were here, as in all Muhammadan places, in great demand, and much prized. A young woman asked me to buy a couple of rings from her, for which I proposed to give in exchange some red printed calico. Wishing to possess a larger piece, she took off another ring and added it to the former ones, on which I increased my quantity. Still she was not satisfied, but taking off rings, ear-rings, and hairpins, one by one, she gradually divested herself of every ornament, until she managed to get several yards of the tempting material. Her last hairpin she held in her hand for some time, looking alternately at it and at the coveted article; but at last, as though thinking that copper rings and brass pins could at any time be got at Hamaruwa, she gave it up, and marched off in triumph with the showy dress, resolving to become for the time the envy of all her acquaintance. I met with but one interruption, from a wild looking, overgrown fellow who suddenly came to the door of our hut, and rudely dragged away a woman with whom I was bargaining for some mats, declaring that she was underselling them."

Description: Cloth composed of 16 strips of hand-spun cotton, hand woven and hand sewn together along the selvedge. The strips are identical in pattern, which is warp-faced and consists of stripes of two shades of indigo divided by narrow lines of white; the weft is of the darker shade of indigo. See Baikie's 'Narrative of an exploring expedition', p.98: near Dagbo on the Tshadda, 17 August 1854 (Dagbo/Daggo is about 100 miles after the Confluence, beginning of Doma territory):
"We went at once to the house of the headman, who, coming to meet us, asked us into a kind of reception court, where mats were spread for us. When all the spectators had paid their humble respects, Zuri came forward, bending lowly on his knees, throwing dust on his head, and repeating ten or a dozen times a short formal salutation, which elicited from the chief a corresponding number of acknowledgments. He then delivered a message from A'ma-A'boko concerning us, which was well received, after which I paid him the usual compliments, and told him the purport of our visit. I gave him a present of red cloth and calicoes, and received from him a fine goat. Seeing people gathering around us with various articles for sale, I said that if they came off at once with us, we would deal with them, to which all present consented …. On returning on board we were followed by numerous canoes, bringing ivory, fowls, eggs, and limes; Shea-butter is said to be plentiful, but none was produced. With these people a brisk trade was carried on for long after dark, and many purchases were made."

Description: Cloth (woman's weave): a single width of hand-woven handspun cotton. Both warp and weft are of the same white cotton, but a pattern has been created in the cloth by varying the pattern of the weave and leaving areas of openwork which form four groups of three stripes across the weft. At both ends, the warps have been twisted to form a fringe.;
Curators Comments:
The Wellcome number 11292 is found allocated to this scarf and to two indigo scarves Af1954,23.957 and 958. A fourth cloth linked by its identical recorded provenance is Af1954,23.1319. The Wellcome slip as transcribed above is incoherent, but it seems to describe a group of cloths, all of which were given by the 'Sultan of Hamarawa' to Dr William Baikie in the 1850s (this question would be settled if the August 1904 Stevens sale catalogue could be found). 
NB Wellcome slips 11277,11278, 11279, and11284 all come from the Stevens sale in August 1904. No.11284 is for a 'leather bag with plaited leather strap', recorded as purchased at Stevens auction August 1904, lot 55, for which the Wellcome slip is annotated in pen 'brought home from the interior by Dr Baikie in the early fifties'. The other three slips all bear similar annoatations, added to the slips at a later date.
See Baikie’s ‘Narrative of an exploring voyage up the rivers Kwora and Binue in 1854’, London 1856, in the steamboat Pleiad. Chapter 6 (on the Upper Benue) records his visit to Hamaruwa [sic], which they were the first Europeans to visit (p.156). This was the farthest limit of the 1854 exploration. Much trading was done (p.158), including a visit to the Sultan (p.164) who gave the three leaders of the expedition ‘three fine Hausa tobes’, three poisoned spears, one unpoisoned and a basket of kola nuts; in return (p.165) Baikie gave the Sultan gifts which included several pieces of coloured calico. See also T J Hutchinson, ‘Narrative of the Niger, Tchadda and Benue expedition’, London 1855, chapter  6, on Hamaruwa. He also records the three tobes and the poisoned spears. In neither account is there any mention of the cloths from the Wellcome collection, but they may have been regarded as too minor to list, or were acquired by trade rather than as a gift.

The dress consists of a simple hip cloth, over which is another piece of cloth fastened round the waist, and reaching variously from just above the knee to half-way down the leg, and in cold weather a thin piece is thrown loosely over the shoulders, or by those who can afford them, Hausa tobes are worn. … Women wear a large piece of cloth from the waist to the knees, leaving the breast generally uncovered. The principal ornaments in fashion are armlets or wristlets, either fine brass ones bought at the Confluence, or smaller ones from the Hausa markets or from Wukari ; but sometimes they are made by loosely twisting round the arm thick brass wire rods. Rings are mostly of brass or copper, more rarely of ivory; anklets are seldom worn ; necklaces of beads or of pebbles, or charms of cowries, are in constant use. The ear ornaments are usually small bits of pebble thrust through the lobe. The men generally carry, as arms, swords from twelve to twenty inches in length, slung over the shoulder ; a sharp-pointed knife, with a hollow handle, through which the hand is thrust ; and also long-handled spears with pointed heads. Less frequently bows and arrows appear, these being reserved … for warfare or hunting. I saw one man with a rough leather sheath, made of bullock's-hide, extending from the wrist nearly to the elbow, to prevent the skin being chafed by the bow-strings, while on the right forefinger was worn a short iron thimble for the same purpose… A very curious currency exists in Doma, and is known as far as Katshina. It is of iron made in the form of a small hoe, with a long spike at one end. These are tied up in bundles of a dozen, or thereabouts, and thirty-six are said to be the ordinary price of a slave."

Description: Sansa; made of wood; rectangular box made of wood, one short side concave; small hole carved approximately in centre of top of box; two slats of wood attached to top of box; eight pieces of cane attached with fibre across slats of wood, pieces of cane longer in centre than on outside.;
Curators Comments:
Register: "The Ibo people. River Niger. From Kew. Dr Baikie's Niger expedition. Mr Barter." This was therefore collected by Charles Barter, the botanist on William Baikie's expedition up the Niger and Benue in 1857-9, and given by Baikie to Kew, from where it was transferred to the British Museum in 1866.
This is the oldest documented sansa in the BM collection. G T Basden, 'Among the Ibos of Nigeria', London 1921, p.189, gives this description of it: 'The ubaw is an instrument which cannot be compared with any foreign one with which I am acquainted. It is composed of thin pieces of a very soft wood (okwe) and its shape resembles an oblong box. It is from five to fifteen inches long, from four to six inches wide, and from one to two inches deep. Thus far it is similar in principle to a violin, but in lieu of strings thin strips of offolaw (the hard outer skin of the frond of the bamboo palm) are used. These are fixed to the tail-end and then pass over a low bridge to which they are also bound. The loose ends are cut to different lengths and separated widely enough to permit freedom in fingering. The instrument is held in both hands, with the tail-piece pointing away from the person, and the thumbs are used for manipulating the strips of bamboo. The thumbs press cleanly on the strips, and are then slipped sharply backwards, and a twanging sound results, the notes varying according to the different lengths of the six or eight keys of the instrument. Occasionally loosely threaded cowrie shells are attached to the tail end of the ubaw , which are shaken to make an accompaniment. The music is not unpleasant, but there is little life in it, the bamboo strips producing a dull note. One notices young men leisurely parading the streets strumming these instruments, but they are not in demand in assemblies: indeed they could not be heard. The ubaw is eminently a solo instrument.'

Curators Comments:
See John Latham, ‘A few notes on swords in the International Exhibition [London 1862]’, in the ‘Journal of the Royal United Service Institution’, VII 1864, p.440: 
“A collection which should contains specimens of all the different patterns of blades made at Solingen would be highly interesting. Solingen supplies a greater variety of markets than any other manufacturing town, and among other places Abyssinia, the African coast, etc. take yearly a considerable number of sword blades. Now the natives in these parts can hardly be suspected of any antiquarian enthusiasm, but they are nevertheless well acquainted with and thoroughly appreciate many of the best known forge marks and mottoes of the early armourers, and among others those of Andrea Ferrara and the old Toledo masters; the Scissors mark of Domenicho Sanchez, the Wolf or Fox of Julian del Rey, the Crown and Cipher of Lupus Aguado and especially the Sun and Moon of Juan Martin. In fact no blade is worth looking at unless it bears a well-known mark, and as the original proprietors of these insignia are obviously unable to supply a demand arising a few centuries after their death and burial, the German manufacturer very practically solves the difficulty by putting these marks on his own blades. In a German pattern-book intended for the South American and African trades, I have seen the oddest possible jumble of old acquaintances. Andrea Ferrara, of course, is the most prominent; ‘God bless the King and the Duke of York’ comes next; the third is grave and sententious ‘Gravidad, Lealdad y Timor di Dios’; and the fourth blade recommends the purchaser, very possibly a naked African, to whom a scabbard to his sword is as unknown as a coat to his back ‘No me sacas sin razon, no me envainas sin honor’ – ‘Draw me not without cause, sheath me not without honour’.”; Listed in Christy Collection Register July 1869-July 1877 fol. 27

Description: Gown (tobe, boubou, riga): body flared towards the bottom by folding over the strips towards the top of the tunic, the broad sleeves longer at the top than below. Composed of narrow strips of a uniform warp-faced pattern using trans-Saharan alaari handspun magenta silk, interspersed with narrow stripes of white and indigo handspun cotton; the weft is of cotton dyed indigo. A pocket has been sewn to the front, and both front and back have been embroidered in white local silk. The embroidery is in the ‘eight knives’ (aska takwas) pattern, using chain and buttonhole eyelet stitch; there is a large spiral at the front and another on the back. The knives themselves are embroidered on top of extra pieces of cloth that have been cut to shape and couched down. The tunic appears to be lined with strips of white cotton.;
Curators Comments:
cf a similar tobe, Af1966,01.13.
This tobe and its associated cap (Af1920,0211.2) were purchased from Mrs F.Florence for £8 in 1920. The acquisition register records that these were the 'Robe and cap of the King of Dahomey given to Vice-Admiral Eardley Wilmot by the King of Dahomey between 1863 and 1866'. The cloth is likely to be Nupe, and the embroidery Hausa.
See Ethdoc 50 - letter from Colleen Kriger to Nigel Barley, 14.7.1986. Ms Kriger identifies the original owner as Arthur P Eardley-Wilmot, RN, CB, Commander of HMS Rattlesnake in West Africa in 1862-66, who is recorded as having paid a visit to the King of Dahomey.
The robe and cap were therefore diplomatic gifts, and since Eardley-Wilmot was representing the British crown, they would have been new and of the best quality.; (LaGamma and C. Giuntini, 2008)
‘Impressive for their lavish use of costly hand woven fabric and virtuoso embroidery, garments of this kind established their wearers status, taste and identification with Islam. In the early 1800s, the reputation of the Nupe as remarkable weavers and producers of such princely gowns based on the Hausa flowing robe type known as riga, was established throughout Nigeria.
The most renowned exports from the regional center of Egga on the Niger River, which served Nupe, Hausa and Yoruba peoples, were gowns like this one, featuring luxury materials such as indigenous silk for dyed silk from North Africa. These elaborate garments were purchased by aristocratic Fulani, Nupe and Hausa patrons; used as tributary payments; and traded to the commercial city of Kano for distribution to other Islamic centers. In the 19th century such garments clearly distinguished the elite of Northern Nigerian emirates from commoners and could only be acquired through inheritance or the award of a title. 
In the early 20th century gowns of this type became widely available commodities. Ironically, as traditional weaving has more recently declined in the face of competition with manufactured cloth, they are once again sought by the elite’  (LaGamma and C. Giuntini, 2008. The Essential Art of African Textiles: Design Without End. The Metropolitan Museum of Art: New York).; Reproduced by John Picton and John Mack, 'African Textiles' BM  1989, p.191 with the following caption:
'Cotton and silk embroidered gown Nupe, Nigeria. This gown was presented to a British Vice-Admiral by the King of Dahomey in about 1863. It was presumably made by Hausa (or possibly Nupe) craftsmen. The cloth itself is woven of magenta imported silk with cotton in the warp, and a cotton weft, in strips about 2 1/4 inches (6cm) wide, embroidered with the 'eight knives pattern'.'
Bib references: Spring & Hudson 2002 / Silk in Africa; Picton & Mack 1989 / African Textiles

Cloth, a single hand-woven long rectangular panel (woman’s weave), perhaps a waist or shoulder cloth, made of hand-spun white and indigo cotton and imported European red cotton yarn. The warp is composed of seven colour bands of equal width: four are made up of alternating indigo and white threads, and these flank three bands of white through which run three evenly-spaced lines of red. The weft is entirely white, with the exception of regular lines of red which create a chequerboard pattern when crossing the lines of red in the warp. There is no use of supplementary weft, with the result that this cloth has a much plainer aspect than the others in this group. The warp ends have been twisted to form long tassels.;

Description: Cloth, a hand-woven (woman’s weave) long rectangular cloth, perhaps used as a waist or shoulder cloth, made of hand-spun white and indigo-dyed cotton and imported European red cotton. The cloth is woven in three strips: a wide central panel and two narrower side panels which share the same design. These have been sewn together along the selvedges. The warp in the central strip is of white cotton through which run lines of indigo; in the side strips there are two wider stripes of indigo, while the remaining areas are white, but appear to be shaded by the inclusion of occasional lines of indigo. The weft is of white cotton, but with four stripes of indigo along both ends. The central panel is decorated with identical and regularly-spaced hour-glass motifs using supplementary threads of indigo and red cotton run over the surface of the cloth (a form of brocading: the threads are held in place by warp threads, and the pattern is barely visible on the back of the cloth); the two outer strips also have along their outer edges a different, but parallel, series of motifs in indigo and red cotton. The warp ends have been twisted to form tassels.;
Acq notes (acq): See Af1981,09.1 for comment on the collection, and its provenance and dating.

Description:
Cloth, a rectangular woman’s wrapper (of men’s weave), composed of fifteen strips of hand-woven cloth sewn together lengthwise. The strips are of unequal width, varying from very narrow to merely narrow, and employ five different patterns, two of which are completely different in colour and appearance from the other three. The white and blue yarn used is hand-spun local cotton, the blue being indigo-dyed. The red and yellow 
yarns are imported from Europe. The variety of structure of this cloth is by far the most complicated of any in the British Museum’s African collection, and defeats any brief description. It employs a very wide variety of techniques, including supplementary weft, openwork, and a brocading of white over white: see the detailed photograph attached to this record. The ends have been hemmed.;
Curators Comments: Reproduced as plate 132 in Duncan Clarke et al, ‘African Textiles’, 2022. This is an astonishing and unparalleled cloth. It stands apart from the other cloths in the Johnstone group, which all appear to belong to a single (unidentified) tradition. See comment on Af1981,09.5.
Acq notes (acq): See Af1981,09.1 for comment on the collection, and its provenance and dating.

Description: Cap hand-woven from white and indigo-dyed cotton with spikes around the sides.;
Curators Comments: This is a typical hat made in the Cameroons, which had presumably been imported into the Niger Delta.
Acq notes (acq):
Af1981,09.1 to 15 were given by Mrs Anne MacDonald, and were (inaccurately) recorded in the donation book as "A collection of textiles from the Cameroons comprising four hats and eleven pieces of textile." 
This was corrected in a letter from Mrs J A Macdonald to the Keeper, M D McLeod, dated 16.5.1981: '...I thought though, that you should know they [the textiles] are not from Cameroons.  My grandfather, Walter Johnstone, brought them home just over 100 years ago and had been stationed in Calabar, Bonny and Opobo [so] that they must have been woven in one of those places, possibly by some of King Jaja's women as my grandfather was very friendly with King Jaja ...' (See Eth.Doc.351).
King Jaja founded Opobo in 1869, and was dethroned in 1887. Walter Johnstone was a partner of Couper, Johnstone and Co. of Glasgow, and looked after King Jaja's son (d.1882) when he was sent to be educated in England. The dating of the collection given here is based on the evidence that he was in the Delta and knew King Jaja in the 1870s.

Description: Cloth, a single hand-woven long rectangular panel (woman’s weave), perhaps a waist or shoulder cloth, made of hand-spun white and indigo cotton and imported European red cotton yarn. The warp is composed of three broad bands of pattern: in the centre is a band of white cotton, all the decoration being supplied in the weft. Flanking this on either side are two identical bands, in which the warp alternates single threads of red and indigo-dyed cotton with the exception of the outer edge which is only of indigo. The area with mixed thread is divided into three equal widths by single lines of white cotton. A chequerboard effect is created in these three widths by adding supplementary weft lines of indigo in squares, which, by overlying the alaari, give the effect of blue; this contrasts with the alternating squares of indigo and red. The ground weft across the whole width is entirely of white cotton. In the central band (alone) extra decoration is created (a) by weaving in three lines of openwork, where holes are created by binding the warp threads together; and (b) by weaving in supplementary threads of indigo and red over the surface of the cloth (a form of brocading: the threads are held in place by warp threads, and the pattern is barely visible on the back of the cloth) to form geometrical patterns that extend over most of the surface of the central band. The warp ends have been left as a short fringe.;
Curators Comments: Af1981,09.5 to 13 (with the exception of 12) share similar characteristics (including the use of float wefts and openwork) that link them together, and this suggests that they belong to a single weaving tradition that has as yet not been identified. Since so far as is known cotton weaving was never carried out in the Niger Delta, these cloths must have been imported from a nearby area. They could be an early variety of Yoruba cloth, perhaps from the Ijebu area, but Dr Duncan Clarke thinks that the small scale float patterns on these cloths are more reminiscent of later Igbo motifs, and suggests that they come from some Igbo group, perhaps the Asaba, along the lower Niger. He observes that in the XXc and presumably earlier the "canoe houses" of the Delta accumulated clothes of all sorts from any available sources. So these could have come down the Niger, or perhaps from the Cross River, although there is less evidence for the weaving in that area.
Acq notes (acq): See Af1981,09.1 for comment on the collection, and its provenance and dating.

Description: Cloth, a hand-woven (woman’s weave) long rectangular cloth, perhaps used as a waist or shoulder cloth, made of hand-spun white and indigo-dyed cotton and imported European red cotton. The cloth is woven in three strips: a narrow central panel and two much wider side panels (a reverse of the make-up of Af1981,09.6), which have been hand-sewn together along the selvedges. The warp in the central panel is entirely white cotton; in the side panels it is mainly white but stripes of indigo and red are run through it. The weft is entirely white in all three strips. The side panels share the same patterns created by regularly-spaced lines of thread, as well as hour-glass motifs and diamonds; in the narrow central panel the designs are more complex and more varied. These are all made using supplementary threads of indigo and red cotton run over the surface of the cloth (a form of brocading: the threads are held in place by warp threads, and the pattern is barely visible on the back of the cloth). The warp ends have been twisted to form tassels.;

Description: Sleeveless tunic, formed from about 26 strips of handwoven cloth, using handspun white and indigo-dyed cotton, and imported magenta alaari silk. The strips all have the same pattern: The wrap has a wide central band of alaari, which is flanked by two narrower bands of indigo through which run lines of white cotton at narrow intervals. The weft is indigo, through which run doubled lines of white cotton, which combine with the lines in the warp create the ‘petuje’ (guinea-fowl) pattern. The strips are tailored together so that the skirt flares out at the bottom. The inside edges are lined with blue cotton cloth, probably imported European white sheeting dyed indigo in Nigeria.;

Description: Man’s trousers, formed of 32 narrow strips, hand-woven from hand-spun thread, which have been hand-sewn together vertically along the selvedges. All the strips have the same pattern of a check of single white lines in warp and weft against a dark indigo (the pattern was known as etu). The waist is enormous, and a strip of European blue cotton sheeting is sewn along the top of the waistband to allow a cord to be inserted which can be pulled tight to hold up the trousers. The same blue sheeting (which may have been locally dyed in indigo) is used as a backing at the two corners where the legs emerge. The leg areas are hand-embroidered using imported green European cotton in chain and buttonhole eyelet stitching to create similar patterns of loops and knots on each leg.;
Technique: embroidered; plain weave; sewn; cut work; dyed
Curators Comments:
For a very similar later cloth from the Beving collection see Af1934,0307.205. 
These trousers may be associated with the cap Af,+.903 and the tobe Af,WA.13.a.

Description: Gown (tobe, tunic, gbariye) with wide oblong sleeves and a large flared skirt. It is composed of 170 narrow strips of handspun cotton, hand-woven and hand-sewn together along the selvedges. The body of the tobe is composed of strips of 4cm wide and has been gusseted with strips 2.5cm wide. The strips are of the same pattern: predominantly dark indigo in both warp and weft, through which run narrow lines of white cotton. This creates a white grid on a blue background. The tunic has been embroidered around the neck and pocket openings with white thread: multiple lines follow the shape of the neck and pocket openings, and there are four 'knots' around each pocket opening and four around the neck. The pockets and neck are lined with blue cotton, and the edges of the skirt and sleeves are lined with a strip of (expensive) fabric with stripes of magenta silk and yellow cotton. The garment has been hemmed at the skirt and neck.;
Curators Comments: This tobe stylistically belongs to a type made by the Yoruba. It is a gown of the finest quality, and since it is securely datable to the 1870s must be the earliest documented Yoruba tobe recorded to date.

Acq notes (acq):
WA slip reads: "West Africa. Tobe of blue cloth striped with narrow white threads, ornamented with native cotton embroidery. (Nigeria). Given by A W Franks. Dumaresq collection."
The Dumaresq collection was acquired by Franks from his widow in 1878. It had been formed by John Dumaresq who was the British Administrator of Lagos between 1874 and 1878.  This tobe does not match any missing object in the sequence of the Dumaresq collection which was registered between Af,+.881 and Af,+.963.a, and between Af,+.2070 and 2083, and was presumably added to the WA series because it was a textile and therefore belonged with other tobes in that group. 
It might be part of a single costume along with the trousers and cap from the Dumaresq collection which are now registered as Af,+.902 and Af,+.903.

Description: Crossbow; made of wood; string mssing.;
Curators Comments:
Acquisition Register later addition by W B Fagg: 'Possibly Ijebu Yoruba or Bini'.; In 2025 a further two objects from the same source (previously recorded as duplicates and not accessioned into the collection) were added to the end of this collection with registration numbers Af1940,22.8-9 (JMH, 2025).; Plankensteiner 2007
The crossbow known in Benin as ekpede was used by Benin warriors.  It fired heavy arrows, which made it a significant weapon of war before the introduction of European firearms.  It was predominantly used by archers who also carried weapons for hand-to-hand.  Benin traditions claim that Ake of Ilobi of Isi, one of the deified heroes of Benin who lived during the reign of Oba Ewuare, who also invented the normal bow, was the creator of the crossbow as well.  Possibly, the Benin model may have been invented by copying a Portuguese model, without being able to replicate the lock.  Bows and arrows were well known locally, it was quite easy to transfer the technology to the manufacture of a simple crossbow.  It is interesting to note though that on Benin artworks crossbows are only depicted as used by Poruguese soldiers.
Arrows for crossbows, know in Benin as ifenmwen ekpede, were produced from treated wooden sticks with sharp pointed metal ends smeared with poisonous substances.  The poison was made by a group of specialists who were versitile in preparing it from plants of harmful  effects and venom.  Such posion for arrow heads was fatal as it was intended to kill the enemy.

Description: Iron spur of European shape, but with the rowel replaced by four fish-like projections. It is attached to a piece of leather which helps attach it to the foot.;
Curators Comments: From acquisition slip "Niger District". Perhaps Fulani.; This is described in J G Wood's 'Natural History of Man' 1868, p.625 as follows: "The Caboceer’s dress consists of an ornamental turban, a jacket, and a loin-cloth, mostly of white, and so disposed as to leave the middle of the body bare. On his feet he wears a remarkable sort of spur, the part which answers to the rowel being flat, squared, and rather deeply notched. It is used by striking or scoring the horse with the sharp angles, and not by the slight pricking movement with which an English jockey uses his spurs. The rowels, to use the analogous term, pass through a slit in an oval piece of leather, which aids in binding the spur on the heel. A pair of these curious spurs are now in my collection, and were presented by Dr. R. Irvine, R.N.

Description: Carved ivory cup, supported by three figures.;
Curators Comments:
Read & Dalton 1899:
Ivory cup of rude work. The bowl is hemispherical with two lines of zigzag ornament; it is connected with the flat circular base by three human figures carved in the round. The first represents a bearded European seated on a stool, wearing a hat and buttoned jacket; from each side of his head issues a long feather or plume which descends vertically to the ground, and is grasped by his hand on each side.  The second is a man in the same style as the female figure on Af.+867, with similar style of hair-dressing, necklace, and three cicatrices on the abdomen as well as the same number on each eyebrow; he holds a spear-like object vertically in his right hand, and a plume  in his left.  The third figure is a native in profile, walking towards the last-described, and  wearing a jacket and breeches, as well as a hat with a brim; in his right hand  he holds a twisted walking-stick, and over the left shoulder he carries a club-like object the end of which is imperfect.; Identified as Yoruba by W B Fagg.
Bib references: Read & Dalton 1899 / Antiquities from the City of Benin and from other parts of West Africa in the British Museum

Description: Cloth (omada); a single length hand-woven in white hand-spun cotton in a complicated sequence forming five bands. Three of the bands (at the centre and the ends) are of plain weave, and are separated by two bands of openwork; the two warp ends are tied together to form long tassels. The completed cloth was subsequently stitch tied and dyed in indigo to form a pattern of lines on the plain weave areas, and stopped with a resist to create a band of white in each of the openwork areas. The ends of the tassels were stopped out in the same way.;
Curators Comments:
Part of the group of 83 cloths dyed with designs in indigo in the Beving collection (Af1934,0307.221 to 303). For comment on the group see Af1934,0307.221. 
C.A.Beving did not know where this cloth came from, and only commented 'the designs in the centre obtained by the use of some kind of resist.’
It has now been recognised by Dr Duncan Clarke as an ‘omada’ cloth, woven by the Okpella in the rocky uplands of the northern part of Edo state in southern Nigeria. See the article by Jean Borgatti in Bernhard Gardi (ed.), ‘Woven Beauty, the art of West African textiles’, Basel 2009, pp.130-3, and her earlier article on these cloths in B.Engelbrecht and B.Gardi (eds.), ‘Man does not go naked’, Basel 1989, pp.175-95. Such cloths were made for female titled elders among the Okpella, and can only be worn by them. Traditionally they are buried with them. By the 1970s only a few women were still weaving these cloths. For another much more recent cloth of the same type, see 2018,2036.145. The Beving example might be the earliest surviving example of this class, and is is not clear how he came to acquire it, as such cloths were (at least in recent years) not made for the market.

Description: Woman’s shawl or wrapper (aso oke), composed of eight strips of handspun and hand-woven cotton 8cm wide, hand-sewn together along the selvages with yellow cotton. All eight strips have the same warp-faced pattern of green and alaari thread with a band of cream-coloured cotton along a central stripe and also along the edges. Each of the six inner strips has three blocks of openwork, each in turn consisting of three individual bands which are aligned across the cloth. The six inner strips and one of the outside strips are all crossed in the weft by regular stripes of green cotton which align across the cloth, though some mis-alignment along the outer strip. The second outside strip (which may have been intended to be at the bottom) has no weft stripes. Neither of the outside strips has any openwork. The warp ends have hand-stitched hems.;
Curators Comments:
A Nigerian aso oke cloth, woven by Yoruba male weavers on a narrow horizontal loom. See comment on Af1934,0307.129. 
For another shawl with openwork see 2018,2036.46.

Object type: gown (object name); textile (object name); tobe (object name)
Description: Man’s gown (boubou, tobe, riga), hand-woven from hand-spun white cotton. The body is formed of 103 narrow strips hand-sewn together along the selvedges vertically, while the sleeves are sewn horizontally. The body of the gown is rectangular in shape, while the sleeves are wider at the top than at the bottom and so flare out at the top. At the front is sewn a large pocket. The gown is hand-embroidered in the ‘two knives’ (aska biyu) pattern. The two knives and the area around the neck are embroidered with a cream coloured local silk thread; the rest of the decoration (five squares and two spirals (tambari), one on the front and one on the back) are in the same white cotton as the body of the gown, and are in chain and buttonhole eyelet stitching. The sleeves of the garment are sewn with a hem; the neck and bottom are not.;
Curators Comments:
This Hausa cloth is very similar to Af1934,0307.208. The label of C.A.Beving reads: 'made from strips woven on a very narrow loom with (probably) European yarns. Embroidered round the neck with European thread.' This may be incorrect, as the thread appears to be local.
For comment on African gowns in the Beving collection, see Af1934,0307.199.

Description: Cloth (woman’s wrapper) composed of eight plain woven narrow strips of unequal width hand-sewn together along the selvages.  All the threads are of handspun silk or cotton. Along one side of the cloth (probably the  bottom) is a single strip with a chequerboard pattern formed from indigo and white cotton warps and wefts, giving an overall indigo appearance. This is followed by three strips with a second pattern: this consists of a different chequerboard of indigo and white warps and wefts, which is laid out to give an overall white appearance; this background is crossed by seven pattern bands created using weft threads of three different colours: magenta silk (alaari) and indigo and white cotton. Along the centre of the cloth is a single width with a third pattern formed of predominantly weft-faced magenta alaari threads, which are separated into five sections by two narrow stripes of indigo and two stripes of white cotton; the weft is of indigo. The remaining three strips of the cloth repeat the three strips of the second pattern. The warp ends are not hemmed.;
Curators Comments: For another Beving cloth that must come from the same area of Nigeria, as yet unidentified, see Af1934,0307.133.

Description: Cloth (Oshogbo society title wrapper) formed of two panels (woman's weave), hand-woven from white and indigo-dyed hand-spun cotton, and then hand-sewn together. The warp and ground weft are both of white cotton, and over this are run supplementary weft bundles of indigo threads (only on the front of the cloth), held in place by white warp threads every 50mm. These are arranged in eight bands of pattern, separated by triple continuous lines, and the pattern is the same on both panels. The bands have mostly geometric decoration of diamonds and rectangles, though three bands have animal figures. The loose warp ends have been twisted into tassels.;
Curators Comments:
This is an early Ijebu cloth, using entirely hand-spun thread. The register has a note by John Picton that this was woven by women on the upright loom as a continuous piece and cut off when complete - hence the fringe.
The acquisition made by the BM from the Church Missionary Society contained a remarkable group of Ijebu cloths: see Af1964,02.52 to 56, as well as this and the following cloth (Af1966,01.26). Another group of mostly early Ijebu cloths is entered as 2018,2034.106 to 112. For the type see comment on 2018,2036.106.
Exhibition history:

1983 Jun-Dec, New York, American Museum of Natural History, African Textiles.

Description: Wrapper (woman’s weave, a single width only), from hand-spun cotton, hand-woven in two shades of indigo cotton and with magenta (alaari) silk in the weft. The warp consists of light indigo and three bands of dark indigo: two of these are very narrow, while the third (along the bottom edge of the cloth) is much broader. The weft is also of light indigo, but with a regular ‘hidden’ weft pattern of alternating narrow (with two threads) and wide (with four threads) weft lines of alaari silk (the silk thread itself being of a thicker gauge than the indigo). At both ends the warp threads have been twisted to form tassels.;
Curators Comments: The 1934 register records in the section of ‘Observations’ that the provenance of this cloth is ‘probably southern Nigeria’. It is typical Yoruba women's weave, but is incomplete, lacking the second panel that would make up the whole cloth which would have been used as a wrapper by women.

Description: Man’s trousers, formed of 32 narrow aso oke strips, hand-woven from hand-spun thread, which have been hand-sewn together vertically along the selvedges. All the strips have the same pattern of a check of single white lines in warp and weft against a dark indigo (the pattern was known as etu). The waist is enormous, and a strip of European blue cotton sheeting is sewn along the top of the waistband to allow a cord to be inserted which can be pulled tight to hold up the trousers. The same blue sheeting (which may have been locally dyed in indigo) is used as a backing at the two corners where the legs emerge. The leg areas are hand-embroidered using imported green European cotton in chain and buttonhole eyelet stitching to create similar patterns of diamonds, loops and knots on each leg.;
Curators Comments: These trousers are very similar to those in Af1934,0307.204 (qv), and might even come from the same workshop. The leg holes have been sewn closed: this suggests that the trousers were acquired new and were never worn.

Object type: gown (object name); textile (object name); tobe (object name)
Description: Man’s gown (boubou, tobe, riga) made from four sheets of European cream coloured cotton sheeting, assembled into a rectangular gown with square body and flared sleeves. At the front is a vestigial large pocket made from another sheet of cotton and sewn down. The area around the neck opening at the front is hand-embroidered in European green cotton with a small pattern of ‘two knives’ (aska biyu) and a spiral; another spiral is on the back of the neck. The sleeves and base of the garment are hemmed using a sewing machine.;
Curators Comments:
The label written by C.A.Beving reads: 'made of bleached European cotton cloth and embroidered around neck with simple embroidery done with European green thread.'
The quality of the embroidery is low when compared with another Hausa gown of the same type in the Beving collection, Af1934,0307.208. 
 For comment on African gowns in the Beving collection, see Af1934,0307.199.

Description: Woman’s wrapper (women’s weave) composed of two identical panels hand-woven and and hand-sewn together along the centre. The design is entirely warp-faced and in white and two shades of indigo cotton. Each strip has the same pattern with alternating stripes of varying colour, with at the bottom two broad dark indigo bands flanking a similar-sized band of lighter indigo variegated with white lines. All the cotton is handspun, and the warp threads at each end have been twisted into tassels.;
Curators Comments: Af1934,0307.149 to 161 is a group of Yoruba blue and white women’s wrappers from the Beving collection, either narrow-strip ‘aso oke’ woven by men, or two-panel cloths of women’s weave. The register records inforamtion from the label attached to this cloth by C.A.Beving: 'Probably Nigeria. Cost some years before 1913 9 shillings'.

Description: Woman’s wrapper (women’s weave) composed of two identical panels hand-woven and hand-sewn together along the centre. Each panel has the same warp-faced pattern formed from two shades of dyed indigo cotton divided by thin white lines of cotton; these are arranged to create a complex design. The weft is mostly of the darker cotton, but at certain points alternates with the lighter shade of cotton to create a ‘hidden’ pattern across the cloth. All the cotton is handspun, and the warp threads at each end have been twisted into tassels.;
Curators Comments: Af1934,0307.149 to 161 is a group of Yoruba blue and white women’s wrappers, either narrow-strip aso-oke woven by men, or two-panel cloths of women’s weave.
Exhibition history:
1979-1982 Dec-Nov, London, Museum of Mankind, African Textiles.
1983 Jun-Dec, New York, American Museum of Natural History, African Textiles.

Description: Man’s gown (boubou, tobe, riga). The body is formed of 126 uniform narrow strips, hand-woven from hand-spun cotton and silk, sewn together along the selvedges. Each strip has in the warp two broad stripes of magenta (alaari) silk separated by thin lines of white, yellow and indigo cotton, and edged on the sides with thin lines of yellow and indigo; the weft is of indigo, which gives the silk a purple tinge.The strips have been hand-sewn together such that the stitching is almost invisible. The strips forming the body of the gown have been sewn vertically, but folded towards the upper half to narrow the strip; the folding opens gradually lower down the sides of the body of the gown so that its skirt flares outwards. The sleeves are sewn horizontally. At the front is added a large pocket. The pocket, shoulder and front are hand-embroidered in green thread with the ‘eight knives’ (aska takwas) pattern in satin stitch and buttonhole eyelet stitch. Along the inside at the bottom of the gown is a lining of white cotton and alaari silk.;
Curators Comments:
Martin S Kisch, a colonial officer in the Sokoto area in 1908-9, made many notes about the tobes (in Hausa ‘riga’) that he saw being worn (published after his early death in ‘Letters and Sketches from Northern Nigeria’, London 1910). These ranged in quality from the very ordinary to the quality seen in this tobe from the Beving gift and the spectacular gowns worn by the Emirs (see below):
“The native cloth most favoured in these parts is of an Oxford blue colour. The Hausa tobe lasts over a hundred years in constant wear; it is handed down from father to son; even when threadbare it makes a sufficient covering. Many of the carriers wear tobes torn in shreds from the seams where the native stuff is sewn together” (p.70)
“This is a portrait of a Hausa [reproduced] with a very poorly decorated riga of light blue stuff and green cotton embroidery. The embroidery usually reaches all down the right side to the bottom [of the pocket]. Note the long sleeves which, when thrown back over the shoulder, show the bare arm and usually a dark blue riga underneath. The trousers are white, with red, blue and green embroidery, with red and black embroidered stripes round the bottom. (pp.140-1)
“I have four messengers and an interpreter, all tremendous ‘bloods’, who ride horses and wear enormous turbans and beautifully embroidered trousers and rigas. They carry their money in the end of the turban that hangs down. They nearly all put part of the cloth over the mouth” (p.100).
“All the natives here dress like tremendous ‘bloods’; all wear turbans and trousers, and two, three or even four rigas besides.” (p.96)
“The Sarikin Gando had a light green silk cape embroidered with silver lace, then a sky-blue silk robe, then a pink silk robe, then a crimson one and lastly a white silk one. As he turned the sleeves up to the shoulder, you could see them all on top of one another. He wore a dark blue silk turban.”; The register gives a transcript of the label added by Charles A.Beving: 'Mahommedan gown from Nigeria made from strips woven on a narrow loom with European waste silk yarns. Embroidered round neck with green European thread. Lined throughout with strips of native woven cloth of indigo and white yarns and around the hem with native woven cloths of grey and waste silk yarns.' 
This type of gown was made in the north of the modern Nigeria, by the Hausa and the Nupe, and widely exported to other areas of West Africa. See Gardi, 'Le boubou c'est chic', 2002, pp.68-77. A large study collection of these gowns and their designs was formed by David Heathcote, and is now in the British Museum (2008,2025.1 to 190). 
The very narrow strip and design points to this cloth having been woven by a Nupe weaver, even though the gown itself may have been embroidered elsewhere.

Description:
Woman’s wrapper (two-panel women’s weave) composed of two panels with completely different warp-faced designs and slightly different lengths, hand-sewn together along the selvages. The two panels are described separately: 
A: two-thirds of the longer panel consists of three groups of five magenta and four white stripes; between these are two areas with blue threads, and these two areas (only) have supplementary weft designs formed by four clusters of five short magenta lines; the remaining third of the panel is entirely of magenta (alaari) silk. 
B: the design of the second shorter panel is also divided into two sections of unequal width; the wider area consists of 23 narrow lines of blue, yellow and red European machine-spun cotton, while the smaller area is entirely of alaari silk. 
The weft in both panels appears to be of alaari silk. The warp threads at the ends have been left loose or have been slightly twisted.;
Curators Comments:
There is a long tear along the warp in panel A. The detail photograph shows that the yellow, blue and red bands in shorter panel are entirely composed of doubled threads of machine-spun imported cotton; the areas of uniform red are of magenta (alaari) silk. The composition of a single cloth from two panels of such different design is most uncommon in Yoruba woman’s weave, where the two panels are usually of the same matching design.
For comment on women's weaving, see Af1934,0307.128.

Description: Woman’s skirt of narrow man’s weave composed of six strips plus one edging strip, which have been hand-sewn together along the selvages. The six strips alternate two completely different designs. The first group of three strips is warp-faced, and consists of magenta (alaari) silk, divided into four sections by narrow lines of white and black thread. The second group is wider and is weft-faced, with a repeating arrangement of horizontal bands of alaari silk and yellow cotton, within which are patterns formed of black and white cotton. The weft-faced strips are cut at the ends; the warp-faced strips have short fringes. The alaari thread is handspun; the black, white and yellow threads appear to be of machine-spun yarn. The edging strip is much narrower than the others and has an extension at one end to allow it to be fastened as a skirt. At the end that acts as a fastener the warp and weft are purely of alaari silk, but in the rest of the strip the alaari weft is alternated in narrow blocks with weft-faced lines of white cotton. In the final two-thirds of this strip, the alaari warp is interspersed with white lines; these appear to have been created by tying white cotton thread to the ends of the alaari.;
Curators Comments: Dr Duncan Clarke has commented that the purely weft-faced strips of the first group of are typical of Yoruba weaving, but that the weft faced patterns of the second group are most unusual. It may well be that the two strip types were woven by different weavers. The closest parallel he knows for the weft-faced strips are the weft-faced cloths woven by a tiny number of weavers in Ogori near the Niger Benue confluence. But the style is itself an anomaly in that area, and it must have come from somewhere else, though no-one knows where. For another Beving cloth that must come from the same unknown area, see Af1934,0307.139. The edging strip, with its white lines that continue the alaari warp, presents another problem, and he remarks that there are many types of African cloth about which we still know nothing.
Exhibition history:
1979-1982 Dec-Nov, London, Museum of Mankind (rooms 7 & 9), African Textiles.
1983 Jun-Dec, New York, Metropolitan Museum of Art, African Textiles.

Description: Cloth, a single width, probably a shoulder cloth or sash rather than a strip from a larger cloth. It is hand-woven from imported European white, yellow, pink, brown, blue and black cotton. The ground weave is white, but there are numerous supplementary weft bands of coloured thread forming lines across the cloth. There are also three discontinuous bands with double diamonds, or drums, placed across the weft. The warp ends have been left at both ends of the cloth, and twisted to form ten tassels.;
Curators Comments:
C.A.Beving correctly suggested that this cloth came from southern Nigeria. It was probably made by the Igbo. See G T Basden, 'Among the Ibos of Nigeria', London 1921. The plate opposite p.96 shows a young woman with a very similar cloth which she is wearing over her shoulder. See p.90 “Ibo women are but little concerned with dress, and in this respect they differ rather from the men. The reason is twofold. In the first place women’s apparel is never found in any interior market, and but very recently at places where there are trading factories [selling imported cloth]. In the second place the men always put an embargo on feminine apparel and until recently have deliberately barred the use of clothing. On the western side of the Niger the fashion is a small white loin-cloth and a sort of shawl thrown loosely round the shoulders, both woven by the women themselves from native-grown cotton. Sometimes the cloth is of sufficient size to cover the body from just beneath the armpits to the knees. On the eastern side it is the custom for girls to go entirely naked up to (and sometimes after) marriage. In places like Onitsha and Asaba the girls now refuse to comply with the injunctions against the use of dress, and as the country is opened up, they will become obsolete altogether.” (Basden was a missionary in Iboland from 1900-1920).
Basden, ‘Among the Ibos of Nigeria’, London 1921, p.178 describes women spinning cotton thread and weaving the thread “on hand looms into strips of cloth from twelve to fifteen inches in width. The finished article is used for making caps and loin cloths, and on the western side of the Niger shawls are made by sewing strips with blue and brown”. The implication is that the ordinary cloth was white and was made up into items of clothing; the other cloth had warp striping using indigo or brown dyes thread, and so would have used for a higher-priced product. He concludes his remarks on women’s weaving with the observation that huge quantities of European cloth were now being imported, and that “In large towns like Onitsha the market is ever growing for foreign cloth, and except among the Hausas and other up-river natives, native cloth is scarcely ever seen nowadays.”

Description: Composite harp; made of wood; triangular prism-shaped box made of pieces of wood tied together with fibre; eight pieces of cane tide to pointed edge of prism; fibre strings strung from ends of cane across rectangular base of prism; rectangular base carved with two rows of ridges; ends of prism painted with black paint; two black stripes painted across rectangular base.;
Curators Comments:
Register: "West African harp". Comment: '?Ibo, south-east Nigeria'.
See G T Basden, 'Among the Ibos of Nigeria', London 1921, pp.189-90: 'Probably the most interesting of the Igbo instruments is the ubaw-akwala, a sort of primitive guitar. It has a triangular-shaped body formed by sewing together three pieces of soft wood with fibre. To the under part, from four to eight pliable canes of different lengths are securely laced, all of them extending well beyond the head of the instrument. They are then bent upwards, and the strings are tied to the ends, crossed over the bridge, and finally fastened to the tail-piece. The strings (awmi) are pieces of fibre taken from the base of the palm tree and carefully rubbed down to the required fineness. The instrument is held like the ubaw (qv), but the method of playing is different, the thumbs lightly twanging the strings, the left and right working an equal number of them. It has rather a sweet sound, not unlike light staccato notes from a violin. The instrument is tuned by bending the canes and passing the strings one or more times round them until the desired pitch is secured. The musician must learn all tunes by heart, or compose his own, which he frequently does.'; A few of the objects in this collection were accompanied by labels or other records which have been transcibed. The other attributions to peoples and places of manufacture have been made by Museum curators.

Description: Pair of trousers nearly four metres across (or nearly eight metres in circumference), assembled from 85 narrow strips 2 inches in width, of hand-spun cotton, hand-sewn together along the selvedges. Each narrow strip has a warp-faced pattern of dark indigo along the edges variegated by lines of white cotton, which flank a central strip of (now faded) magenta alaari silk. The weft also uses alaari silk to create irregular weft patterns of lines or blocks. At the two corners, the leg opening is embroidered in green cotton with a design resembling a house façade. The waistband of the trousers is made from a single width of machine cotton dyed blue (now faded).;

Description: Cloth, perhaps a shawl, hand-woven in a single loom width, with a chequered pattern formed by a mostly warp-faced design of yellow, blue, white and red coloured threads crossed by broad and regularly-spaced ‘hidden’ weft bands of red and indigo. All the threads appear to be European machine-spun and dyed cotton. The speckled pattern seen in two stripes was created by alternating pairs of blue and white threads in the warp and using red in the weft. The warp ends have been twisted to form tassels.;
Curators Comments: The 1934 acquisition register records that this cloth came from Zaria, in the north of Nigeria, and that it is a ‘woman’s headdress native woven in one width ... purchased pre-War for 2/6d’. This information must have come from Charles A.Beving and the place of acquisition and the price must have been found in the firm’s records. This might suggest that it was woven by Hausa craftsmen. Dr Duncan Clarke however thinks it more likely to be Yoruba than Hausa, in which case it would have been traded north to Zaria for sale.

Description: Man’s trousers, formed of about 48 narrow aso oke strips hand-woven from hand-spun thread which has been hand-sewn together vertically along the selvedges. The strips all have the same pattern: two stripes of magenta (alaari) silk are set against indigo cotton which is itself variegated by lines of white cotton running along the warp; blocks formed of six stripes of white cotton are irregularly placed along the weft. The waist is enormous, and a strip of imported blue cotton sheeting is sewn along the top of the waistband to allow a cord to be inserted which can be pulled tight to hold up the trousers. The same blue sheeting is used as a backing at the two corners where holes are left for the legs. The leg openings are hand-embroidered using green cotton in chain and buttonhole eyelet stitching to create the same pattern of diamonds, loops and knots on each leg. The trousers are partly lined with European cloth.;
Curators Comments: The aso oke strips are of Yoruba men’s weave and were cut from a single roll of woven cloth. Embroidery of this kind is characteristic of the Hausa in northern Nigeria, but was also done in Bida and Ilorin.

Description: Garment; six wide strips, hand-sewn together at seams. White and indigo-dyed cotton in basket weave pattern. Bright pink-dyed cotton warp and weft stripes and supplementary weft float patterns. Hand-sewn hems at both ends.;

(Comment from Duncan Clarke) This six strip woman's wrapper is probably nineteenth century, and is made of hand spun cotton and magenta silk. It has a "basket weave" background with silk pinstripes, and supplementary weft float "arrow" motifs. It was collected in south-west Nigeria, but the cloth is of an undocumented type of which no other example has yet been published.

Description: Woman’s wrapper (aso oke) formed of 19 strips of unequal width and with three different patterns, hand-woven and hand-sewn together along the long sides. The design is entirely warp-faced and in white and two shades of indigo cotton. Reading from the top downwards, the first strip is composed of six same-sized stripes, three of white, two of dark and one of lighter indigo. The second strip is narrower, and has a checked pattern of white and light indigo formed by the crossing of warp and weft lines. The third strip is the most complicated and is built up by stripes of varying width of two shades of indigo. The sequence of the three patterns of strip is as follows: 1,2,3,2,1,3,2,1,2 etc (each of the first and third patterns being separated by a strip of the second pattern). All the cotton is handspun, and the warp ends are hemmed.;
Curators Comments: Af1934,0307.149 to 161 in the Beving collection is a group of Yoruba blue and white women’s wrappers, either narrow-strip aso oke woven by men, or two-panel cloths of women’s weave.

Description: Wrapper with a waist-tie (aso oke), formed of 18 strips each 9.2cm wide, hand-woven and hand-sewn together along the selvages. 16 of the strips have an identical design consisting of dyed dark blue indigo between five narrow bands of white cotton. The weft is of the same dark indigo, but is replaced at irregular intervals by bands of white cotton that form a pattern across the cloth. The topmost band takes the form of a tie with long extensions at both ends; it shares the same design of dark indigo between five narrow bands of white cotton, but instead of irregular weft bands in white, it has regular very thin lines of white cotton all along its length. The band below it follows this pattern for half its length, but then reverts to the same pattern as the other 16 strips. All the cotton is handspun, and the warp threads at the ends have not been hemmed.;
Curators Comments: Af1934,0307.149 to 161 is a group of Yoruba blue and white women’s wrappers, either narrow-strip aso-oke woven by men, or two-panel cloths of women’s weave. The 1934 register records a remark on the old Beving label that this has ‘interesting strings woven on, compare with Af1934,0307.134 which has material sewn on.’
Condition: Good.

Description: Woman’s skirt composed of 22 narrow strips with two warp-faced patterns, hand-woven and hand-sewn together along the selvages; in addition there is a longer edging strip at the top of indigo-dyed cotton thread (with no patterning) which serves as a tie. All the thread is handspun. 19 of the strips have the same pattern, with a central band of magenta silk (alaari) thread flanked by two narrower bands of indigo-dyed cotto, and with two stripes of six threads of white cotton down the centre of the magenta band, while two threads of cotton separate the magenta from the indigo. The remaining 3 strips have a wide band of alaari silk and a narrow band of indigo, but no band of white cotton; these strips form a wide band of silk in the centre and another along the bottom edge, in such a way as to imitate a two-panel cloth of woman’s weave. The weft is of indigo, and the cloth has not been hemmed.;
Curators Comments: The strips have been sewn together along the centre with a join that is only visible on close inspection; as a consequence it creates what is seen as a single band of indigo. Dr Duncan Clarke has pointed out that the individual strips are only 5.3mm (2 inches) wide, and that this implies that the work is not of Yoruba origin but from Nupe. For Nupe cloths with similar narrow width strips, see Af1920,0211.1 and 2018,2036.147.
Exhibition history: 1983 Jun-Dec, New York, American Museum of Natural History, African Textiles.

Description: Woman’s wrapper (aso oke) formed of 14 strips each 9.7cm wide, of two different designs, hand-woven and hand-sewn together along the selvages. 12 of the strips are of the same design, and the other 2 strips seem to have been added to the cloth as an afterthought, perhaps to form a band along the bottom of the cloth when worn. Description: Cloth (woman’s weave), a single width hand-woven from European machine-spun cotton. The warp threads are of salmon pink with three stripes of orange along the outside edges. The main field has a variety of parallelograms of varying shape, in yellow, white and black, created by discontinuous weft supplementary floats; these are arranged in 21 lines across the cloth, and are only visible on the front of the cloth. Short lengths of supplementary black and yellow thread have been woven in along each side to form a fringed pattern, and lines of yellow and black have been added at each end. The warp ends have been twisted into a fringe.;
Curators Comments:
The following notes are taken from the entry by Alisa LaGamma and Christine Giuntini when this cloth was lent to the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York in 2008 for the exhibition ‘The essential art of African Textiles’, where it was no.14 in the catalogue.
‘The complex stripe motifs at the edges of this panel exactingly frame a field containing a graceful seemingly random arrangement of elements. Woven as an integral unit on a vertical single-heddle loom with a continuous warp, this work comes out of an influential tradition of textiles produced and traded by Igbo female weavers and centered in the town of Akwete in south-eastern Nigeria. Akwete textiles are distinctive for their breadth, which dramatically contrasts with the occasionally narrower 8-24 inch width of strips produced by female weavers elsewhere in the region (the present cloth is atypical, an especially narrow example of the genre). In Akwete all women are expected to know how to weave from an early age, and most of them do so as full time professionals. Over a month an Akwete weaver may produce as many as four cloths. The work is in great demand and is disseminated to a wide spread assortment of regional patrons of other ethnicities’ (LaGamma and C. Giuntini, 'The Essential Art of African Textiles: Design Without End. The Metropolitan Museum of Art: New York, 2008).
Exhibition history:
Exhibited:
1995, London, Barbican Art Gallery, The Art of African Textiles
2008-2009 Sep-Apr, New York, Metropolitan Museum of Art, The Essential Art of African Textiles: Design without end

Object type: gown (object name); textile (object name); tobe (object name)
Description: Man’s gown (boubou, tobe, riga), hand-woven from hand-spun white cotton. The body is formed of 116 narrow strips hand-sewn together along the selvedges vertically, while the sleeves are sewn horizontally. The body of the gown is rectangular in shape, while the sleeves flare out being wider at the top than at the bottom. At the front is sewn a large pocket. The gown is hand-embroidered in the ‘two knives’ (aska biyu) pattern. The two knives and the area around the neck are embroidered with a silk-like thread (possibly a  local silk thread, tsamiya); the rest of the decoration (five squares and two spirals (tambari), one on the front and one on the back) are in the same white cotton as the body of the gown, and are in chain and buttonhole eyelet stitching. The sleeves of the garment are sewn with a hem; the neck and bottom are not.;
Curators Comments:
Charles Beving Collection Label 'woven in narrow strips ... (probably) native yarns. Embroidered around neck with two kinds of thread; the more yellowish is probably European.'
For a similar Hausa white gown in the Beving collection, see Af1934,0307.202. Other white gowns are Af1934,0307.211 and Af1934,0307.212. The five squares are also found in the category of boubou from Mali that Bernhard Gardi calls ‘tilbi’ (see ‘Le Boubou – c'est chic, les boubous du Mali et d’autres pays de l’Afrique de l’Ouest’, Basle, 2nd ed. 2002, p.97).  
For comment on African gowns in the Beving collection, see Af1934,0307.199.
