Description: Cloth, probably a head-tie, formed of five hand-woven strips (aso oke) with two different designs. The strips have been assembled alternately, and hand-sewn together along the selvages. All the thread is handspun. Three of the strips have warp-faced designs with five stripes of magenta (alaari) silk and indigo, the stripes being divided by white cotton: of these the centre stripe is of indigo, the two flanking stripes are of alaari, and the outer stripes are a mixture of indigo and alaari. The second pattern seen on the other two strips is of indigo and white cotton making a check formed by the crossing of the two colours of warp and weft: over this are woven seven weft-faced blocks of supplementary alaari thread floated across the face of the cloth (ie. the alaari is not visible on the back). Two of these are in the shape of a Koran board and the remainder form rectangular blocks. The cloth has a hand-sewn hem.;
Curators Comments:
The acquisition register records this cloth as ‘probably’ from Ilorin, and continues that is has 'alternate strips of two designs, one containing interesting examples of 'crammed' work.'
Weft-faced float patterns of the type seen in this cloth are indeed associated with the city of Ilorin in the Muslim northerly part of the Yoruba country (see comment on Af1934,0307.142), but the proenance from Ilorian must be an attribution by C.A.Beving, rather than information based on documentation.

Description: Tray made of brass.;
Curators Comments:
Af1963,06.8 to 19 is a group of Efik brass trays or dishes. The type is described by Sir Harry Johnston in ’The story of my life’, 1923, pp.207-8: [on the Efik people of Old Calabar which he visited in 1887-8] “They were very fond of brass-work. They obtained sheets of brass from European traders and having cut out circular plates they would stamp on these fantastic designs by means of a large-headed, sharp-pointed nail and a stone used as a hammer. The work was usually done by women, quite untaught. The designs were in many cases really graceful and chiefly consisted of flowers and fruit in conventional forms. Some traders said they introduced ‘mermaids’. They may have learnt this myth from the Portuguese who revived old Mediterranean stories at the sight of the manati suckling its young at the breast.”
This reveals that the plates were being made in the 1880s, and suggests that a reasonable dating of the group lies between the 1880s and the 1910s.
For a recent study, see J Coote & J Salmons, 'Mermaids and Mai Wata on brassware from Old Calabar', in H J Drewal (ed.), 'Sacred waters, arts for Mami Wata and other divinities in Africa and the Diaspora', Indiana University Press 2008.
Condition: Good.
Acq notes (acq): Af1963,06.1 to 21 were given by Miss Maud Denny (see her biography). Nos.1 to 7 are mostly Nupe; nos.8-19 are Efik (Calabar trays); 20 is Yoruba; 21 is Asante.

Description: Man’s gown (boubou, tobe, riga). The body is formed of 49 uniform strips, hand-woven and hand-sewn together along the selvedges; each strip has three broad stripes of hand-spun magenta (alaari) silk separated by narrower bands of machine-spun European white and yellow cotton; the weft is indigo, which gives the alaari a purple tinge. Four gussets of locally-spun and woven white cotton are inserted along the skirt of the main body in order to make the skirt flare; the sleeves are wider at the top than the bottom and as a result fan out. At the front is sewn a large pocket. The pocket, shoulder and front are hand-embroidered in European green thread with the ‘eight knives’ (aska takwas) pattern in chain and buttonhole eyelet stitch; there is a small spiral at the front and another on the back. Along the inside at the bottom of the gown is a lining of European printed cotton with a 'paisley' boteh motif printed in black, blue and white, and with a background in red. All the edges have a hand-sewn hem.;
Curators Comments:
The label written by C.A.Beving reads: "Native Mohammedan garment made from strips of cloth woven on a narrow loom with ... (European waste silk) yarns. Embroidered round neck with green European thread. Hemmed with a piece of European printed cotton and small piece of woven cloth."
Dr Duncan Clarke observes that the cloth is woven by Nupe weavers, although the tailoring and/or embroidery could have been done by people from other groups such as the Hausa. For a gown with a similar design see Af1934,0307.200.
 For comment on African gowns in the Beving collection, see Af1934,0307.199.

Object type: gown (object name); textile (object name); tobe (object name)
Description: Man’s gown (boubou, tobe, riga), hand-woven from hand-spun white and indigo cotton. The body is formed of 60 narrow strips hand-sewn together along the selvedges vertically, while the sleeves are sewn horizontally. At the front is a large pocket. All the strips have the same design of indigo crossed in both warp and weft by lines of white cotton that form a large rectangular check (petuje in Yoruba). The front of the cloth is decorated in white cotton by hand with embroidery in the ‘eight knives’ (aska takwas) pattern. The areas with the knives are cut out from another piece of cloth, then embroidered in European thread and couched down; the rest of the decoration is embroidered directly on the cloth, with chain and buttonhole eyelet stitching, some in herringbone patterns, forming knots, a spiral and other interlaced patterns; there is a second small spiral on the back. Before being embroidered, the areas around the neck were lined on the inside with light blue cotton sheeting imported from Europe; the blue might be locally dyed indigo.;
Curators Comments:
Charles Beving Collection Label: ' Gown made from strips of cloth of one design woven on a narrow loom. Embroidered at the front with white thread (European).'
This type of gown was made in the north of the modern Nigeria, by the Hausa and the Nupe, and by the Yoruba in Ilorin, and widely exported to other areas of West Africa. The quality of the design and embroidery is not as high as in a similar gown from the Beving collection, Af1934,0307.207.  For comment on African gowns in the Beving collection, see Af1934,0307.199.

Description:
Cloth (woman’s weave), a single width hand-woven from European machine-spun cotton. The warp threads are pink cotton regularly varied with dark blue threads; the bands along the edges are only in pink. The weft is also in pink. Across the cloth are ten bands of decoration in supplementary weft, arranged in the order 1,2,1,3,1,4,1,3,1,2. These are composed as follows:
1. Alternating blue and white stripes highlighted with small yellow stars
2. A pattern of repeating six point stars in blue and white
3. Alternating pink and white blocks flanked by white and blue stripes
4. A repeating 'wave' pattern flanked by blue and white stripes
Short lengths of supplementary black and yellow thread have been woven in along the pink bands on each side to form a fringed pattern. The warp ends have been twisted into a fringe.;
Dimensions: 199.00 centimetres including fringe ;  104.00 centimetres including fringe ;
Curators Comments: A cloth woven in Akwete: see comment on Af1934,0307.104.

Description: Wrapper, cloth; composed of two panels hand-sewn together. Natural coloured cotton warp and weft with single indigo-dyed cotton warp stripe at one side. Supplementary weft float patterns in red- and indigo-dyed cotton. Hand sewn hems at both ends.;
Technique: plain weave; supplementary weft; dyed; sewn
Curators Comments:
One of the group of seven Ijebu Ode cloths in the 2018 gift. See comment on 2018,2036.106. Despite its small size and having only two panels, this cloth is certainly complete, since there is no sign of the removal of a strip. The colours, the thick handspun thread and the design all point towards its belonging to the group of Ijebu Yoruba "aso olona" title cloths for the Ogboni (or Oshugbo) society. Duncan Clarke, who bought the cloth in Ibadan, recorded that the person from whom he bought it had stated that it came from an Ijebu woman. 
The cloth can be dated to the late XIXc or early XXc from the use of hand-spun white and indigo cotton, with imported red cotton. The design is unusually minimalist.
Condition: Good.

Description: Man’s gown (boubou, tobe, riga), hand-woven from hand-spun white cotton. The body is formed of 176 narrow strips hand-sewn together along the selvedges vertically, while the sleeves are sewn horizontally. The body of the gown flares out towards the bottom by folding the tsrips at the top; the sleeves are wider at the top than at the bottom and so flare out at the top. At the front is sewn a large pocket. The gown is hand-embroidered in the ‘eight knives’ (aska takwas) pattern with a large spiral on front and back. The decoration is in white cotton, and is in chain and buttonhole eyelet stitching. The sleeves of the garment are sewn with a hem; the base is lined with a length of magenta alaari silk.;
Curators Comments: This is a remarkable early Hausa gown, now very hard to read in the photographs. The extremely narrow strips may have been imported from Nupe.
Exhibition history:
1979-1982 Dec-Nov, London, Museum of Mankind (rooms 7 & 9), African Textiles.

Description: Man’s trousers, with 126 narrow strips, hand-woven from hand-spun white and dyed indigo cotton. The weave forms a very narrow check pattern (known as saki in Hausa, and etu in Yoruba). These strips have been hand-sewn along the selvedges in vertical and horizontal directions, and leave the centre baggy and the waist enormous. A strip of white cotton sewn along the top acts as the waistband, with a green cotton pull cord made of green mercerized cotton yarn plaited by hand; this can be pulled tight with a draw-string to hold up the trousers. Attached to the bottom ends are two short narrow leggings covered in embroidery and lined with blue machine-woven cotton sheeting. Both the front and back of the trousers are hand-embroidered with white, red, green, blue and pink imported European cotton in a pattern of diamonds, loops and knots.;
Curators Comments: Trousers such as these were worn together with men’s gowns of the type seen in Af1934,0307.199, and were made by the Hausa and Nupe.

Description: Woman’s wrapper (two-panel woman’s weave) composed of two hand-woven panels hand-sewn together along the selvages. The panels are warp-faced and have identical designs; one, however, is slightly narrower and shorter than the other. The design is made up of stripes of varying width of magenta (alaari) silk and two shades of indigo-dyed cotton (both handspun), which are separated by thin lines of European machine-spun white cotton. The weft is of indigo-dyed cotton. The warp-ends have been twisted to form tassels.;
Curators Comments: Early examples of wrappers of Yoruba woman’s weave are often seen where the two panels are of unequal width and length even though they are composed of the same count of threads. The explanation must lie in the difficulty of getting the same tension and length when using the wide vertical woman’s loom.

Description: Man’s gown (boubou, tobe, agbada). The body is formed of 24 aso oke strips hand-woven and hand-sewn together along the selvedges vertically, while the sleeves are sewn horizontally; the strips in the upper section are folded, and gradually unfolded below so as to make the skirt flare. The strips on the body and sleeves have the same design. This consists of alternating warp stripes of indigo within which are lines of single threads of white hand-spun cotton, and stripes of magenta (alaari) silk; the weft is indigo. The area around the opening of the neck is hand-embroidered in chain stitch on the front and back with lines of white cotton and four star-like squares or knots. The same decoration is embroidered around two vestigial openings on the chest. The neck opening is lined with plain blue cotton (possibly locally dyed), and the edge of the skirt is lined with pink and white machine-woven European printed cotton with a design of red and white stripes and red circles.;
Curators Comments:
The label of C.A.Beving reads: ' made from strips woven on a narrow loom with European waste silk and cotton yarns. Embroidered with white European thread around the neck and belt holes. Lined at neck with European calico native dyed and around hem with European printed cotton.'
This is a Yoruba ‘agbada’ gown: see Bernhard Gardi, ‘Le Boubou – c'est chic, les boubous du Mali et d’autres pays de l’Afrique de l’Ouest’, Basle, 2nd ed. 2002, pp.72-3. The two oval gaps on the chest are not pockets, but in origin were left to pass the hands through when holding the reins of a horse.  For comment on African gowns in the Beving collection, see Af1934,0307.199.

Description: Cloth, being the width of a whole cloth that has been cut across the middle, and was probably originally three times as long. The thread is imported European white and two shades of brown hand-spun cotton that has been hand-woven with a warp-faced pattern of narrow stripes. The warp ends on the surviving end have been left loose and frayed.;
Curators Comments: C.A.Beving plausibly suggested that this cloth came from southern Nigeria. The unusually wide loom width and the swelling of the cloth towards the end, might suggest that it comes from Akwete, but it is not similar to the other Akwete cloths in Beving's collection (eg. it lacks any supplementary weft decoration). It might have been woven elsewhere in the Niger delta, or represent a stage of Akwete weaving before the innovations attributed to Dada Nwakata (see sv Af1934,0307.104) in the late XIXc.

Description: Woman’s wrapper (aso oke) formed of ten strips hand-woven with two different designs, one warp-faced, the other primarily weft-faced, hand-woven and hand-sewn together along the selvages.  All the thread is handspun and locally dyed. The ten strips have been arranged to form two identical groups of five strips which are repeated twice. Each group is made up of five strips, in which three warp-faced stripes alternate with two strips with supplementary weft float designs. The warp-faced strips are striped with magenta silk (alaari) and yellow, white and two shades of indigo cotton. The weft-faced strips have a uniform narrow check pattern of indigo and white cotton, formed by the crossing of the blue and white threads of the warp and weft, which forms the background to eight blocks of supplementary float weft of alaari silk (the alaari is not visible on the verso); three of these are in the shape of Koran boards, a fourth is in the shape of a drum and the other four are groups of parallel lines. The cloth has not been hemmed.;
Curators Comments:
Recorded in the 1934 acquisition register as coming from Ilorin, and as having been ‘Purchased some years before 1913 for 3/6d’.
Af1934,0307.137, 142, 143 in the Beving collection have very similar layouts and designs.

Description: Woman’s wrapper (aso oke) formed of ten strips hand-woven with two different designs, one warp-faced, the other balanced plain weave, hand-sewn together along the selvages. Description: Woman’s wrapper (aso oke) formed of ten strips hand-woven with two different designs, one warp-faced, the other primarily weft-faced, all hand-woven and hand-sewn together along the selvages. All the thread is handspun. The ten strips have been arranged to form two near-identical groups each of five strips, in which three strips with warp-faced stripes separate two strips with weft float designs. The warp-faced strips are (with one exception) striped with white and two shades of indigo cotton: the exception is one strip with a different pattern of stripes of magenta silk (alaari), and cotton in white and two shades of indigo. The weft-faced strips have a uniform narrow check pattern of indigo and white cotton, formed by the crossing of the blue and white threads of the warp and weft, over which are floated seven blocks (in repeated pairs) of supplementary weft motifs of alaari silk (the alaari is not visible on the verso); two of these in each strip are in the shape of Koran boards. The cloth has not been hemmed.;
Curators Comments: This cloth has a very similar layout to Af1934,0307.137 and 142. Following the fall of Oyo around 1830 to the Fulani jihad and to its own internal strife, the main centres of Yoruba aso oke weaving were Ilorin, Iseyin, and in smaller numbers the re-established New Oyo. In the 1920s and 1930s there was a revival of fashion for supplementary float motifs. These were then woven in Ilorin but not in Iseyin, and on that basis it has been assumed that float motifs in the nineteenth-century were also woven at least predominantly in Ilorin. (Note by Dr Duncan Clarke)

Description: Cloth (woman’s weave), a single width hand-woven from European machine-spun cotton in white, dark blue and pink. The warp is of white cotton, varied by a regular occasional thread of dark blue. The weft is of white cotton, with occasional bands of pink. Along the selvedge edges the cloth has been left white, but short supplementary lines in pink have been woven in from the borders on either side; these abut two long broad lines of dark blue along the length of the cloth. The central field so defined is occupied by six bands of supplementary weft decoration, placed between seven bands of lines in pink and blue. Four of the six bands have geometric shapes of stars and rectangles; the main two bands have patterns referred to as ikaki (tortoise) motifs. The unwoven warp ends have been twisted to form a fringe of tassels.;
Curators Comments:
A detail of this cloth is reproduced by Lisa Aronson, ‘Akwete Weaving: Tradition and Change’, in B.Engelbrecht & Bernhard Gardi (eds), 'Man Does Not Go Naked; Textilien und Handwerk aus afrikanischen und anderen Ländern', Basel, 1989, p.39, fig.5, where it is stated to have been collected in 1880. There is no evidence for this date, and it is most unlikely. Beving began working as an a trader around 1880 and died in 1913: hence the date range given on the BM records for many of his cloths is 1880-1913. This can, however, be narrowed with great probability to the years 1900-1913, when he had become a calico printer, and moved from trading into production. It was to provide ideas for potential designs that he formed large study collections in the early 1900s. His indigo cloths from Senegal and Nigeria can be securely dated to these years, and his large group of Akwete cloths most probably does as well. It speaks for the high reputation that the Akwete weavers had already gained in the trade that Beving thought it worth acquiring such a large collection of their work. (AVG); Illustrated in Picton & Mack, 1989, with the following caption:
'Detail of a cotton textile, Igbo, Nigeria. A single piece of cloth, woven on the upright single-heddle loom by a woman at the southern Igbo village of Akwete, of imported machine-spun yarn with supplementary weft float patterns.'
See comment on Akwete cloths on Af1934,0307.104. The ikaki motifs derive from those commonly in use in Ijebu Ode.
Bib references: Picton & Mack 1989 / African Textiles
Exhibition history:

Description: Man’s gown (boubou, tobe, riga), hand-woven from hand-spun white/cream cotton. The body is formed of 82 narrow strips hand-sewn together along the selvedges vertically, while the sleeves are sewn horizontally. A large pocket is added at the front. The gown is hand-embroidered in white in the ‘two knives’ (aska biyu) pattern. The two knives and the area around the neck are embroidered with European thread onto a cotton base that has been couched down onto the tunic. Other areas are embroidered in cotton with chain and buttonhole eyelet stitching forming diamonds, squares and loops; there are large spirals on both the front and the back of the robe. The gown is unlined, and the sleeves of the garment are sewn with a hem; the neck and bottom are not.;
Curators Comments:
Charles Beving Collection Label: ' Gown made from strips woven on a very narrow loom with native looms. Embroidered with white European thread round neck. Unlined neck hole is sewn up and garment may never have been worn.'
This is a typical work made by the Hausa and Nupe in northern Nigeria. White gowns, patterned with white against white, were prestigious in Muslim societies. See Bernhard Gardi, ‘Le Boubou – c'est chic, les boubous du Mali et d’autres pays de l’Afrique de l’Ouest’, Basle, 2nd ed. 2002, p.68-77. For three other white gowns in the Beving collection, see Af1934,0307.208, 211 and 212.
The 1934 register records (from the donor's label) that the neckhole is sewn up, and the garment may never have been worn. Dr Duncan Clarke suggests that this may indicate that it was intended to be used as a shroud for burial with the body.

Description: Woman’s wrapper (aso oke) formed of 10 identical strips each 11.9cm wide, hand-woven and hand-sewn together along the selvages. The design is entirely warp-faced and in white and two shades of indigo cotton. Each strip has two main areas, one with a wide dark blue stripe flanked by two narrower lighter blue stripes edged with white, and a second area with alternating thin white and light blue lines. The weft is of the darker shade of indigo. All the cotton is handspun, and the ends have sewn hems.;
Curators Comments: Af1934,0307.149 to 161 in the Beving collection is a group of Yoruba blue and white women’s wrappers, either narrow-strip aso oke woven by men, or two-panel cloths of women’s weave. The label supplied by C.A.Beving suggested that these are 'probably European yarns', but this seems unlikely.

Description: Shawl, formed of a single loom width, and hand-woven in balanced weave using European industrial cotton. The warp consists of numerous narrow stripes of coloured threads in white, green, yellow, blue, red, and brown. The wefts also consists of numerous narrow stripes in white and green; there are also three triple bands of openwork that extend from one edge across about a quarter of the width of the cloth. The crossing of warp and weft and the colours employed create a checked design that imitates imported Indian Madras cloth.;
Curators Comments:
The 1934 register records in the section of ‘Observations’ that this cloth has ‘coloured and white yarn imported from Europe’ and that it is ‘probably southern Nigeria’.
Dr Duncan Clarke thinks that the use of openwork suggests that it is probably a Yoruba cloth, although he adds that the colour combination is unlike any other he has seen. If it were blue and white it would obviously be classified as Yoruba.

Description: Woman’s wrapper (aso oke) composed of 10 narrow strips of uniform width, hand-sewn together along the selvages. All the thread is handspun, and the cotton is locally dyed. The strips fall into two groups of completely different patterns, which alternate across the cloth. The design of the first group of five strips is entirely warp-faced, and is predominantly composed of magenta (alaari) silk; the alaari is broken up by three sets of narrow lines of white, green and yellow cotton. The second group of strips is weft-faced with a uniform narrow check pattern of indigo and white cotton formed by the crossing of the blue and white threads of the warp and weft: the indigo in the weft is sometimes replaced by lines or bands of white cotton. Over this background are floated complex supplementary weft designs of horned animals, Koran boards, and geometric shapes (none of which are visible on the verso) in magenta ‘alaari’ thread or in green cotton. The warp ends of the strips which have weft designs are twisted into short tassels, the others being left unhemmed.;
Curators Comments: This cloth is recorded in the acquisition register as ‘probably Ilorin’. It is reproduced by Venice Lamb & Judy Holmes, ‘Nigerian Weaving’, 1980, p.54, where it is described as a ‘Gandere cloth from Ilorin’. Dr Duncan Clarke points out that such figurative or anthropomorphic weft float motifs are rarely seen in Yoruba weaving at this period, and became associated with Ilorin in later years.

Description: Woman’s wrapper or shawl composed of six virtually identical wide weft-faced strips 20 cm wide, hand-spun and hand-sewn together along the selvages. Each strip has a warp of white cotton. The weft is primarily of magenta silk (alaari), while indigo-dyed cotton is used to create various patterns, either of bands (of which there are six where the indigo is bordered by lines of white cotton) or alternating lines of indigo and white. In addition to these, there are five bands of discontinuous supplementary weft of indigo cotton: the outer pair are geometric, the inner pair have Koran boards, and the central band has lizards. All the thread is handspun; the white warp ends have short fringes.;
Curators Comments:
The 1934 acquisition register records the cloth as coming from the ‘Nupe district … cost pre-War 6/-’ (six shillings). The cloth however is not characteristic of known Nupe weaving, though it could well come from some unknown sub-area in that country or have been imported from further afield.
Lamb & Holmes, in 'Nigerian Weaving', 1980, p.154 ill.222, described this cloth as an ‘old Jukun kyadze cloth’. It is, however, unlike most Jukun textiles. 
See Duncan Clarke in ‘African Textiles’ 2002, no.133 where this cloth is illustrated. He reports the traditional attribution to the Jukun, and notes that although the alternating weft pattern of white and blue can be paralleled in early Jukun cloths, the overall effect is very different, and the effect more similar to some early Yoruba cloths -  though the float motifs of lizards and Koran boards cannot. There are other early Nigerian cloths composed of six wide strips which are equally obscure in their origin, and the problem has yet to be investigated properly. He dates the cloth to the XIXc.

Object type: gown (object name); textile (object name); tobe (object name)
Description: Man’s gown (boubou, tobe, riga), hand-woven from hand-spun cotton dyed indigo. The body is formed of 141 narrow strips hand-sewn together along the selvedges vertically, while the sleeves are sewn horizontally. The body of the gown is rectangular in shape, while the sleeves flare out being wider at the top than at the bottom. At the front is sewn a square pocket. The gown is hand-embroidered in a different blue cotton thread in the ‘two knives’ (aska biyu) pattern around the neck and pocket. There are small spirals on the front and back of the garment. There is a hand-sewn hem around the neck and sleeves.;
Curators Comments:
The label of C.A.Beving reads :"Nigeria: Mohammedan garment worn by Haussa native. Made from strips of cloth woven on a very narrow loom and dyed indigo. Embroidery around neck. The whole garment appears as if it had been finally dyed as a whole." This is glossed by the 1934 register: ‘the whole cloth appears to have been dyed when finished; it is of a uniform shade of indigo’. This is very probably correct. Dr Duncan Clarke observes that cloths of this kind were primarily made for the Tuareg and pastoral Fulani. They were made of white thread, and were dyed indigo after the embroidery was completed.
For comment on African gowns in the Beving collection, see Af1934,0307.199.

Object type: gown (object name); textile (object name); tobe (object name)
Description: Man’s gown (boubou, tobe, riga). The body is formed of 161 uniform strips, hand-woven and hand-sewn together along the selvedges; the strips are uniform and use indigo-dyed cotton in both warp and weft, with lines of white cotton inserted frequently and regularly in both warp and weft to create a checked appearance of a blue/grey colour (known as ‘saki’ by the Hausa’ and ‘etu’ by the Yoruba). The body of the cloth is not shaped, while the sleeves are wider at the top than the bottom and as a result fan out. At the front is sewn a large pocket. The pocket, shoulder and front are hand-embroidered in white European cotton in a very large rectangle that extends beyond the pocket. The embroidery is in chain and buttonhole eyelet stitch, and in the ‘eight knives’ (aska takwas) pattern; there is a large spiral at the front and another on the back. The knives themselves are embroidered on top of extra pieces of cloth that have been cut to shape. The tunic is unlined and unhemmed except around the neck and sleeves.;
Curators Comments:
Illustrated in Picton & Mack 1989, p.192: the caption reads:
'Cotton embroidered gown, Hausa, but woven of Nupe cloth, Nigeria.' This gown is embroidered with an expanded form of the 'eight knives' pattern' (cf Af1920,0211.1 for an earlier version). This is a gown from Nigeria of very high quality. The strips are certainly Nupe work. The embroidery is as likely to be Nupe as Hausa.
For comment on African gowns in the Beving collection, see Af1934,0307.199.

Curators Comments: This is a complicated 'aso oke' Nigerian cloth with stips of four different patterns. The rpesence of alaari silk in one of the strips elevates it into a higher level of cost and distinction.

Description: Tunic ("riga yaki" in Hausa language) formed of cotton strips one inch wide sewn together, and covered on both sides with Islamic decorations and painted inscriptions and patterns (such as prayers, Qur'anic inscriptions, 99 Beautiful Names of God, magic squares and amuletic motifs). 51 leather-covered amulets have been sewn to the inside of the upper part of the tunic.;
Curators Comments:
Reproduced in John Picton and John Mack, 'African Textiles', BM 1989, p.164 with the following caption: 'Cotton tunic, probably from northern Nigeria, The drawn inscriptions are derived from Koranic texts. Small leather charm cases which probably also contain extracts from the Koran, are attached to the inside of the garment.' On p.163 they describe the process of making a cloth of this type that was commissioned by David Heathcote in 1971 from a Hausa craftsman.; (LaGamma and C. Giuntini, 2008)
‘Every inch of this simple cotton tunic was inscribed and invested with prayers by an itinerant Hausa artist who sought to transform it into a mantle of invulnerability. The extraordinary measures taken suggest that the garment was made for an important warrior to wear into battle. The Islamic belief in the power of the Koran’s written word is manifested here in a creation configured so its Koranic texts encase the body, affording a line of mystical defence superior to armour’ (LaGamma and C. Giuntini, 2008. The Essential Art of African Textiles: Design Without End. The Metropolitan Museum of Art: New York).; Captain Fuller was a collector and must have acquired this tunic on the London market with no provenance. The acquisition register records this as a 'Jibbeh' and from 'West Sudan?'. Later H.J.Braunholz added 'N.Nigeria?'

Description: Man’s gown (boubou, tobe, riga) of hand-spun white and indigo cotton. The body is formed of 56 narrow strips hand-woven and hand-sewn together along the selvedges vertically, while the sleeves are sewn horizontally. The body of the gown is rectangular in shape, while the sleeves are wider at the top than the bottom and therefore fan out along the top. A large pocket is sewn onto the front. All the strips have the same design of indigo cotton crossed in both warp and weft by lines of white cotton that form a narrow check (etu). The front of the cloth is embroidered by hand in white European cotton in the ‘eight knives’ (aska takwas) pattern. The areas showing the knives are embroidered on other pieces of cloth, which were then couched down; the rest of the decoration is embroidered directly on the strips in chain and buttonhole eyelet stitching, with knots, spirals and other interlaced patterns; there is also a second small spiral on the back. The gown is unlined, and has been hemmed around the neck and sleeves.;
Curators Comments:
The label of C.A.Beving reads: ' made from strips of cloth woven on a narrow loom, with European yarns, the blue probably native dyed. Embroidered with white European thread around the neck.' Despite this remark, the yarn in the body of the gown seems to be native-spun and dyed in indigo; the white yarn used in the embroidery might be imported from Europe.
For a similar Hausa gown but of inferior quality, see Af1934,0307.203. For comment on African gowns in the Beving collection, see Af1934,0307.199.

Description: Woman’s wrapper (aso oke) composed of 10 identical hand-woven narrow strips each 11.3cm wide, hand-sewn together along the selvages. Each strip is designed with seven stripes of warp-faced pattern arranged symmetrically: the two outermost stripes are of very dark indigo through which run three or four thin white lines; within these are three stripes of magenta (alaari) silk, which are separated by two stripes of white cotton that have been ikat-dyed with a lighter shade of indigo. The weft appears to be of white cotton. All the thread is handspun, and the weft ends have not been hemmed.;
Curators Comments:
For Yoruba men's weave, see comment on Af1934,0307.129.
The stitching that joins the strips is barely visible: the pattern has been designed with considerable sophistication so that the indigo stripe continues without a break across the strips. The place of acquisition is recorded in the acquisition Register (taken from the original Beving Collection label) as Abeokuta, a Yoruba city on the far west of Nigeria, and this information must come from Beving’s records. The town is not known to have been a weaving centre, but the cloth may very easily have been purchased there.
The following description of this cloth by Alice LaGamma and Christine Giuntini is taken from the 2008 Metropolitan Museum of Art exhibition catalogue, ‘The essential art of African textiles’, cat.10: ‘The stripes that alternate blue and white were created by a method of resist-dying yarns before they are woven that is widely known as ikat. To carry out this technique, the exact amount of warp yarn needed for the ikat-patterned areas must be measured out, held taut, and secured so that it will not shift during subsequent steps in the process. The sections that are to remain white are tightly wrapped and tied in order to resist the dye; then the prepared yarns are dipped in indigo until they reach the desired intensity and allowed to dry before the binding strings are removed. These fibres are then placed onto the loom with other yarns in the order defined by the pattern. The richly-blended magenta and indigo design of this cloth is composed from ten strips of hand-spun silk and cotton. Each contains the same sequence of stripes: a broad indigo and white pinstripe alongside an alternation of solid magenta stripes with blue-and-white ikat ones. Despite the regular repetition, however, no two of the ikat-patterned elements are perfectly aligned, and this asymmetry creates a sense of infinite variation.’

Description: Cloth (woman’s weave), a single warp-faced width, using European machine-spun cotton in white, dark blue, pink, yellow and red. It is hand-woven in a pattern formed by 17 bands of weft decoration: five bands are of parallel coloured stripes, two bands have repeating diamond shapes, two bands have three large coloured blocks set against a dark blue background, and eight bands consist of five or six supplementary weft float motifs set against a dark blue background. At the warp ends is a fringe of twisted warp threads.;
Curators Comments:
The 23 cloths, Af1934,0307.104 to 126, were all woven in Akwete, the town to the east of Port Harcourt in the Igbo area in the Niger delta. It became in the late XIXc, and remains today, the centre of weaving a new class of single-panel cloths on a much wider vertical woman’s loom than had been customary in Africa. The cloths share a common feature in that they all splay out to become wider at one end than at the other. In Akwete they are said to have been pioneered by a lady named Dada Nwakata. She must be credited with the invention of what was a new category of cloth in Africa which has proven highly successful. The designs were derived from patterns that were in fashion in other centres (among them Ijebu Ode), but show considerable originality. They make use of the wide range of colours supplied by European machine-spun and industrially dyed threads. 
The group of 23 Akwete cloths in the Beving collection must be dated between 1900 and 1913 (see comment on Af1934,0307.115), and it is the largest and best known such early collection. Another early collection is in Liverpool. There are other Akwete cloths in the BM collection, a total of some 50 in all.

Acq notes (acq): The Wellcome Historical Medical Museum (WHMM) deposited 1300 cases of cases of ethnographic material at the Museum in 1949. The Museum was given first choice of objects and advised on the other dispersals. Material was distributed in ten batches from 1949 to 1954. The BM selected over 10,000 objects, but not all were intended for registration [see ‘Annual report for the Department of Ethnography for the year 1954’, by A Digby. June 1955; Central Archive]. The transfer was formally recorded as a donation from the WHMM in 1954. Sir Henry Wellcome acquired much of his collection through auction houses (eg. Christie’s, Sotheby’s, Glendining). Some material was also purchased directly from collectors or exhibitions (eg. 1924 Wembley British Empire Exhibition).

Description: Box made of wood, cylindrical, and entirely covered with white cowries, strings of which also hang from the openings in the cover. [An ori container];
Dimensions: 73.00 centimetres a+b ;  42.80 centimetres a ;  36.00 centimetres b ;  44.50 centimetres a ;  55.00 centimetres b ;  38.30 centimetres a ;  53.00 centimetres b ;
Curators Comments:
Slip records: "The Adamu Oresha, or worship of Eleda, the genii of the head, is sometimes very elaborate. The box of white cowries is the sacred emblem. The cover is intended to represent a crown for the head. The whole is placed before a great chief at his councils, or when entertaining guests kolah-nuts are placed in the upper part for the refreshment of guests. (Mr Justice Smalman Smith in the 'Handbook to West African Court' (Col. & Ind. Exh. 1886), p.20."
ADD This is the first such Ori container to be acquired for the British Museum. For a more recent account, see Anthony Jack, ‘Africa, relics of the colonial era’, London, 1991 p.34: "In Yoruba culture a man’s head is regarded as the essence of his personality, character and destiny – a divine gift which should be honoured. As a symbolic representation, and as an object of reverence, a stylised crown was made and kept inside a container or coffer of more elaborate form. Both were heavily decorated with cowrie shells, which as currency represented prestige and wealth. On the death of the owner, the small image and its coffer were usually destroyed and the cowries recycled as money."

Description: Cloth (itagbe, made for the Oshogbo/Ogboni society) woven from handspun white cotton used in both warp and weft. The cloth is rough on one side, this being created using 'shag' (shaki) in the supplementary weft. It is undecorated with the exception of two stripes of indigo supplementary weft at either end of the cloth. The two ends have been woven to form nine triangular points bound together with indigo thread just before the final termination with a pompom.;
Curators Comments:
The slip has a comment: 'Shaki or cloth upon which the Edan (no.2) is carried by Oshogbo messenger'. Added by W B Fagg: 'Ijebu-Ode cloth?'. This is confirmed both by the provenance and by the points into which the ends have been bound. See comment on 2018,2036.106.
'King Docemo of Lagos' is Dosunmu (c.1823-86), Oba of Lagos from 1853. It was he who ceded Lagos to Britain in 1861.

Description: Gelede mask made of coloured wood in the form of a head with figures on top.;
Curators Comments:
Slip records the entry from the 1886 exhibition catalogue: "Lagos No.515. One Gelede mask used in plays." The pair of masks are attributed by the Drewals to Ota, capital of the Awori Yoruba, which was the source of carvings for much of the Lagos area. See 'Yoruba, nine centuries of African Art and Thought’, Centre for African Art New York, 1989, p.227. It is there suggested that it might have been carved by the father of Olabimtan Odunlami.
This mask is typical of those representing hierarchy, with three figural elements arranged one on top of another. See H.M. Cole (ed.), 'I am not myself: the art of ma', Los Angeles monograph series, no. 26 (Museum of Cultural History, University of California, 1985).

Description: Man’s gown (tobe, boubou, riga saki). The body is formed from 125 narrow uniform strips, hand-woven and hand-sewn together along the selvedges. The strips are uniform and use indigo-dyed cotton in both warp and weft, with lines of white cotton inserted frequently and regularly in both warp and weft to create a checked appearance of a blue/grey colour (known as ‘saki’ by the Hausa’ and ‘etu’ by the Yoruba). The body of the cloth is not shaped, while the sleeves are wider at the top than the bottom and as a result fan out. At the front is sewn a large pocket that occupies a quarter of the front of the gown. The pocket, shoulder and front are hand-embroidered in white European cotton in a very large rectangle that extends beyond the pocket. The embroidery is in chain and buttonhole eyelet stitch, and in the ‘eight knives’ (aska takwas) pattern; there is a large spiral at the front and another on the back. The knives themselves are embroidered on top of extra pieces of cloth that have been cut to shape. The tunic is unlined and unhemmed except around the neck and sleeves.;
Curators Comments:
This ‘riga saki’ tobe is described on pp.407-8 of Freeman’s book, 'Travels and life in Ashanti and Jaman' (1898) though without stating that he owned the garment or giving any clue as to where he acquired it, though it was certainly during his years in West Africa, 1887-91. This must be one of the earliest such careful descriptions of the Hausa ‘riga’, of which this is a very fine specimen.
‘The characteristic garment of the Mohammedan men is what is called by the Europeans a ‘tobe’ and by the Hausas a ‘riga’. This is a wide-sleeved gown of ample proportions and varying length, reaching in some cases barely to the knees and in others nearly to the ankles. Among the poorer classes it often forms the only garment, but generally it is supplemented by loose drawers or ‘wondo’. Complete as this garment looks when it is being worn, it is not so great an advance on the simple country cloth or ‘ntama’ as it at first appears, for in its simplest form it is nothing more than a square of cloth with a hole in the centre and the corners sewn together. Nevertheless, it is an extremely handsome garment even when quite simple in material and design, and the long vertical folds that drop from the shoulder impart to the wearer, especially if he be a tall man of good bearing, a dignified and even commanding aspect. It is seldom, however, that the tobe is left quite without ornament: usually it is decorated with a kind of embroidery the colour of which depends upon that of the cloth on which it is worked, and its elaborateness upon the value of the material. The most highly prized material is a cotton cloth of a dark bluish grey speckled with white, the speckles running in narrow lines, which is known among the Arabs as ‘filfil’ or pepper, and by the Hausas as ‘riga saki’. Tobes made of this cloth are generally very handsomely embroidered in white, the greatest amount of ornamentation being bestowed upon the immense pocket that occupies the whole of the left breast and often extends nearly to the bottom of the gown. When the material of the tobe is white, the embroidery is generally of a dark buff or light brown colour ….The scheme of colour is as a rule extremely severe and restrained … the finest fabrics of the northern cities present a plain ground of creamy white or some quiet neutral shade, upon which a few pots of brilliant colour are introduced with great judgement and severity of taste, and with a very fine effect.’
For another similar ‘riga saki’, which has a larger area of embroidery and is perhaps ten or twenty years later, see Af1934,0307.215. The strips are certainly Nupe work. The embroidery is as likely to be Nupe as Hausa. See the article by Judith Perani, ‘The cloth connection: patrons and producers of Hausa and Nupe prestige strip-weave’, in ‘History, design and craft in West African strip-woven cloth’, Smithsonian Institute Washington, 1982, pp.95-112.

Description: Commemorative head; lost-wax cast in brass. In form of human head, hollow with opening in top.  Three raised  scarification marks above eyes. Openwork coral bead cap  decorated with additional large beads; single bead at front over forehead.  Strands of beads and braids at sides of face and at back. Deep  coral bead collar over chin to below mouth. Flanged base with various symbols in low relief.;
Curators Comments:
Trustees Committee minutes, 8 July 1961 and Special Report by Adrian Digby, 26 June 1961 record : 'The tusk [Af1961,09.2] is probably of the nineteenth century, and the head was almost certainly cast in1888 when Oba Adolo died and his son, Ovonramwen, on his accession, set up an altar in his memory. '; Heads of ths late type show the exaggerated choker of coral beads and complex coral headdress worn by the king of Benin on ceremonial occasions. The latter is said to recall the ada sword that symbolises the right to take human life. Around the base are depictions of leopards, rams' heads and other manifestations of power.
(Label text: Man and Metal in Ancient Nigeria, 1991).; See Collection File: Af1961,09.1-2.; Register 1961:
'Brass casting of a head, aperture at top,  circular flange at base ornamented with various animals and objects.
BENIN- probably made in 1888, taken at the Benin Expedition, of 1897.'

Acq notes (acq):
Af1928,0711.9 to 23 is a group of raffia and cotton cloths. The register records that they were all 'bought in the market at Lagos, acquired in 1889-1894'. The date is certain as Sir Robert Johnstone was only in Africa in those years. Although all bought in Lagos, they do not form a uniform group. 9 is a mat and stands apart. 10 and 11 are also somewhat different. 12 to 19 go closely together, and are a mixture of raffia and cotton. 20 to 22 are quite different. The function of the single strips is uncertain – they may be baby-ties.
Dr Duncan Clarke comments that all of this group from 10 to 23 are most likely to be Yoruba, although it is entirely possible that some come from other peoples along the Niger and were brought to the market in Lagos.

Description:
Cloth (wrapper) composed of 10 hand-woven strips of cotton, hand-sewn together along the selvedges. The cotton threads used are a mixture of imported European industrial thread (see for example in the yellow), handspun local cotton (see for example in the indigo blue), and imported magenta alaari silk. There are three different patterns of strip arranged in the following order: 1,2,3,1,2,3,2,1,3,2.
1. Grey, blue, pink, yellow and white warps and blue and white wefts. This combination is used to create a series of coloured warp stripes which are crossed at regular intervals by groups of white weft stripes.
2. Pink, yellow and grey warps and blue wefts. This combination is used to create alternating stripes of pink and yellow/grey.
3. White and pink warps and wefts. This combination is used to create a pink warp stripe flanked by two white stripes, which are crossed at regular intervals by groups of pink weft stripes.
The warp ends have been cut but not hemmed.;
Curators Comments: Dr Duncan Clarke thinks that this must be an unusual early variety of Yoruba aso oke cloth.

Description: Cloth (perhaps a baby-tie): a single width, hand-woven from raffia of a single shade of brown, and imported European machine-spun cotton. The warp is formed primarily of raffia, but on one side of the cloth strips of white cotton have been run through the raffia, and there are two places in which there are groups of stripe formed from red and yellow cotton. Description:
Photograph [black and white] view of a seated man wearing a cloak and crown. On the right is a younger man wearing a formal Westernised jacket with a watch chain and holding a hat. On the left is a woman wearing a Western-style crinoline dress with her left hand on the shoulder of the seated man, and holding a fan. Calabar, Nigeria. 
Albumen print;
Inscription: Inscription type: annotation Inscription position: Underneath the image in the album Inscription language: English Inscription quoted: Creek Town King Eyo Honesty 7th, Old Calabar, Nov 16th 1890;
Curators Comments:
There appears to be writing on the back of the photograph that is fainlty visible, however this photograph is stuck down in the album and is thus inaccessible.
This album belonged to Minnie Gunn, her name is inscribed in pencil at the beginning of the album; she was the elder sister of Livingston Daniel Gunn, a distinguished long-term trader in West Africa.
The following information was provided by Donald Gunn (deceased), a nephew of Minnie Gunn (courtesy of Robert Gunn who donated the album).
On Wednesday 18th July 1881, just past his 18th birthday, Livingston left England from Liverpool, sailing on the SS Angola, to work for Hatton and Cookson at Cabenda (also spelt Kabinda),  a small Portuguese enclave, and now a province of Angola. Livingston Daniel was always known to his family as Livy, which distinguished him from his father who was also named Livingston.
In a long and affectionate letter to his father dated a week after his arrival Livy gave an account of the voyage describing: “bullock carts in Funchal, flying fish, porpoises, sharks, whales, Kroo boys and some coral”, which he bought for Minnie with comments on Cape Coast Castle and Sir Garnet Wolsey’s exploits in the Ashanti War. Livy arrived in Cabinda on 13 August 1881. No further details from surviving letters came to light before he went home at the end of his tour in 1887.
Before Minnie died, she jotted down some pencil  notes about Livy’s tour of duty and leaves in England:
July 1881- end of 1887 – Cabinda for Hatton and Cookson
March 1888-89 – Ambriz for Millingtons
January 1890- February 1895 – Niger
October 1895- November 1905 – Division Agent for the Royal Niger Company
March 1906 – 18 May 1910 – Onitsha, Niger.
The album dates from 1891, Minnie would have been around 27/28 years old, and visually documents the period in which Livy was working in the Niger Delta. Presumably Livy was sending photographs back home to Minnie and advising her on the subject matter which she used to annotate the album. The 1891 census shows that she was living with her father Livingston, who was a widower (aged 65) and Minnie was a Ladies Attendant in the Theatre. She also lived with one of her brothers George H Gunn.
Livy and Minnie’s father Livingston died in April 1895 and Minnie left the house they had lived in since 1891 at 36 Filey Street, Sheffield and took a 3 year lease of 12 Hanover Square on 20th August 1895 at £25pa.
Livy continued to work in Nigeria and had a relationship with a local Nigerian woman named Ma Agubi, and they had a daughter together.
Livy was taken ill in 1910 in Minvukor(?)  and  got himself to Oguta, about 40 miles down the tributary of the Niger from Onitsha. A Dr E. W. Graham went by open launch to Oguta to bring him to Onitsha hospital but on the journey they were caught in a tropical storm and Livy was drenched when already very ill. He died a few days later on 19th May 1910. The doctor in Abo had diagnosed liver abscess now thought to have been amoebic but Dr Graham decided that we was too ill, with double pneumonia, to be examined. Donald Gunn notes that had he gone to hospital as soon as he felt ill he might just possibly have survived. But Livy sent a message for medicine with instructions not to reveal his identity.
Livy seems to have spoken to Dr Graham of giving up Africa and retiring as he could have in comfort. He was just short of 47 years old when he died.
Minnie received many letters of regret and sympathy from Nigeria including one from the Governor of South Nigeria, Sir Walter Egerton and one from the Provincial Commissioner Central Province. Dr Graham wrote that all departments were represented at the funeral including the White Fathers- Roman Catholics. Someone who had known him and worked under him for 16 years wrote “a  kinder and more considerate Divisional Agent it would be impossible to meet”…I believe he could talk in no less than seven native dialects, knew their customs used to swear in juju with them and went where no other white man has been amongst them”
Inscribed on Livingston’s grave in Accra: “20 years in the service of the Niger Company by whom this monument is erected”.
Minnie Gunn died in 1947 in Middlesex.
This information is a précis of a typed account from Donald Gunn, a nephew of Minnie and Livy. The account includes some scanned photographs, which include a picture of Livy aged about 18; a photograph of Ma Agubi; Old Calabar Christmas 1893 and Livingstone’s grave in Accra.

Description: Ceramic group of figures on a stand, made of pottery. In the centre is a man holding a drinking-horn in his left hand and a fan in his right, both signs of his status. Either side of him are two pregnant women, probably his wives, with elaborate hairstyles and scarification, and holding fans, the right-hand one holding a child. Seated in front is a servant or child with a gong and a fowl, possibly a sacrifice for the yam deity, Ifejioku; and a brazier.;
Curators Comments:
Illustrated in Nigel Barley, ‘Smashing Pots’, BMP 1994, p.137, with a commentary:
The vessel was made for the altars of the yam deity, Ifijioku, probably in the late XIXc. The central male figure represents a chieftain with signs of status such as a hat, fan and carved elephant tusk. Over one shoulder he wears a manilla, the currency of the area and thus a sign of wealth. The women on either side are heavily scarified and sport elaborate hairstyles. The one on his left is pregnant. The one on his right is suckling a child. Before them sits an attendant with a gong and an altar of the hand by which a notable may gain good fortune. The top of the chicken is a removable lid. Decoration of possessions and the body with lined patterns such as those on the front of the vessel (known popularly as ichi lines) is a traditional mark of high standing.; Register 1951:
Pottery group on a stand, consisting of a chieftain in the centre, holding a fan & horn; a wife on either side, holding fans;  the right-hand witfe holding a child, the other having a seated attendant figure in front holing a gong.  On the ground in front are a fowl and a brazier.
Addition by W B Fagg: "Group of figures, 'ifijioku', used in the yam cult among the KWALE IBO of OSISA village, (probably OGBE ISELE quarter) & representing a family group of consisting of a chief with the 2 wives & an attendant figure."
See Herbert M Cole & Chike Aniankor, 'Igbo Arts, Community and Cosmos', Hearst Museum UCLA 1984, p.80 where Cole reproduces this work, and states (for reasons that are unclear) that it had been collected in 1880. For a similar statement of date see Frank Willlett, 'African Art, an introduction', London 1971, p.93, where another similar vessel, now returned from Britain to Lagos, is reproduced.
Malcolm McLeod and John Mack, 'Ethnic Sculpture', BMP 1985, p.29:
Such elaboration of pottery is almost always indicative of an exceptional function. Pots of his type were made among the western Ibo for a cult connected with the growing of yams, a staple food. The figures represent family heads, their wives and attendants.; A similar example of an Osisa pot was shown in Tom Phillips (ed), ‘Africa, the art of a continent’, Royal Academy 1995, cat.5.54 with a text by Herbert Cole, who states that only a handful of such ceramics are known and that these were collected in the late 19th century – the tradition does not seem to have lasted into the 20th century. This group rises out of a hollow ceramic base with a textured surface; at the back it is attached to a kind of openwork screen with several decorative loops.
"Around the late nineteenth and early twentieth century, the Igbo people of southern Nigeria made clay altars or shrines with a number of figures. The main crop of the Igbo was yam, and these altars were used at the new yam harvest festival to help produce good harvests and to emphasize the importance of the family in Igbo society. In this region, as in most of sub-Saharan Africa, the potters are women. Normally only men are permitted to make representational and naturalistic figures. However, the creator of this piece was probably a post-menopausal woman who was perceived by society as having relinquished her female status."

Description: Woman's ceremonial wrapper; two panels of women's weave hand-sewn together at seams. Combination of white, dark and medium indigo-dyed hand spun cotton and alaari (magenta silk) stripes. Fine white cotton weft stripes. Embroidered in alaari (magenta silk) and three shades of indigo-dyed cotton in repeated patterns of zigzag clusters. Hand-sewn seams at both ends.;
Curators Comments:
The embroidery added to this cloth is exceptional, and has been associated with the cult of Shango by Duncan Clarke, who has commented as follows on his blog:
Amongst the Yoruba and other Nigerian peoples embroidery was not a domestic pastime but a professional skill exercised by full or part-time male craftsmen, most if not all of whom were Muslim. Perhaps as a result, the technique was applied only in specific contexts, notably in the decoration of male ceremonial robes and trousers. Recognised patterns were handed on from one generation to the next,often in Koranic schools, and although designs could be modified over time and novel variations introduced, these took place within an established repertoire and context. This repertoire was based to a large extent on Islamic inspired motifs shared, with local variants, across a wide area of West Africa.
In addition to its intrinsic beauty, this cloth is notable as an exceptional example of Yoruba embroidery in an unexpected context and in an otherwise unfamiliar style. As this is the only known example to date we cannot know whether it represents a unique and idiosyncratic innovation or whether its use was once more widespread.
The cloth is a woman’s ceremonial wrapper cloth, woven by a woman weaver using a vertical single heddle loom, in two panels joined horizontally at the centre. It is woven from quite fine hand spun indigo dyed cotton and pink, probably cochineal dyed, silk from the trans-Saharan caravan trade. Comparison with related cloths in museum collections, and the use of silk, allow it to be dated to around the end of the nineteenth century or the early years of the twentieth. Quite unusually for this type of cloth the use of a repeated pattern of stripes in the weft, partially but not entirely hidden by the predominance of the warp, allows for a subtle check effect in the paler blue areas. The use of silk, along with the sophistication of the weaving and the fineness of the thread, reveals that this was a prestige piece commissioned at considerable expense for the use of a high status patron.
The embroidery uses the same pink silk as the ground cloth, along with three shades of indigo dyed cotton, and is in the form of repeated clusters of zigzags of various lengths. The layout of the embroidery contrasts in colour with the background, and the placement seems most focussed on the area of the cloth that would be visible in use. The similarity in the colours chosen, in particular the rather unusual shade of pink, suggests the embroidery was done quite soon after the cloth was woven.
Why might a wealthy Yoruba woman at the turn of the nineteenth century choose to have zigzags woven on her expensive wrapper cloth ? We can only speculate based on the association of zigzag designs in other contexts in Yoruba visual culture. Sculptures called anarugba Sango show a bowl supported by a cluster of figures, dominated by a female devotee. They formed part of the cult paraphernalia of the Yoruba orisa (deity), Shango, god of thunder and lightning, and some have contained the collection of Neolithic stone axe heads that were believed to be the physical embodiment of thunderbolts. The zigzag designs that were painted on both the bowl and the female figure depict the power of Shango in its manifestation as thunder and lightning.
Condition: Fiar; damage to supplementary patterns. Silk damaged in places.

Livy arrived in Cabinda on 13 August 1881. No further details from surviving letters came to light before he went home at the end of his tour in 1887.

July 1881- end of 1887 – Cabinda for Hatton and Cookson
March 1888-89 – Ambriz for Millingtons
January 1890- February 1895 – Niger
October 1895- November 1905 – Division Agent for the Royal Niger Company
March 1906 – 18 May 1910 – Onitsha, Niger.
The album dates from 1891, Minnie would have been around 27/28 years old, and visually documents the period in which Livy was working in the Niger Delta. Presumably Livy was sending photographs back home to Minnie and advising her on the subject matter which she used to annotate the album. The 1891 census shows that she was living with her father Livingston, who was a widower (aged 65) and Minnie was a Ladies Attendant in the Theatre. She also lived with one of her brothers George H Gunn.
Livy and Minnie’s father Livingston died in April 1895 and Minnie left the house they had lived in since 1891 at 36 Filey Street, Sheffield and took a 3 year lease of 12 Hanover Square on 20th August 1895 at £25pa.
Livy continued to work in Nigeria and had a relationship with a local Nigerian woman named Ma Agubi, and they had a daughter together.
Livy was taken ill in 1910 in Minvukor(?)  and  got himself to Oguta, about 40 miles down the tributary of the Niger from Onitsha. A Dr E. W. Graham went by open launch to Oguta to bring him to Onitsha hospital but on the journey they were caught in a tropical storm and Livy was drenched when already very ill. He died a few days later on 19th May 1910. The doctor in Abo had diagnosed liver abscess now thought to have been amoebic but Dr Graham decided that we was too ill, with double pneumonia, to be examined. Donald Gunn notes that had he gone to hospital as soon as he felt ill he might just possibly have survived. But Livy sent a message for medicine with instructions not to reveal his identity.

Dr Graham wrote that all departments were represented at the funeral including the White Fathers- Roman Catholics. Someone who had known him and worked under him for 16 years wrote “a  kinder and more considerate Divisional Agent it would be impossible to meet”…I believe he could talk in no less than seven native dialects, knew their customs used to swear in juju with them and went where no other white man has been amongst them”
Inscribed on Livingston’s grave in Accra: “20 years in the service of the Niger Company by whom this monument is erected”.
Minnie Gunn died in 1947 in Middlesex.

Description: Cloth (Oshogbo society aso olona title wrapper) formed of four panels, hand-woven (woman's weave) and then hand-sewn together. The white thread is locally hand-spun, while the green, pink, yellow and blue threads are of imported European manufacture. The warp is primarily of white cotton, but through this are run single green threads that have been used to hold in place the supplementary weft threads. The ground weft is of white cotton, and over this are run supplementary weft bundles of pink, yellow and dark blue threads (only visible on the front of the cloth), held in place by the green warp threads. The supplementary weft is arranged in nine bands, with a continuous line framing either end of the cloth. The pattern is the same on all four panels, and all the bands, with the exception of the central one, are based on animal figures. The loose warp ends have been twisted into tassels.;
Curators Comments: This Ijebu cloth is perhaps later than Af1966,01.25, but is certainly an early example. See comment on Af1966,01.25, and for the type see comment on 2018,2036.106.

Description: Cloth; two panels of women's weave hand-sewn together at seams. Combination of white, indigo-dyed cotton and alaari (magenta silk) stripes. Supplementary weft float patterns in alaari (magenta silk) and indigo-dyed cotton. Hand-sewn seams at both ends.;
Technique: plain weave; dyed; sewn; supplementary weft
Curators Comments:
Although this two-panel cloth belongs within the category of Yoruba women's weaving, its complex style with koran boards and bands of alternately placed red and blue blocks, places it apart from the main tradition. As yet it is the only known complete cloth of this type, and its place of manufacture has yet to be determined.
Duncan Clarke comments on the extremely complicated design as follows. Each of the two panels is divided warpwise by three narrow magenta silk and white cotton warp stripes, creating four broad bands that mimic the effect of narrow strip cloth. Each of these bands is broken up by four sets of supplementary weft float patterning in local indigo dyed cotton and magenta knitting wool (of European origian, imported via the coastal trade). Blue and white threads are alternated in the warp to create a lined effect across the cloth, while blocks of white cotton, indigo cotton, and magenta silk are used for the weft.
Condition: Fiar; damage to supplementary patterns. Silk damaged in places.

Description: Garment; five wide strips, hand-sewn together at seams. Combination of white and indigo-dyed hand spun cotton and alaari (magenta silk) warp and weft stripes. Hand-sewn hems at both ends.;
Curators Comments:
(information from Duncan Clarke)
Four very similar cloths of this type have so far been recorded. One is in the Princeton University Art Museum; another is in the collection of Karun Thakar: see ‘African Textiles, the Karun Thakar collection’, Prestel 2015, p.121, where it is speculated that the chequered pattern was influenced by imported cloths from India. All four were collected in the Yoruba speaking region, and if they are Yoruba they may have been made in the Ilorin area. It is also possible that they are from further north and are Nupe in origin. There is some evidence that strip width varied more widely during the XIXc than in the XXc when the 4 inch (10 centimetre) standard became the norm. All the thread is handspun, and the cloth is very fine and and light in weight.
One strip of this cloth had been detached, probably so that it could be used as a separate head-tie, but it has recently been resewn by a tailor in Ghana.
Condition: Fiar; damage to supplementary patterns. Silk damaged in places.

Description: Man's gown. Rectangular, rounded neckline, two front slit pockets. Embroidered around openings in natural-coloured ?cotton. Tunic composed of repeating narrow strips (aso oke) sewn together. Warp stripes in dark indigo-dyed and white cotton and alaari (magenta silk), with alaari weft stripe. Embroidered with repeating knot designs in white cotton on front and back.;
Curators Comments:
The following comment has been supplied by Duncan Clarke: 
The unique feature of this classic late XIXc Yoruba robe is the cloth from which it was tailored. One of the most prestigious and expensive patterns of Yoruba aso oke strip weave was dark indigo hand spun cotton with a very fine check pattern of lighter blue or white cotton. This pattern was called etu, meaning "guineafowl" after the bird's speckled plumage. Etu, for those with a deep understanding of Yoruba cultural tradition, formed one of a triumuvirate of prestige textiles, along with local wild silk sanyan, and magenta silk, called alaari, that was imported across the Sahara to northern Nigeria from the XIXc until the start of the XXc. Sometimes the fine check of etu was changed to a larger check, then called petuje, which can be roughly translated as "surpasses etu". This robe is the only example I have seen where expensive alaari silk has been used to form a large check petuje pattern that was used to tailor a man's robe. 
The robe is sewn by hand throughout, and is decorated with well-executed hand embroidery in a classical Yoruba style, using the Yoruba knot motif 'pako' (literally 'chewing stick').
Bib references: Lamb & Holmes 1980 / Nigerian Weaving
Condition: Good.

Description:
Photograph [black and white] view of in the foreground seven children bent forwards; the children in the centre are holding brushes and those on the left and rights are holding adzes. Behind them are a line of eight seated men. This group is observed by a large group of seated and standing men and women, some of whom wear indigenous clothing and others wear Westernised clothing and uniforms. The scene takes places in front of a long thatched building. Calabar, Nigeria. 
Albumen print;
Inscription: Inscription type: annotation Inscription position: Underneath the image in the album Inscription language: English Inscription quoted: Chief Effiom’s House. Dance Palaver;
Curators Comments:
This album belonged to Minnie Gunn, her name is inscribed in pencil at the beginning of the album; she was the elder sister of Livingston Daniel Gunn, a distinguished long-term trader in West Africa.
The following information was provided by Donald Gunn (deceased), a nephew of Minnie Gunn (courtesy of Robert Gunn who donated the album).
On Wednesday 18th July 1881, just past his 18th birthday, Livingston left England from Liverpool, sailing on the SS Angola, to work for Hatton and Cookson at Cabenda (also spelt Kabinda),  a small Portuguese enclave, and now a province of Angola. Livingston Daniel was always known to his family as Livy, which distinguished him from his father who was also named Livingston.
In a long and affectionate letter to his father dated a week after his arrival Livy gave an account of the voyage describing: “bullock carts in Funchal, flying fish, porpoises, sharks, whales, Kroo boys and some coral”, which he bought for Minnie with comments on Cape Coast Castle and Sir Garnet Wolsey’s exploits in the Ashanti War. Livy arrived in Cabinda on 13 August 1881. No further details from surviving letters came to light before he went home at the end of his tour in 1887.
Before Minnie died, she jotted down some pencil  notes about Livy’s tour of duty and leaves in England:
July 1881- end of 1887 – Cabinda for Hatton and Cookson
March 1888-89 – Ambriz for Millingtons
January 1890- February 1895 – Niger
October 1895- November 1905 – Division Agent for the Royal Niger Company
March 1906 – 18 May 1910 – Onitsha, Niger.
The album dates from 1891, Minnie would have been around 27/28 years old, and visually documents the period in which Livy was working in the Niger Delta. Presumably Livy was sending photographs back home to Minnie and advising her on the subject matter which she used to annotate the album. The 1891 census shows that she was living with her father Livingston, who was a widower (aged 65) and Minnie was a Ladies Attendant in the Theatre. She also lived with one of her brothers George H Gunn.
Livy and Minnie’s father Livingston died in April 1895 and Minnie left the house they had lived in since 1891 at 36 Filey Street, Sheffield and took a 3 year lease of 12 Hanover Square on 20th August 1895 at £25pa.
Livy continued to work in Nigeria and had a relationship with a local Nigerian woman named Ma Agubi, and they had a daughter together.
Livy was taken ill in 1910 in Minvukor(?)  and  got himself to Oguta, about 40 miles down the tributary of the Niger from Onitsha. A Dr E. W. Graham went by open launch to Oguta to bring him to Onitsha hospital but on the journey they were caught in a tropical storm and Livy was drenched when already very ill. He died a few days later on 19th May 1910. The doctor in Abo had diagnosed liver abscess now thought to have been amoebic but Dr Graham decided that we was too ill, with double pneumonia, to be examined. Donald Gunn notes that had he gone to hospital as soon as he felt ill he might just possibly have survived. But Livy sent a message for medicine with instructions not to reveal his identity.
Livy seems to have spoken to Dr Graham of giving up Africa and retiring as he could have in comfort. He was just short of 47 years old when he died.
Minnie received many letters of regret and sympathy from Nigeria including one from the Governor of South Nigeria, Sir Walter Egerton and one from the Provincial Commissioner Central Province. Dr Graham wrote that all departments were represented at the funeral including the White Fathers- Roman Catholics. Someone who had known him and worked under him for 16 years wrote “a  kinder and more considerate Divisional Agent it would be impossible to meet”…I believe he could talk in no less than seven native dialects, knew their customs used to swear in juju with them and went where no other white man has been amongst them”
Inscribed on Livingston’s grave in Accra: “20 years in the service of the Niger Company by whom this monument is erected”.
Minnie Gunn died in 1947 in Middlesex.
This information is a précis of a typed account from Donald Gunn, a nephew of Minnie and Livy. The account includes some scanned photographs, which include a picture of Livy aged about 18; a photograph of Ma Agubi; Old Calabar Christmas 1893 and Livingstone’s grave in Accra.

Description: Cloth (aso-oke); woman's wrap-around garment. Warp-faced weave. Composed of fourteen strips, hand sewn together. Repeating warp strips in indigo-dyed and white cotton and magenta silk (alaari). Narrow white cotton weft stripes. Hand-sewn hems at both ends.;
Curators Comments:
(Comment supplied by Duncan Clarke)
This cloth is called an iro, and would have been worn as a wrap-around skirt by a wealthy Yoruba lady on an important occasion such as a wedding or a chieftaincy ceremony. It would have formed part of a set of cloths woven in the same pattern, along with two or three smaller pieces worn as shawl, head-tie, and sometimes a hip cloth. The quality of the indigo dyeing is exceptional. Very dark, almost black, indigo dyed strip weave cloth was prestigious and expensive because of the high number of immersions in the dye required to achieve that colour. When patterned as a fine check or plaid of lighter blue or white threads, it was known as etu, or guinea fowl, after the speckled plumage of the bird. In the Yoruba aso oke tradition etu formed part of a threefold classification of high status cloths along with magenta silk alaari obtained from the trans-Sahana caravan trade network, and local beige wild silk called sanyan. The three threads used in this cloth, indigo 'etu', silk alaari, and white cotton, are all handspun.
Condition: Good; some loose stitching along seams.

Curators Comments:
The original account of their origin is most unlikely. The donor was a London-based surgeon and collector, who had nothing to do with the Benin expedition.
 The figures were later identified as northern Yoruba ibeji figures by W B Fagg.

Acq name (previous): Donated by: Sir John Bland-Sutton, 1st Baronet

Description: Figure carved in wood with a central ridge on the head, squared shoulders and arms outstretched.;
Curators Comments:
Recorded on acquisition as "Aro plains, Cross River Nigeria". With a later note added by W B Fagg: "probably from Langtang, near Pankshin, Yergum tribe, northern Nigeria. cf five figures in possession of Miss Jane Drew, 1951". 
See Ethdoc 416 - Jane B Drew FRIBA, Accra/W Fagg, 28 Aug. 1951 enclosing notes on Yergum Idols made by Rev. W L Broadbent, Langtang, from a tract published in 1907.  Mr Fagg has noted that 'Miss Drew's 5 figures - apparently those collected by the Rev. W L Broadbent - are in the same style as 1923-15'.

Description: Head tie (gele). Composed of four narrow (aso oke) strips, hand-sewn together. Alternating warp strips: indigo-dyed cotton with fine white cotton stripes; and indigo-dyed and white cotton check with supplementary weft float patterns in alaari (magenta silk). Description: Pottery vessel with a row of figures beneath the lip.;
Curators Comments:
Reproduced in William Fagg & Margaret Plass, ‘African Sculpture, an anthology’, Dutton Vista (London) 1964, p.139: “Between Benin and the Niger live certain western Igbo groups, and among them the Kwale Igbo formerly practised a form of pottery sculpture of considerable merit, if not of great material strength. Fragments of this style can still be found in the village of Osisa, but the existing complete examples seem to have come to England in the 1880s. They were made for the cult of the Yam Spirit, Ifijioku, and whereas most of them are freestanding groups representing the family making sacrifices to the spirit, they include this pot with smaller figures under the lip. This is among the most humanistic (though not naturalistic) of African arts.”
The caption for this piece in William Fagg and John Picton, 'The Potter's Art in Africa', The British Museum, 1970  states: "Pot for the cult of the Yam Spirit, Ifijioku, at Osisa, an Ibo village north of Aboh on the west bank of the lower Niger,  Nigeria; collected there about 1880.  19in (48cm)"
Acq notes (acq): Acquisition details unknown.

Description: Standing male figure wearing top hat made of wood. Facial scarification. Painted with white spots on dark brown surface.;
Curators Comments:
Text from William Fagg, ‘The Tribal Image’, BMP, 1977, no.22
This figure was collected by John Main, an engineer stationed in the Niger Delta between 1891 and 1901, and was presented in in 1952 by his son. There is no documentation to show what the figure represents. The top hat suggests a chief, but could simply be a way of doing honour to a familiar or protective spirit. The styles of the western and eastern Ijo prescribed so precisely what figures and masks should look like as to leave little room for individual variations, but there is always room for the subtler forms of artistry.
Also reproduced in William Fagg & Margaret Plass, ‘African Sculpture, an anthology’, Dutton Vista (London) 1964, p.97. It “probably represents a ‘spirit companion’ shown as a chief, to judge by the European hat, of a type which was quickly adopted as a status symbol of chieftainship or civic importance by the Nigerian coastal tribes in the early nineteenth century.”

Description: Cloth (perhaps a sash or waist-cloth), a single width of woman’s weave, using entirely hand-spun thread. The design is warp-faced, and consists of wide stripes of magenta alaari thread, through which are run six narrow stripes of indigo which alternate between two shades. The warp ends have been twisted to form a fringe of tassels.;
Curators Comments: This luxury cloth, using almost entirely expensive silk alaari thread, was presumably used for display as a sash or waist-cloth. John Picton catalogued it as Yoruba work with a question mark: this seems more likely than that it was made by the Nupe or Hausa.
