Description: Cloth (aso-oke); woman's headtie (gele). Warp-faced weave. Composed of twelve narrow strips, hand sewn together. Two repeating warp stripe patterns: magenta silk (alaari) and white cotton; and white cotton and indigo-dyed cotton ikat strip. Hand-sewn hems at both ends.;
Curators Comments: This cloth originally formed part of a set of three identically-patterned cloths. It was the smallest, and so must have been intended as the head-tie. The other two were also sold by Dr Duncan Clarke and were seen by the donors who were not able to afford to acquire them at the time. They would have been used as a waist-wrapper and as a second cloth to wrap on the upper half of the body.; Both male and female Yoruba weavers use the ikat technique in their cloths. Warp threads are tie- dyed before weaving to give characteristic fluctuating light and dark colours.
Condition: Good.

Description:
Photograph [black and white] view of a European man in white uniform and pith helmet standing behind a group of twenty-four seated and kneeling African men wearing uniforms and white hats.  Five sets of stacked guns are behind the group and a set of drums are located centre front. The groups are situated on sand and in the background is a wooded environment with a thatched hut. Curators Comments:
George F. Annesley was appointed Vice-Consul in 1890. The role of a vice-consul was to cultivate and maintain friendly relations with the indigenous people, opening up roads and markets and generally preserving peace and order in their respective areas. They were also responsible for the proper working of the Customs, Postal and Treasury Departments in their areas of jurisdiction.

July 1881- end of 1887 – Cabinda for Hatton and Cookson
March 1888-89 – Ambriz for Millingtons
January 1890- February 1895 – Niger
October 1895- November 1905 – Division Agent for the Royal Niger Company
March 1906 – 18 May 1910 – Onitsha, Niger.
The album dates from 1891, Minnie would have been around 27/28 years old, and visually documents the period in which Livy was working in the Niger Delta. Presumably Livy was sending photographs back home to Minnie and advising her on the subject matter which she used to annotate the album. The 1891 census shows that she was living with her father Livingston, who was a widower (aged 65) and Minnie was a Ladies Attendant in the Theatre. She also lived with one of her brothers George H Gunn.

Graham went by open launch to Oguta to bring him to Onitsha hospital but on the journey they were caught in a tropical storm and Livy was drenched when already very ill. Description: Cloth; two panels of women's weave hand-sewn together at seams. Alternating warp strips: white and indigo-dyed hand spun cotton stripes with supplementary weft float patterns in alaari (magenta silk); and plain alaari (magenta silk) stripes. Hand-sewn seams at both ends.;
Technique: plain weave; dyed; sewn; supplementary weft
Curators Comments: This cloth imitates the type of weft patterns found in Yoruba men's weaving of the same period. Because it is of two panels, rather than the 12 strips that would have been employed in men's weave, the float motifs are aligned precisely across each of the two panels in a way that would not be found in men's weave. Both the cotton thread and the alaari are hand-spun. This is an  exceptional cloth and unlike anything so far published from any collection and more elaborate than any yet seen on the market.
Condition: Fiar; damage to supplementary patterns. Silk damaged in places.

Description: Cloth made of a single width of raffia fibre. The warp threads have been left as fringes at both ends. One end only is decorated with narrow bands formed of supplementary white cotton thread; this same end also has a single line of supplementary dark brown-dyed raffia thread inserted under and over the warp threads immediately before the fringe.;
Curators Comments:
WA slip reads: "Africa West. Long scarf of finely woven grass cloth, fringed at both ends."
The WA [West Africa] series was put together in ca.1877 (the date found on some of the slips) and included newly arrived textiles as well as earlier acquisitions. 
This cloth appears at first sight to come from the Congo, but the bands of supplementary weft in cotton and raffia are uncharacteristic of that part of Africa. It is perhaps an example of a local Nigerian weaving tradition that did not last to the end of the XIXc.
Condition: Poor; split along central fold. Grubby and stained throughout. Small pin holes along one edge.
Acq notes (acq): Acquisition details unknown.

Description: Shawl; two panels of women's weave hand-sewn together. Composed of combination of white, pink-dyed cotton and ?alaari (magenta silk) warp stripes. Some supplementary weft float patterning in pink ?cotton. Woven holes. Fringes braided at both ends.;
Technique: plain weave; dyed; sewn; supplementary weft; braided
Curators Comments:
There are two colours of ped/pink in this cloth. The best guess is that the darker magenta colour is alaari silk imported across the Sahara, while the lighter pink is a local imitation madder dye which has now faded. The braided ends show that this cloth was designed to be used as a shawl. 
A very similar cloth was lot 74 in the sale of textiles from the collection of Lord (Alistair) McAlpine at Sotheby's Olympia 7 June 2006.
Condition: Fiar; damage to supplementary patterns. Silk damaged in places.

Description: Cloth; three panels of women's weave hand-sewn together at seams. Combination of white, dark and light indigo-dyed cotton and alaari (magenta silk) warp stripes. Hidden white cotton weft stripes. Hand-sewn seams at both ends.;
Curators Comments: A worn and fragile cloth. Typically cloths of women's weave are formed of two panels, and were intended for use as wrappers for women. This three-panel cloth is much larger and must have been intended to be worn by a man toga-style. Yoruba cloths, whether of aso oke or women's weave, intended for the use of men are unusual. By the late XIXc Yoruba men seem to have adopted the tobe or boubou of Muslim origin as their preferred garment.
Condition: Fiar; damage to supplementary patterns. Silk damaged in places.
Acq name (acq): Donated through: Antony Griffiths (Cultural Gifts Scheme)

Description: Cloth (aso oke), formed of seven narrow strips about 4 inches wide of hand-spun and hand-woven cotton, which have been sewn together along the selvedges by machine. The strips are of two patterns that have been arranged alternately across the cloth. Four have warp threads of dark indigo, through which single lines of a lighter indigo have been run at regular intervals. The other three have a purely white ground thread in both warp and weft; over this are run supplementary weft bundles of magenta alaari silk (only on the front of the cloth), held in place by warp threads some 50mm apart. The alaari patterns are the same in each strip (though sometimes arranged in a different sequence), and are primarily geometric though some are recognizable as Koran boards. The warp ends have been hemmed by machine.;
Curators Comments: This is a classic example of Yoruba aso oke weaving of a type that was made c.1900 (compare Af1900,-.37 to 41, given by Dr Coker Adams in 1900.) The acquisition register has a comment by John Picton that it came from Ilorin. This was most probably based on the general understanding that such complicated weft-float compositions were primarily made there. The strips would have been hand-sewn together originally, and the machine sewing is a later replacement or repair.

Before Minnie died, she jotted down some pencil  notes about Livy’s tour of duty and leaves in England:
July 1881- end of 1887 – Cabinda for Hatton and Cookson
March 1888-89 – Ambriz for Millingtons
January 1890- February 1895 – Niger
October 1895- November 1905 – Division Agent for the Royal Niger Company
March 1906 – 18 May 1910 – Onitsha, Niger.
The album dates from 1891, Minnie would have been around 27/28 years old, and visually documents the period in which Livy was working in the Niger Delta. Presumably Livy was sending photographs back home to Minnie and advising her on the subject matter which she used to annotate the album. The 1891 census shows that she was living with her father Livingston, who was a widower (aged 65) and Minnie was a Ladies Attendant in the Theatre. She also lived with one of her brothers George H Gunn.
Livy and Minnie’s father Livingston died in April 1895 and Minnie left the house they had lived in since 1891 at 36 Filey Street, Sheffield and took a 3 year lease of 12 Hanover Square on 20th August 1895 at £25pa.
Livy continued to work in Nigeria and had a relationship with a local Nigerian woman named Ma Agubi, and they had a daughter together.
Livy was taken ill in 1910 in Minvukor(?)  and  got himself to Oguta, about 40 miles down the tributary of the Niger from Onitsha. A Dr E. W. Graham went by open launch to Oguta to bring him to Onitsha hospital but on the journey they were caught in a tropical storm and Livy was drenched when already very ill. He died a few days later on 19th May 1910. The doctor in Abo had diagnosed liver abscess now thought to have been amoebic but Dr Graham decided that we was too ill, with double pneumonia, to be examined. Donald Gunn notes that had he gone to hospital as soon as he felt ill he might just possibly have survived. But Livy sent a message for medicine with instructions not to reveal his identity.
Livy seems to have spoken to Dr Graham of giving up Africa and retiring as he could have in comfort. He was just short of 47 years old when he died.
Minnie received many letters of regret and sympathy from Nigeria including one from the Governor of South Nigeria, Sir Walter Egerton and one from the Provincial Commissioner Central Province. Dr Graham wrote that all departments were represented at the funeral including the White Fathers- Roman Catholics. Someone who had known him and worked under him for 16 years wrote “a  kinder and more considerate Divisional Agent it would be impossible to meet”…I believe he could talk in no less than seven native dialects, knew their customs used to swear in juju with them and went where no other white man has been amongst them”
Inscribed on Livingston’s grave in Accra: “20 years in the service of the Niger Company by whom this monument is erected”.
Minnie Gunn died in 1947 in Middlesex.
This information is a précis of a typed account from Donald Gunn, a nephew of Minnie and Livy. The account includes some scanned photographs, which include a picture of Livy aged about 18; a photograph of Ma Agubi; Old Calabar Christmas 1893 and Livingstone’s grave in Accra.

Description: Garment; two panel cloth of women's weave, hand-sewn together at seams. Alternating warp strips: white sanyan (wild silk) and sanyan (beige silk) warp stripes. White hand spun cotton weft. Rows of openwork holes between triple alaari (magenta silk) supplementary weft float stripes. Hand-sewn hems at both ends.;
Curators Comments: This and the previous cloth (2018,2036.89) belong to a group of Nigerian two-panel cloths of women's weave of which the origin is uncertain. They are probably Yoruba, but stand apart from the main tradition. A similar cloth is illustrated by Venice Lamb and Judy Holmes, 'Nigerian Weaving', 1980, pl.300, where it is captioned "a very old pure silk Yoruba cloth." Duncan Clarke has seen three other cloths of this type. The warp is local beige and white wild silk sanyan, the weft white hand spun cotton, while the design alternates rows of openwork holes with threefold lines of supplementary weft float woven from thick loosely spun magenta silk from the trans-Saharan trade. On this cloth loose fibres from the magenta silk have spread onto adjacent beige and white fibres in places, creating an appearance similar to slight colour bleeding.

Description: Cloth: seven narrow weft-faced strips of hand-spun and hand-woven cotton, hand-sewn together along the selvedges. The warp is of white cotton, while the weft uses white, purple and indigo cotton to form complex bands of design across the cloth. At each end of the cloth there are stripes of plain blue, purple and white cotton. One end of the cloth retains its original finish and warp ends; the other end has (almost certainly later) been hemmed.;
Curators Comments:
The acquisition register has a comment that in this and the previous cloth (Af1952,16.22), the mauve dye was probably derived from the leaves of the guinea-corn when red; this produces a mauve colour. An alternative explanation (which requires re-examination of the cloth) is that the purple/mauve is alaari dyed silk.
According to Dr Duncan Clarke, this cloth belongs to a small group of unstudied weft-faced Nigerian cloths of which some other examples are in the BM (see Af1934,0307.133 and 2018,2036.130 - from Ogori). Although looking at first glance like a cloth from Mali, it is certainly Nigerian, but it is not from Ogori. It belongs to some more widespread tradition, but its origins cannot be more closely determined at present.

Description:
Photograph [black and white] view of a group of women. Two of the women stand at the back and are wearing cloth aprons. The figure on the right carries a rectangular wooden box on her shoulder containing a pot and a calabash. The two women in the centre of the composition are seated and facing each other with their hands wrapped around the neck of a large pot; they are wearing waist belts made of bells and beaded necklaces. The two women at the front of the composition are in a semi-reclined position and are wearing waist belts made of bells, brass leg ornaments and beaded necklaces. Bonny, Nigeria.
Albumen print;
Inscription: Inscription type: maker's mark Inscription position: reverse of photograph Inscription language: English Inscription quoted: J.A.Green Artist Photographer Bonny, Opobo, &c, &c.;
Curators Comments:
A similar photograph entitled “Bonny Girls” is held at the Eliot Elisofon Photographic Archives, National Museum pf African Art, Smithsonian Institution, Nigerian Photographic Album, EEPA 2000-003-0058. Dated before 1900.
Anderson and Aronson (2017) propose that this photograph represents “a rite performed in conjunction with iria, but the contrived composition suggests that Green recruited the young women to pose for him. A British curator named Richard Quick published it in a 1900 article in the Reliquary and Illustrated Archaeologist. The photo, mislabelled “Benin Girls” occupies most of the second page, but Quick makes little account of it, saying only that “marriageable girls of Benin City wear an apron consisting entirely of brass bells” (p:224).
The composition of the photograph is interesting because of the positioning and postures of the women, and has been compared to “the type of trophy display that ethnographers, as well as big-game hunters, favoured at the time” (Anderson and Aronson, 2017:225). Jonathan Green emulated European modes of photography but as Anderson and Aronson (2017) observe “he may have been drawing on other sources, including layouts favoured by illustrated journals. “Bonny Girls” is the only known photo in which employs the trope of the reclining nude – or semi-nude - female….the unnatural posture calls attention to the women’ lack of clothing but it also conforms to Green’s preference for symmetry, as noted by Aronson, in the majority of his group portraits”(p.225).

Description: Cloth: two panels of hand-spun cotton, hand-woven and hand-sewn together along the selvedges. The design is warp-faced, and consists of stripes of cotton, either white or dyed to two different shades of indigo. The weft is of the lighter shade of indigo cotton. The two panels have the same design, but are of somewhat different lengths and widths. The warp ends have been twisted to form a fringe.;
Curators Comments:
This is one of five cloths (Af1952,26.19 to 23) among a collection of 44 objects made by the father of the donor, William Main (qv), 'mainly between 1891 and 1901, in southern Nigeria' (so the acquisition register for 1952). The register suggests (with a question mark) that this comes from northern Nigeria. It is however characteristic Yoruba work of woman's weave. 
The varying loom width and length is often found in early cloths woven by Yoruba women. It is a consequence of the fact that the panels were separately woven and with a varying loom tension.

Curators Comments:
A similar photograph entitled “Marriage Ceremony (women winding thread)” is held at the Eliot Elisofon Photographic Archives, National Museum of African Art, Smithsonian Institution, Nigerian Photographic Album, EEPA 2000-003-0009. Dated before 1903.
Author, Gertie de S. Webster in her 1903 article in the English Illustrated Magazine did not publish the photo but provides an explanation for such local “marriage” customs:
“After a due amount of vocal, instrumental, and gastronomic demonstrations they [the brides] repair to the spot selected for the necessary formalities, where it is discovered a slave holding a skein of wool. The Brides then become seated, the bridegroom remaining standing, while the skein of wool is slowly unwound, at the conclusion of which ceremony they are legally man and wives, their vows being supposed to have been bound up in the ball of wool!” (Anderson, 2017:225)

Original Description: "Mahomedan Mosque Lagos" [manuscript note on album paper].;
Curators Comments:
The Shitta-Bey Mosque, located at Martins Ereko Street in Lagos, was built in 1892 and is one of the oldest mosques in Nigeria. It was funded by philanthropist and businessman Mohammed Shitta Bey, who was the son of Sierra Leonean parents of Yoruba descent. The mosque was built in the Afro-Brazilian architectural style by a Brazilian architect, Joao Baptisa da Costa, assisted by a Nigerian builder, Sanusi Aka, at a reported cost of £3,000.  It was designated a National monument by the Nigerian Commission for Museums and Monuments in 2013.; The mosque is likely to have been built by Yoruba slave traders who had come back from south America. (N F Barley, 04/06/1996.)

Description: Cloth (Akwete cloth): two fragments reassembled from the same cloth, but still incomplete with less than half the cloth remaining. The cloth is hand-woven from imported European thread. The ground weave is formed of blue cotton warps and wefts. The textile is patterened with supplementary wefts in yellow, red, pink, green and white cotton, which are used to create geometric shapes, oblongs and chevrons being the most prominent. The remaining warp end has been twisted to form tassels.;
Curators Comments: The acquisition register records that Af1952,20.52 to 54 were joined together to make a curtain. The correct observation was added that they were all 'Akwete cloths from Ibo-Ijaw country, S.E.Nigeria'.
Acq notes (acq): Af1952,20.1 to 142 were collected by Sir Raymond Menendez during the years he spent in West Africa between 1894 and 1908. There is no record of when or where he acquired the objects, and the provenances have been supplied by BM curators.

Description:

Leather saddle-bag, of brown leather, with embroidery in leather, coarse white cotton, and inset triangles of green leather.  With large flap tucked inside.;
Curators Comments: Nos.76-79 are all registered as from north Nigeria. But Menendez worked in Lagos, and there is evidence of leather work among the Yoruba in P Amaury Talbot, 'Peoples of Southern Nigeria', 1926, II p.938: "Leather work is scarce [in southern Nigeria] except among the Yoruba, many of whom show considerable skill in the making of bags, saddlery, sheaths, cushions, sandals etc. Black, white, green and yellow are the principal colours used. The most usual skin employed is that of goats, but quite good fans are made by Edo from cowhide, which are much like an ancient Egyptian type. The Bantu often make bags out of Colobus monkey skins."
Acq notes (acq): Af1952,20.1 to 142 were collected by Sir Raymond Menendez, Chief Justice of Nigeria, who worked in Nigeria between 1894 and 1908, and were given to the BM by his widow.

Description: Cloth (Akwete cloth), a single width of hand-woven cloth using imported European thread. The warp is a mixture of blue and red, as is the ground weft. There are a large number of patterns inserted in supplementary weft using thread of red, white/beige, yellow and green. The warp ends have been twisted to form tassels.;
Curators Comments:
Register 1952 entry: 'Cotton woven cloth, woven on a broad loom, indigo with red warp lines, brocaded with red, white, green, buff & yellow in bands of patterns.' The register records that
Af1952,20.52 to 54 were joined together to make a curtain. The correct observation was added that they were all 'Akwete cloths from Ibo-Ijaw country, S.E.Nigeria'.
Acq notes (acq): Af1952,20.1 to 142 were collected by Sir Raymond Menendez during the years he spent in West Africa between 1894 and 1908. There is no record of when or where he acquired the objects, and the provenances have been supplied by BM curators.

Description:
Photograph [black and white] view of a group of a dozen children in various postures and groupings; behind on the left is a wooden canoe and they stand in front of tropical vegetation. Bonny, Nigeria. 
Albumen print.;
Inscription: Inscription type: maker's mark Inscription position: reverse of photograph Inscription language: English Inscription quoted: J.A.Green Artist Photographer Bonny, Opobo, &c, &c.;
Curators Comments:
A similar photograph from the National Museums of Liverpool is part of the Howie Album.
This is one of two portraits of children that were taken by Green on Christmas Day in 1894. This one shows them barely dressed, but the accompanying photograph depicts the same children “wearing European attire, apparently to suggest before and after views of ‘civilisation’“(Aronson, 2017:93 and fig. 3.8). This photograph was subsequently printed in a collotype postcard format.
Bib references: Anderson and Aronson 2017 / African Photographer J.A.Green: reimagining the Indigenous and the Colonial

Description: Cloth, perhaps a baby tie; hand-woven in plain weave from imported European white and red cotton. The cloth is warp-faced with narrow stripes of red cotton interrupting the white; the weft is entirely of white cotton. The warp ends have been twisted to form a fringe.;
Dimensions: 155.50 centimetres;  29.50 centimetres at the widest point ;
Curators Comments: The three cloths Af1952,20.44 to 46 are closely related and must have been acquired as a group together. The 1952 register observed that they were 'probably Nupe', and this suggestion was followed by Venice Lamb & Judy Holmes in their 'Nigerian Weaving', 1980, where the three cloths are illustrated on p.236. An alternative suggestion is that they are Hausa.
Acq notes (acq): Af1952,20.1 to 142 were collected by Sir Raymond Menendez during the years he spent in Africa between 1894 and 1908. There is no record of when or where he acquired the objects, and the provenances have been supplied by BM curators.

Description: Saddle-cloth (with fringe) made of leather.;
Curators Comments:
See the letter dated 19 May 1922 from Claude Beddington to T A Joyce. "In the year 1899 I brought back from Kumasi, Ashanti, two of King Prempeh's war drums which had been given to me by the then Chief Commissioner, Sir Donald Stewart. Should they be of interest to you, I should be glad to give them to the Museum. In the same year I also brought back from Ashanti a collection of leather Hausa work articles, beautifully worked bridle, saddle bags etc. which I should also be glad to give to the Museum if they would be of any interest." He was visited by Braunholtz and the gift was accepted. 
The drums must have come from the Ashanti campaign of 1895-6. If he returned to England in 1899, the Hausa leatherwork must have been bought in Asante or northern Nigeria (it is not certain which) around 1895-99, when he is known to have been in Africa.
Acq notes (acq): Af1922,0608.1 to 17 were given by Colonel Claude Beddington, who had acquired them between 1895-99. Nos.1 to 14 are Hausa work. Nos.15 and 16 come from Kumasi.

Photograph (black and white), from an album; view of a chief and his wives.  All wear traditional Bonny attire, and the women wear bracelets, necklaces, earrings, and have elaborately styled hair.  A row of children are seated on the ground in front of the adults. Bonny
Albumen print.;
Inscription:
Inscription type: annotation Inscription quoted: Album Title: "1st BENIN. WARRI. & SAPELE. 2nd NEW CALABAR. BONNY. OPOBO & QUA COUNTRY." [manuscript note on album paper].
Original Description: "Capt Hart & wives." [manuscript note on album paper]; "Abbey Hart & his wives (a large Bonny Chief)" [manuscript note on back of print]; "J. A. Green, Artist Photographer, Bonny, Opobo, &c., &c." [stamp on back of print].;
Curators Comments:
At least 12 of Green's photographs feature a chief surrounded by his wives, sisters, children and slaves - indicating his status. As Anderson and Aronson (2017) state " Positioning of figures, as well as displays of women's adornments, communicates the chief's standing - particularly in relation to the women and children in his household - in Green's group portrait of Chief Orugne Abbey Hart. The most important woman of the household, either a wife or sister, sits next to the head of the household. Those of lower status, such as the wives of slaves are always in the back row, and children - most particularly, the potential heir(s) to the throne - are always seated on the ground in front (p:140); Albums Af,A46 and Af,A47 were originally in one album containing 176 photographs.

Main themes of album: Views of indigenous and European settlements, trading stations, roads, and Christian cemeteries. Portraits of European and indigenous people.

Description:
Photograph (black and white), from an album; view of the rear of a colonial style building. Some men farming in field in foreground. Corrugated iron sheds beside fenced trees in middle-ground. Akwete
Albumen print.;
Inscription:
Inscription type: annotation Inscription quoted: Album Title: "1st BENIN. WARRI. & SAPELE. 2nd NEW CALABAR. BONNY. OPOBO & QUA COUNTRY." [manuscript note on album paper].

Curators Comments:
This building served as a trade station in Akwete during the 1890s. The building was moved in the 1990s to its present location in Aba, Abia State, and is now the Museum of Colonial History. Its collection consists of objects relating to the colonial period in Nigeria and the country’s path to nationhood, old Nigerian money and relics of the slave trade era.; Akwete, a town in Abia state, Nigeria, is located 18 km northeast of Port Harcourt and 18 Kkm southeast of the commercial city of Aba. Akwete is known in West Africa for its unique weaving.

Photograph (black and white), view of group of African men wearing light-coloured short and shirts and rounded hats, holding a large log above their heads in order to demolish a house. A white man wearing a pith helmet and smoking a pipe looks on. Benin, Nigeria
Silver gelatin print;

Description:
Photograph (black and white/sepia); image of brass relief plaque (Ama) from Benin City, Nigeria. Single figure wearing coral bead regaila. Crocodile heads in each corner. River leaf background design.
Photographic process.;
Inscription: Inscription type: annotation Inscription position: reverse of photograph Inscription language: English Inscription quoted: 17 Inscription note: Handwritten in pencil.;
Curators Comments:
During the British expedition to Benin City (Edo) in 1897 objects made of brass, ivory, coral, and wood were looted from the royal palace, its storerooms, and compounds. Some of these objects subsequently passed as official 'spoils of war' to the British Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs. Among this loot were 304 brass relief plaques that were lent to the British Museum and displayed in the Assyrian Saloon in September 1897. Subsequently, the Museum petitioned successfully for the acquisition of 203 of these plaques that were donated to the Museum by the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs and were accessioned into the collection in January 1898. A further 11 plaques were added to the original list and of these remaining 112 plaques, 14 were sold to UK museums, 50 were sold to German museums, 39 were sold to a private dealer, Miss Eva Cutter, 8 were retained by the Foreign Office and 1 was unrecorded. Description: Wooden headpiece in the form of a human head and neck with painted crest, coloured black and white.;
Curators Comments:
The register records an old label: "Wooden headpiece worn by Benin warriors. About 20 of these were found lying about in the bush after a sharp attack at Gwato ... 4.1.97".
Reproduced by Frank Willlett, 'African Art, an introduction', London 1971, p.105: 'This mask is one of seven which were used in the cult of the water spirit Igbile at Ughoton (Gwatto), the old port of Benin. They were brought out to invoke the help of Igbile against the Punitive Expedition of 1897. Their style appears to be derived from that of the Western Ijo of the Niger Delta, via the Ilaje Yoruba, for the songs used in the cult are in the Ilaje dialect.'
Acq notes (acq): acquired by Beasley 20.1.1937

Description:
Register 1956:
Wood carving representing a massive quadruped with gaping mouth, surmounted by a top-hatted human figure which is supported by two smaller figures; heavy wood painted black.;
Curators Comments:
Register 1956 note by W B Fagg:
Probably from the western IJO, S.NIGERIA.
Reproduced by Frank Willlett, 'African Art, an introduction', London 1971, p.149: 'An ejiri of the Western Ijo representing the head of the household making sacrifice to the family guardian spirit represented below as a strange animal, commonly said to be an elephant, though the trunk never appears to be represented. The Urhobo also have similar sculptures used in a warrior cult'.
Exhibition history:
Exhibited:
1977 London, BM, Animals in Art
Acq notes (acq): This was purchased from Mrs J Trew, and registered by W B Fagg as 'probably western Ijo' but now is thought to be a characteristic piece from the Urhobo. The vendor stated that it had been collected at the time of the Benin expedition of 1897 by her father-in-law, who was the  Fleet Paymaster to the Expedition. There is no suggestion that this work came from Benin itself.

Description:
Photograph (black and white); view of a group of six seated Europeans (members of the British Expedition to Benin City in 1897) wearing western clothing and pith helmets or wide-brimmed hats. One man in uniform. Surrounded by objects from the royal palace, shrines and compounds. Other members of the expedition in roofed building in background. 
Gelatin silver print.;
Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: Typed below mounted photo Inscription quoted: Contributed by Paymaster Rear Admiral H. S. Measham. Benin Expedition 1897.;
Acq notes (acq): Photograph taken by Dr Robert Allman, Principal Medical Officer on the British Expedition to Benin City in 1897. Dr Allman took a number of photographs in Benin City (including in the palace and its compounds). He remained in Benin City for several weeks after the main British forces had withdrawn and took additional photographs during this period.

Af1920,1106.1 to 35 is a series purchased from Arthur Harold Unwin, an expert in forestry, who worked in Nigeria from 1904 to 1917.

Acq notes (acq): The previous owner (Ethel MacDonald)'s husband, Sir Claude Maxwell MacDonald (1852-1915) was a British diplomat and colonial official. In 1889, MacDonald led a mission to the Niger and Benue rivers to hold interviews with all the emirs, kings, and chiefs over whom the Royal Niger Company claimed jurisdiction. From 1891 until 1896, MacDonald served as Commissioner and Consul General of Oil Rivers Protectorate (later Southern Nigeria Protectorate). In 1896, MacDonald retired from the British Army and continued his diplomatic career in Japan, Korea and China. The manillas were therefore most likely acquired before 1897.

Title: Overami - King of Benin
Description:
Photograph (black and white), view of Overami, Oba of Benin,  wearing patterned robes, coral necklace and elaborate headdress. Seated on his left and right are two women (the Oba’s wives) wearing European dress. Behind stand two young boys, and an adult man and woman (slaves). Seated at the feet of the Oba are two children wearing European dress. Calabar, NIgeria
Silver gelatin print;
Curators Comments:
Ovonramwen Nogbaisi (ruled 1888–1897), also called Overami, was the Ọba (king) of the Kingdom of Benin up until the British Punitive Expedition of 1897. He was exiled to Calabar where he died in 1914.
This photograph is likely to have been taken in Calabar during his exile.
Condition: good

Description:
Photograph (black and white); portrait of Oba Ovonramwen seated in a wicker chair with three soldiers, carrying bayonets, standing beside and behind him. The Oba wears a velvet gown; his bare feet are shackled together with chains. The soldiers wear knee-length trousers, long-sleeved shirts, caps with tassels, and belts; bare feet. Soldiers at right proper and centre wear medals. 
Albumen print.;
Inscription:
Inscription type: annotation Inscription quoted: Album Title: "1st BENIN. WARRI. & SAPELE. 2nd NEW CALABAR. BONNY. OPOBO & QUA COUNTRY." [manuscript note on album paper].
Original Description: "King of Benin" [manuscript note on album paper]; "J. A. Green, Artist Photographer Bonny, Opobo, &c. &c" [stamp on back of print].;
Curators Comments:
Photograph taken by Nigerian photographer J. A Green on board the S. S. Ivy, a British Government vessel, under the command of Captain Herbert Child. Oba Ovonramwen was exiled and sent to Old Calabar in eastern Nigeria in September 1897. The soldiers in this photograph are British-trained members of the Niger Coast Protectorate force. 

By 1905 Green's portrait of the exiled king appeared as a hand-painted, coloured colotype on a postcard.; Photographs in the collections Af,A46 and Af,A47 were originally contained in a single album containing 176 photographs.
Bib references: Kaplan 1991 / null; Anderson and Aronson 2017 / African Photographer J.A.Green: reimagining the Indigenous and the Colonial

Curators Comments: This loom is reproduced by Lisa Aronson, ‘Akwete Weaving: Tradition and Change’, in B.Engelbrecht & Bernhard Gardi (eds), 'Man Does Not Go Naked; Textilien und Handwerk aus afrikanischen und anderen Ländern', Basel, 1989, p.40 fig.7 as an 'Akwete loom collected in 1899 with three narrow pieces of cloth woven simultaneously with one set of apparatus'. The BM record only refers to its coming from Calabar, and the gift from Major Gallwey implies that it had very recently been collected for presentation to the BM. If it is an early precursor of the development of the Akwete loom, as Aronson suggests on p.44, it would imply that the development of the wide loom characteristic of Akwete weaving must post-date 1900, and predate 1905, the acquisition date of the Akwete loom in Edinburgh that she reproduces as fig.6. Curators Comments:
This document records 304 brass relief plaques looted during the British Expedition to Benin City in 1897. Deposited with the Foreign Office (through the Crown Agents for the Colonies) and lent to the British Museum for exhibition in September 1897. Of the original 304 plaques listed here the British Museum successfully petitioned to retain 200 as a gift. The remaining 104 plaques were subsequently offered for sale to external institutions/dealers or returned to the Foreign Office. This list was created around 1899 by Charles Hercules Read (Keeper of British & Mediaeval Antiquities and Ethnography) following publication of 'Antiquities from the City of Benin' (Read & Dalton, 1899). 
The annotations on the document indicate the following:
- single angled line in black ink: plaques retained by the British Museum and published in Read & Dalton 
- double crossed lines in black ink: plaques retained by the British Museum but not published in Read & Dalton
- circled in black ink with single horizontal line in red ink: not retained by the British Museum 
The red ink numbers at the foot of each column indicate the total number of plaques not retained by the British Museum.
Bib references: Read & Dalton 1899 / Antiquities from the City of Benin and from other parts of West Africa in the British Museum

Acq notes (acq): Given by H Fitzgerald Marriott, and recorded as "Ibibio tribe, Kwa Iboe River, Niger Coast Protectorate. Probably a mask of the 2nd grade of the Egbo Society. The ring on the head may be intended to represent that worn by Idiong men."

Description:
Register 1960
Split palm petiole screen rolled up and secured with lashings of cane. The thin strips of palm petiole are joined at six points with interwoven raphia fibre to form a flexible screen.;
Materials: bamboo leaf; raffia palm fibre; cane
Curators Comments:
Register 1960
"Sun screen made with the split petioles of the Bamboo Palm bound together with fibre from the leaves of the same palm made by prisoners in Old Calabar. 24.4.99." (The palm referred to is R[aphia] vinifera.) Collected by J H Holland.
Acq name (acq): Donated by: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew
Acq name (previous): Donated by: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew
Acq notes (acq): Af1960,20.1 to 246 is a large collection of African material transferred to the British Museum by the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew in 1960. Most of these works had been given to Kew in the XIXc, and the recorded provenances refer to those who gave the objects to Kew together with the date of acquisition by Kew.
